sections.title: Lesson 1 — Encapsulate What Varies, Program to an Interface, Composition
sections.html:
1. Encapsulate what varies (sl. 2–5)

Find the parts of the program that change, and separate them from the parts that stay the same. The change is then localised: you edit one method or one class, not many.

Method level (sl. 2–3)

// BEFORE: tax rules are mixed into the total computation
double getOrderTotal(Order order) {
    double total = 0;
    for (Item item : order.items) total += item.price * item.quantity;
    if (order.country.equals("US")) total += total * 0.07;   // US sales tax
    else if (order.country.equals("EU")) total += total * 0.20; // EU VAT
    return total;
}
// AFTER: the part that varies (tax rate) gets its own method
double getOrderTotal(Order order) {
    double total = 0;
    for (Item item : order.items) total += item.price * item.quantity;
    total += total * getTaxRate(order.country);
    return total;
}
double getTaxRate(String country) {
    if (country.equals("US")) return 0.07;
    if (country.equals("EU")) return 0.20;
    return 0;
}

Class level (sl. 4–5)

When the tax logic grows (state rules, product rules, Chinese tax …), move it out of Order into its own class TaxCalculator(getTaxRate(country, state, product), getUSTax, getEUTax, getChineseTax). Order now delegates; it has one job.

2. Program to an interface, not an implementation (sl. 6)

Depend on abstractions. Example: Cat.eat(Sausage) works only for sausages. Introduce interface Food (getNutrition()) and write Cat.eat(Food). Any new food can be added without touching Cat.

The slide warns: right after this change you feel no benefit and the code is more complex. Do it only where you expect an extension point.

3. Favour composition over inheritance (sl. 7–9)

  • Diamond problem (sl. 7): if ClassA and ClassB both implement doSomething() and ClassC extends both, the compiler cannot decide which one ClassC inherits. Java therefore forbids multiple class inheritance.
  • Tight coupling (sl. 8): Company creates Designer, Programmer, Tester directly — Company depends on every concrete employee class, so a new kind of company or employee forces edits in Company.
  • Fix (sl. 9): abstract Company with abstract getEmployees(); GameDevCompany and OutsourcingCompany override it; Employee is an interface with doWork(). Company now depends only on Employee. (This is the Factory Method idea — Lesson 5.)

4. Cohesion and coupling (textbook — asked 2018-19, 2017-18)

MeaningWant
CohesionHow strongly the responsibilities inside one module/class belong togetherHigh (tight) cohesion — one focused job
CouplingHow much one module depends on the internals of anotherLow (loose) coupling — talk through narrow interfaces
Exam-ready answer

Tight cohesion means each class does one well-defined job (SRP); loose coupling means classes interact only through abstract interfaces and know little about each other (DIP). Together they make a design easy to understand, test and change: a change stays inside one cohesive class, and because coupling is low it does not ripple into others. Example: Order with an embedded tax algorithm has low cohesion; moving tax to TaxCalculator behind an interface raises cohesion and lowers coupling.

5. Subclassing vs delegation (2010-11 Q3(c))

The two techniques in that question are inheritance (subclassing) and delegation (object composition). Both fix the added behaviour at compile time. Composition/delegation should be preferred: it does not expose the parent's internals, avoids the diamond problem and deep hierarchies, and the delegate can be swapped at run time (this is how Strategy, Decorator and Bridge work).

Exam approach

  1. Name the principle in one line (quote the slide wording).
  2. Show a 'before' with the smell (conditionals, concrete dependencies, fat class).
  3. Show the 'after' with the extracted method/class or interface.
  4. Finish with the benefit: what change is now local.

Practice — Lesson 1

(a) Actual — 2017-18 Q7(c). (b) Actual — 2018-19 Q3(c). (c) Actual — 2010-11 Q3(c).

(a) What is tight cohesion and loose coupling? How does it influence software design? (8)

(b) Discuss cohesion and coupling in brief in the context of software engineering. (8)

(c) Extending a system by subclassing vs by copying operations and delegating to another class: name the two techniques. Should one get preferential treatment? (5)

Show solution

(a) Use the EXAM-READY ANSWER in §4, then add an example: Company that creates Designer/Programmer/Tester itself is tightly coupled (sl. 8); after introducing Employee and getEmployees() it is loosely coupled (sl. 9). Influence: changes stay local, classes are reusable and testable in isolation, parallel development is easier.

(b) Cohesion = degree to which elements of a module belong together (aim high: functional cohesion). Coupling = degree of interdependence between modules (aim low: data coupling through parameters/interfaces, not content or common coupling). Good design = high cohesion + low coupling.

(c) Inheritance (subclassing) and delegation (composition). Prefer delegation: it keeps encapsulation, allows behaviour to be changed at run time, and avoids multiple-inheritance problems — 'favour composition over inheritance'.

sections.title: Lesson 2 — SRP and the Open/Closed Principle
sections.html:
1. SOLID (sl. 10)

LetterPrincipleOne-line rule
SSingle ResponsibilityA class should have just one reason to change.
OOpen/ClosedClasses should be open for extension but closed for modification.
LLiskov SubstitutionA subclass object must work wherever the parent object works.
IInterface SegregationClients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they do not use.
DDependency InversionHigh- and low-level classes both depend on abstractions.

Cost (sl. 10): applying them blindly can make a program more complicated than it should be.

2. Single Responsibility Principle (sl. 11)

Every class has a single responsibility, entirely encapsulated by the class. Example: Employee that also prints a time-sheet report has two reasons to change (employee data, report format). Move printing to TimeSheetReport.print(employee).

Benefits listed on the slide: less fragile code, low coupling, high cohesion, changeability, maintainability, testability and easier debugging.

3. Open/Closed Principle (sl. 12–17)

Once a class is complete, it is modified only to fix errors; new features come through new classes (sl. 13). Shipping example (sl. 12): Order.getShippingCost() with if (shipping == ground) … else if (air) … must be edited for every new method. Extract interface Shipping with Ground and Air implementations — a Strategy.

Worked example — AreaCalculator (sl. 14–17, C# on the slides, Java here)

// sl. 15 — every new shape forces an edit here (VIOLATES OCP)
double area(Object[] shapes) {
    double a = 0;
    for (Object s : shapes) {
        if (s instanceof Rectangle) { Rectangle r = (Rectangle) s; a += r.width * r.height; }
        else { Circle c = (Circle) s; a += c.radius * c.radius * Math.PI; }
    }
    return a;
}
// sl. 16–17 — closed for modification, open for extension
abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }
class Rectangle extends Shape { double width, height; double area() { return width * height; } }
class Circle    extends Shape { double radius;        double area() { return Math.PI * radius * radius; } }
class Ellipse   extends Shape { double major, minor;  double area() { return Math.PI * major * minor; } } // added later
class AreaCalculator {
    double area(Shape[] shapes) { double a = 0; for (Shape s : shapes) a += s.area(); return a; }
}
Memorize

OCP smell = a type code or instanceof chain that must be edited for every new type. Cure = polymorphism: push each branch into an overriding method (refactoring 'Replace Conditional with Polymorphism').

Practice — Lesson 2

(a) Actual — 2016-17 Q8(d). (b) Constructed.

(a) Which class design principle does the following code violate? Rewrite the code to remove the violation.

(b) State SRP. Show a class that violates it and fix it.

class GraphicEditor {
    public float getArea(Shape s) {
        if (s.m_type == 1) return s.width * s.width;
        else if (s.m_type == 2) return 3.1416 * s.r * s.r;
    }
}
class Shape { int m_type; }
class Rectangle extends Shape { int width; Rectangle(int width) { super.m_type = 1; this.width = width; } }
class Circle extends Shape { int r; Circle(int radius) { super.m_type = 1; this.r = radius; } }
Show solution

(a) It violates the Open/Closed Principle: GraphicEditor must be modified every time a new shape is added (another m_type branch), and it reaches into the fields of every subclass. (There is also a bug: Circle sets m_type = 1, so a circle's area is computed as a square.) Rewrite — each shape computes its own area:

abstract class Shape { abstract double getArea(); }
class Rectangle extends Shape {          // the paper's 'Rectangle' is a square: width * width
    private final int width;
    Rectangle(int width) { this.width = width; }
    double getArea() { return width * width; }
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    private final int r;
    Circle(int radius) { this.r = radius; }
    double getArea() { return 3.1416 * r * r; }
}
class GraphicEditor {                    // closed for modification
    double getArea(Shape s) { return s.getArea(); }
}
// new Triangle extends Shape { double getArea() {...} }  -> no change to GraphicEditor

(b) SRP: a class should have only one reason to change. Violation: class Employee { calculatePay(); saveToDatabase(); printTimeSheetReport(); } — pay rules, storage and report format are three reasons. Fix: Employee (data + calculatePay), EmployeeRepository.save(e), TimeSheetReport.print(e).

sections.title: Lesson 3 — LSP, ISP and DIP
sections.html:
1. Liskov Substitution Principle (sl. 18–20)

  • You must be able to pass a subclass object wherever a parent object is expected without breaking the client.
  • When overriding, extend the parent's behaviour; do not replace it with something different.
  • Violation (sl. 19): ReadOnlyDocument extends Document and overrides save() to throw an exception. Project.saveAll() must now check the type — the subclass is not substitutable.
  • Fix (sl. 20): Document has only open(); WritableDocument extends Document and adds save(). Project keeps allDocs and writableDocs, and saves only writable ones.

2. Interface Segregation Principle (sl. 21–22)

Clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Make interfaces narrow.

Example: a fat CloudProvider interface (storeFile, getFile, createServer, listServers, getCDNAddress). Amazon can implement all, but a Dropbox adapter must leave hosting/CDN methods empty or throwing. Split into CloudHostingProvider, CDNProvider and CloudStorageProvider; Amazon implements all three, Dropbox only CloudStorageProvider.

3. Dependency Inversion Principle (sl. 23–31)

  • High-level classes shouldn't depend on low-level classes; both depend on abstractions.
  • Abstractions shouldn't depend on details; details depend on abstractions.
  • sl. 24–25: BudgetReport → MySQLDatabase is inverted to BudgetReport → «interface» Database ← MySQL, MongoDB.
  • How it works (sl. 26): the high-level module defines the interface it needs; low-level modules implement it.

Worked example — the power switch (sl. 27–31)

// Without DIP: ElectricPowerSwitch can only switch a LightBulb
public class ElectricPowerSwitch { public LightBulb lightBulb; ... lightBulb.turnOn(); ... }

// With DIP
public interface Switch     { boolean isOn(); void press(); }
public interface Switchable { void turnOn(); void turnOff(); }
public class ElectricPowerSwitch implements Switch {
    public Switchable client; public boolean on;
    public ElectricPowerSwitch(Switchable client) { this.client = client; this.on = false; }
    public boolean isOn() { return on; }
    public void press() {
        if (isOn()) { client.turnOff(); on = false; } else { client.turnOn(); on = true; }
    }
}
public class Fan implements Switchable { public void turnOn()  { System.out.println("Fan: Fan turned on..."); }
                                          public void turnOff() { System.out.println("Fan: Fan turned off..."); } }
public class LightBulb implements Switchable { /* same with 'Bulb' messages */ }
Trap

DIP is not the same as 'dependency injection'. Injection (passing the Switchable in the constructor) is just a technique; the principle is that both sides depend on the Switchable abstraction.

Practice — Lesson 3

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q2(c). (b) Actual — 2012-13 Q4(b). (c) Constructed.

(a) Give an example of the Interface Segregation Principle. (8)

(b) What is the primary motivation behind ISP? Explain ISP with a suitable 'bad example'. (14⅔)

(c) Show an LSP violation with Rectangle/Square and fix it.

Show solution

(a)/(b) Motivation: a fat interface couples every client to every method; implementers are forced to write dummy methods, and a change to one method forces recompiling/retesting clients that never use it. Bad example:

interface Worker { void work(); void eat(); void attendMeeting(); }
class Robot implements Worker {
    public void work() { ... }
    public void eat() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }        // forced, meaningless
    public void attendMeeting() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}
// ISP: split by client need
interface Workable  { void work(); }
interface Eatable   { void eat(); }
interface Meetable  { void attendMeeting(); }
class Human implements Workable, Eatable, Meetable { ... }
class Robot implements Workable { public void work() { ... } }

The CloudProvider/Dropbox example of sl. 21–22 is an equally good answer.

(c) Square extends Rectangle and setWidth() also sets height. A client that does r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); expects area 20 but gets 16 → Square is not substitutable. Fix: make Rectangle and Square siblings under abstract Shape { double area(); } with no setters that break invariants.

sections.title: Lesson 4 — What a Design Pattern Is
sections.html:
1. Definition (sl. 2)

  • A standard solution to a common programming problem — a design structure that achieves a particular purpose.
  • A description or template of how to solve a problem, usable in many situations.
  • A technique for flexible/efficient code: reduces coupling and memory overhead.
  • Shorthand for describing a design (a vocabulary).

2. The Gang of Four catalogue (sl. 3–6)

CategoryConcernPatterns (23)
Creational (5)How objects are instantiatedFactory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton
Structural (6 in syllabus)How objects/classes are combined into larger structuresAdapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Flyweight, Proxy
Behavioral (8 in syllabus)How objects communicate and share responsibilitiesTemplate Method, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Observer, State, Strategy, Visitor

3. Essential elements of a pattern (sl. 7)

ElementWhat it states
Intent (name)Design goal of the pattern; the name gives a shared vocabulary
ProblemWhen to apply it: the problem and its context
SolutionElements of the design, their relationships, responsibilities and collaborations (a template, not code)
ConsequencesBenefits and trade-offs of applying it

4. Why patterns are needed (sl. 8–10)

Requirements always change: users' view changes after talking to developers; developers' view of the domain changes as they learn it; the environment changes. Design should accommodate change, and patterns give code that absorbs change easily.

Reasons to study (sl. 10): reuse proven solutions; common terminology; higher-level thinking; decide whether a design is right, not just working; individual and team learning; modifiability; better alternatives even without the pattern; alternatives to large inheritance hierarchies.

Practice — Lesson 4

(a) Actual — 2011-12 Q4(c). (b) Actual — 2014-15 Q6(a).

(a) What are the four essential elements of a design pattern? Discuss briefly. (8)

(b) What is the difference between structural and behavioral patterns? Give criteria for classifying a new pattern, explaining why current patterns are classified as they are. (10)

Show solution

(a) Name/intent, problem, solution, consequences — table in §3, one sentence each with Observer as the example (problem: dependents must be updated on change; solution: Subject keeps a list of Observer interfaces and calls update(); consequence: loose coupling, but unexpected update cascades).

(b) Structural patterns are about composition — how classes and objects are assembled into larger structures while staying flexible (Adapter wraps to change an interface, Composite builds trees, Decorator wraps to add responsibilities). Behavioral patterns are about interaction — algorithms, control flow and assignment of responsibility between objects (Observer: who notifies whom; Strategy: which algorithm runs; Mediator: who talks to whom).

Criteria for a new pattern: (1) If its main purpose is to define the static shape of a structure — which object contains, wraps or refers to which, so that a larger object is formed — it is structural. (2) If its main purpose is to distribute a run-time responsibility or communication protocol among objects — message flow, choice of algorithm, state changes — it is behavioral. (3) If it is mainly about creating objects, it is creational. Decorator is structural because its essence is a wrapping structure with the same interface; Strategy is behavioral because its essence is selecting an algorithm at run time, even though both use composition.

sections.title: Quick Notes — Design Principles
sections.html:
Revision points for Lessons 1–4.

L1 · Encapsulate, interfaces, composition

  • Encapsulate what varies: getTaxRate() method → TaxCalculator class.
  • Program to an interface: Cat.eat(Food), not eat(Sausage).
  • Diamond problem → Java bans multiple class inheritance. Favour composition/delegation.
  • High cohesion + low coupling; subclassing vs delegation → prefer delegation.

L2 · SRP, OCP

  • SRP: one reason to change (TimeSheetReport out of Employee).
  • OCP: open for extension, closed for modification. Type-code if-chains → abstract method per subclass.
  • 2016-17 Q8(d): GraphicEditor violates OCP; each Shape gets getArea().

L3 · LSP, ISP, DIP

  • LSP: subclass substitutable; ReadOnlyDocument.save() throwing = violation → WritableDocument.
  • ISP: no fat interfaces; CloudProvider → Hosting / CDN / Storage; Worker → Workable / Eatable.
  • DIP: both depend on abstraction; Switch/Switchable with Fan and LightBulb.

L4 · Pattern basics

  • Syllabus slide lists: creational 5, structural 6, behavioral 8 (Facade, Command, Chain of Responsibility, Interpreter are not in this term's syllabus).
  • Elements: intent/name, problem, solution, consequences.
  • Structural = composition of structure; behavioral = interaction/responsibility.

sections.title: Lesson 5 — UML Recap and Factory Method
sections.html:
1. UML relationships used in pattern diagrams (sl. 2)

RelationshipArrowReadingSlide example
Generalizationsolid line, hollow triangle → parentis-a / implementsRectangle → Shape
Dependencydashed line, open arrowuses temporarilyLottery ⇢ Random
Aggregationhollow diamond at the wholeis part of (part can live alone)Car ◇— Engine
Compositionfilled diamond at the wholeis entirely made of (parts die with whole)Book ◆— Page

2. Intent and problem (sl. 4)

Memorize

Factory Method — Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate. Factory Method lets a class defer instantiation to subclasses.

Problem: a framework standardises the architecture for a range of applications, but each application defines its own domain objects and their creation. The creator defers product creation to a subclass.

3. Structure and participants (sl. 5)

        Creator                                   «interface»
 ---------------------                          Product
 # factoryMethod(): Product   - - - creates - ->  + operation()
 + anOperation()  { p = factoryMethod(); ... }        ^
           ^                                          |
           |                                          |
    ConcreteCreator                              ConcreteProduct
 # factoryMethod(): Product  { return new ConcreteProduct(); }
ParticipantRole
ProductInterface of the objects the factory method creates
ConcreteProductImplements Product
CreatorDeclares factoryMethod() returning Product; its other code works only with Product
ConcreteCreatorOverrides factoryMethod() to return one ConcreteProduct

4. Slide examples (sl. 6–14)

  • Drawing (sl. 6–7): Shape interface (draw), Circle/Square/Rectangle; ShapeFactory.getShape(type) returns the right shape; the client asks the factory instead of calling new. (This parameterised version is often called a 'simple factory'.)
  • Kiosk (sl. 8): PaymentProcessor (processPayment) with Cash, CreditCard, Coupon; GetPayment.getProcessor(type).
  • Electricity bill (sl. 9–11): abstract Plan(rate; getRate(); calculateBill(units) = units × rate); DomesticPlan 3.50, CommercialPlan 7.50, InstitutionalPlan 5.50; GetPlanFactory.getPlan(planType); GenerateBill reads plan + units and prints the bill. E.g. 100 commercial units → 100 × 7.50 = 750.
  • Logistics (sl. 12–13): code coupled to Truck; adding Ship would touch everything. Logistics.createTransport() is overridden by RoadLogistics (Truck) and SeaLogistics (Ship); planDelivery() works with Transport. Dialog.createButton(): WindowsDialog → WindowsButton, WebDialog → HTMLButton.
  • UI framework (sl. 14): to make the framework use RoundButton, subclass UIFramework as UIWithRoundButtons and override createButton(). Use Factory Method when users of a library must be able to extend its internal components.

5. Consequences (sl. 15–16)

  • Code for an interface, not an implementation; instantiation is removed from client code → less coupling, easy to extend.
  • Single Responsibility (creation in one place) and Open/Closed (new products without breaking clients).
  • Cost: many new subclasses (one creator per product).

Exam approach

  1. Cue words: 'client must not construct the concrete class', 'centralised creation', 'add new types without modifying'.
  2. Draw Product interface + concrete products, Creator with abstract factory method + concrete creators.
  3. Write the interface, two products, the creator hierarchy and a main() that uses only the abstract types.
  4. End with one line on extension: 'new type = new product + new creator; no existing class changes' (OCP).

Practice — Lesson 5

(a) Actual — 2024-25 (22 batch) Q1(a). (b) Actual — 2016-17 Q5(c). (c) Actual — 2010-11 Q3(d).

(a) A travel company offers Adventure and Regular packages, each with its own activities, pricing and description. Implement it with a pattern so that client code never constructs a concrete class, packages are created through a centralised creation component, and new package types need no change to existing code. (15)

(b) Syntax highlighting: choose a parser (.c, .cpp, .java, .html …), all implementing Parser, from the file extension. Which pattern? Give a Java implementation. (3+7)

(c) XMLReaderFactory has a static createXMLReader() that returns an XMLReader implementation chosen from a system property. Does it implement the Factory pattern? (5)

Show solution

(a) Factory Method. The creator PackageCreator owns the creation step (createPackage()); each concrete creator decides the class. Client code holds only PackageCreator and TourPackage references.

«interface» TourPackage                      PackageCreator {abstract}
 + getName(), getPrice(),                     # createPackage(): TourPackage   «factory method»
   getDescription(), getActivities()          + orderPackage(): TourPackage
     ^                ^                              ^                  ^
AdventurePackage  RegularPackage            AdventureCreator      RegularCreator
                                            createPackage() -> new AdventurePackage()
                                            createPackage() -> new RegularPackage()
// 2024-25 Q1(a) — Factory Method: client never names a concrete package class
import java.util.List;

interface TourPackage {
    String getName();
    double getPrice();
    String getDescription();
    List<String> getActivities();
}
class AdventurePackage implements TourPackage {
    public String getName() { return "Adventure"; }
    public double getPrice() { return 25000; }
    public String getDescription() { return "For thrill-seekers"; }
    public List<String> getActivities() { return List.of("Mountain hiking", "River rafting"); }
}
class RegularPackage implements TourPackage {
    public String getName() { return "Regular"; }
    public double getPrice() { return 12000; }
    public String getDescription() { return "For leisure travellers"; }
    public List<String> getActivities() { return List.of("City sightseeing", "Museum visits"); }
}

// Creator = the centralised creation component
abstract class PackageCreator {
    protected abstract TourPackage createPackage();          // the factory method
    public TourPackage orderPackage() {                       // common logic works on the interface
        TourPackage p = createPackage();
        System.out.println("Booked " + p.getName() + " (" + p.getPrice() + "): " + p.getActivities());
        return p;
    }
}
class AdventureCreator extends PackageCreator {
    protected TourPackage createPackage() { return new AdventurePackage(); }
}
class RegularCreator extends PackageCreator {
    protected TourPackage createPackage() { return new RegularPackage(); }
}
// New type later: HoneymoonPackage + HoneymoonCreator. No existing class is edited.

public class TravelDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PackageCreator creator = new AdventureCreator();   // chosen by configuration / UI
        creator.orderPackage();
        new RegularCreator().orderPackage();
    }
}

Output: Booked Adventure (25000.0): [Mountain hiking, River rafting] / Booked Regular (12000.0): [City sightseeing, Museum visits].

(b) Factory (Factory Method family): the selection logic is one creation component that maps an extension to a Parser; the editor uses only the Parser interface. Assumptions: extension = text after the last dot; unknown extension → exception. A registry map keeps the factory closed for modification (new language = register()).

// 2016-17 Q5(c) — choose a parser from the file extension (factory with a registry)
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

interface Parser { void parse(String fileName); }
class CParser    implements Parser { public void parse(String f) { System.out.println("C parser: " + f); } }
class CppParser  implements Parser { public void parse(String f) { System.out.println("C++ parser: " + f); } }
class JavaParser implements Parser { public void parse(String f) { System.out.println("Java parser: " + f); } }
class HtmlParser implements Parser { public void parse(String f) { System.out.println("HTML parser: " + f); } }

class ParserFactory {
    private static final Map<String, Supplier<Parser>> REG = new HashMap<>();
    static {
        REG.put("c", CParser::new);
        REG.put("cpp", CppParser::new);
        REG.put("java", JavaParser::new);
        REG.put("html", HtmlParser::new);
    }
    static void register(String ext, Supplier<Parser> s) { REG.put(ext, s); }  // new language
    static Parser getParser(String fileName) {
        String ext = fileName.substring(fileName.lastIndexOf('.') + 1).toLowerCase();
        Supplier<Parser> s = REG.get(ext);
        if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("No parser for ." + ext);
        return s.get();
    }
}
public class ParserDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (String f : new String[]{"main.c", "a.cpp", "App.java", "index.html"})
            ParserFactory.getParser(f).parse(f);
    }
}

(c) Yes. createXMLReader() is a static factory method: it returns an object of some class implementing XMLReader, the concrete class is chosen inside the method (from a system property), and the client depends only on the XMLReader interface. Strictly it is the 'simple/static factory' variant — no subclass overrides a creator method — so it is the Factory idea, not the full GoF Factory Method structure.

sections.title: Lesson 6 — Abstract Factory
sections.html:
Memorize

Abstract Factory — Provide an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.

Problem (sl. 17): a portable application must encapsulate platform dependencies — several look-and-feels, several DBMSs.

1. Structure (sl. 18)

«interface» AbstractFactory              «interface» ProductA      «interface» ProductB
 + createProductA(): ProductA                  ^          ^              ^          ^
 + createProductB(): ProductB              ProductA1  ProductA2      ProductB1  ProductB2
        ^                 ^
 ConcreteFactory1    ConcreteFactory2      Client --> AbstractFactory, ProductA, ProductB only
 createA()->A1        createA()->A2
 createB()->B1        createB()->B2        (factory 1 always makes family 1: A1 + B1)

2. Slide examples (sl. 19–33)

  • Furniture shop (sl. 19–22): products Chair, Sofa, CoffeeTable × variants ArtDeco, Victorian, Modern. Customers get angry with non-matching furniture. Declare an interface per product, then FurnitureFactory (createChair, createSofa, createCoffeeTable); ModernFurnitureFactory makes only Modern pieces.
  • Cross-platform GUI (sl. 23–29): GUIFactory (createButton, createCheckbox) with WinFactory and MacFactory. ApplicationConfigurator reads the OS at start-up and passes the right factory to Application; the rest of the code works with Button and Checkbox interfaces only.
  • Car factory (sl. 30): HondaFactory (createEngine, createTrans) with CivicFactory and AccordFactory → CivicEngine/CivicTrans or AccordEngine/AccordTrans.
  • Factory of factories (sl. 31–33): AbstractFactory (getShape, getColor), ShapeFactory, ColorFactory, FactoryProducer.getFactory("SHAPE" | "COLOR").

3. Consequences (sl. 34–35)

BenefitLiability
Isolates concrete classes; client sees only interfacesSupporting a new kind of product is hard: every factory interface and class must get a new create method
Exchanging a whole product family is easy (swap one factory object)More interfaces and classes
Promotes consistency — products of one family are used together
No conditional logic in the client (unlike a parameterised factory)
Trap

Factory Method creates one product through inheritance (subclass overrides one method). Abstract Factory creates a family through object composition (the client is given a factory object). Each create method inside an Abstract Factory is often a factory method.

Exam approach

  1. Cue words: 'families', 'region/platform/brand-specific', 'must match', 'consistent', 'sensitive to their orders', 'easily extendable to new countries/platforms'.
  2. Make a table: rows = families (countries, menus, companies), columns = product kinds (crust/sauce, rice/main/fry, car/moto).
  3. One interface per column; one concrete factory per row with one create method per column.
  4. Client receives the factory once and never names a concrete product.

Practice — Lesson 6

(a) Actual — 2023-24 Q5(a). (b) Actual — 2021-22 Q3(a). (c) Actual — 2017-18 Q7(b). (d) Actual — 2014-15 Q6(b).

(a) Pizza delivery in Italy and America with distinct crust and toppings; each pizza must use region-specific ingredients and the system must extend easily to more countries. Identify the pattern, justify, and implement. (15)

(b) Four set menus (Veggie Harvest, Chicken Delight, Beef Fiesta, Sea Shanty), each a rice item + a main dish + a fried item made in kitchens Rice Station, Main Mania and Fry More; users are very sensitive to their orders. Identify the pattern, give the UML and an implementation. (20)

(c) Uber and Pathao compute car fares n·d·18·f (f = 1.8/1.2/0.9) and n·d·20·f (f = 1.5/1.15/0.9), and moto fares 25 + 12d and 30 + 11d. Input distance, passengers and t (1, 2, 3); output the cost for each app. Class diagram + code. (6+15)

(d) Give one design pattern that reduces dependence on hardware and/or software platforms and explain how. (12)

Show solution

(a) Abstract Factory. Each country is a family of matching ingredients (crust, sauce, topping). The pizza code receives a PizzaIngredientFactory and cannot accidentally mix an Italian crust with an American topping; a new country is one new factory class plus its ingredient classes, with no change to RegionalPizza (OCP).

PizzaIngredientFactory «interface»: createCrust(), createSauce(), createTopping()
   ^ ItalyIngredientFactory   -> ThinCrust,     MarinaraSauce,   Mozzarella
   ^ AmericaIngredientFactory -> DeepDishCrust, PlumTomatoSauce, Pepperoni
Crust, Sauce, Topping «interface»     RegionalPizza(f: PizzaIngredientFactory) -- uses --> the three interfaces
// 2023-24 Q5(a) — Abstract Factory: each region creates a consistent family of ingredients
interface Crust   { String name(); }
interface Sauce   { String name(); }
interface Topping { String name(); }

class ThinCrust       implements Crust   { public String name() { return "thin crust"; } }
class MarinaraSauce   implements Sauce   { public String name() { return "marinara"; } }
class Mozzarella      implements Topping { public String name() { return "fresh mozzarella, basil"; } }
class DeepDishCrust   implements Crust   { public String name() { return "deep-dish crust"; } }
class PlumTomatoSauce implements Sauce   { public String name() { return "plum-tomato sauce"; } }
class Pepperoni       implements Topping { public String name() { return "cheddar, pepperoni"; } }

interface PizzaIngredientFactory {                 // abstract factory
    Crust createCrust();
    Sauce createSauce();
    Topping createTopping();
}
class ItalyIngredientFactory implements PizzaIngredientFactory {
    public Crust createCrust()     { return new ThinCrust(); }
    public Sauce createSauce()     { return new MarinaraSauce(); }
    public Topping createTopping() { return new Mozzarella(); }
}
class AmericaIngredientFactory implements PizzaIngredientFactory {
    public Crust createCrust()     { return new DeepDishCrust(); }
    public Sauce createSauce()     { return new PlumTomatoSauce(); }
    public Topping createTopping() { return new Pepperoni(); }
}
class RegionalPizza {                              // client: never names a concrete ingredient
    private final Crust crust; private final Sauce sauce; private final Topping topping;
    RegionalPizza(PizzaIngredientFactory f) {
        crust = f.createCrust(); sauce = f.createSauce(); topping = f.createTopping();
    }
    public String toString() { return crust.name() + " + " + sauce.name() + " + " + topping.name(); }
}
public class PizzaDemo {
    static PizzaIngredientFactory factoryFor(String country) {   // chosen once
        switch (country) {
            case "Italy":   return new ItalyIngredientFactory();
            case "America": return new AmericaIngredientFactory();
            default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(country);
        }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Italy:   " + new RegionalPizza(factoryFor("Italy")));
        System.out.println("America: " + new RegionalPizza(factoryFor("America")));
    }
}

(b) Abstract Factory. Rows = set menus (families), columns = kitchens (product kinds). 'Users are very sensitive to their orders' means a menu's three items must come from the same family — exactly the consistency Abstract Factory guarantees. (A Builder would assemble one order, but would not stop a builder step from mixing items of two menus.)

SetMenuFactory «interface»: prepareRice(): RiceItem, prepareMain(): MainDish, prepareFried(): FriedItem
  ^ VeggieHarvestFactory   Mushroom Rice      | Paneer Masala    | Fried Vegetable Pakora
  ^ ChickenDelightFactory  Chicken Fried Rice | Butter Chicken   | Fried Chicken Wings
  ^ BeefFiestaFactory      Beef Fried Rice    | Beef Chili Onion | Fried Beef Bacon
  ^ SeaShantyFactory       Rice with Shrimp   | Crab Masala      | Fried Calamari
Restaurant.deliver(f: SetMenuFactory) — the client
// 2021-22 Q3(a) — Abstract Factory: one factory per set menu; one product type per kitchen
interface RiceItem  { String name(); }   // made in Rice Station
interface MainDish  { String name(); }   // made in Main Mania
interface FriedItem { String name(); }   // made in Fry More

class Dish implements RiceItem, MainDish, FriedItem {
    private final String n;
    Dish(String n) { this.n = n; }
    public String name() { return n; }
}
interface SetMenuFactory {
    RiceItem prepareRice();
    MainDish prepareMain();
    FriedItem prepareFried();
}
class VeggieHarvestFactory implements SetMenuFactory {
    public RiceItem prepareRice()   { return new Dish("Mushroom Rice"); }
    public MainDish prepareMain()   { return new Dish("Paneer Masala"); }
    public FriedItem prepareFried() { return new Dish("Fried Vegetable Pakora"); }
}
class ChickenDelightFactory implements SetMenuFactory {
    public RiceItem prepareRice()   { return new Dish("Chicken Fried Rice"); }
    public MainDish prepareMain()   { return new Dish("Butter Chicken"); }
    public FriedItem prepareFried() { return new Dish("Fried Chicken Wings"); }
}
class BeefFiestaFactory implements SetMenuFactory {
    public RiceItem prepareRice()   { return new Dish("Beef Fried Rice"); }
    public MainDish prepareMain()   { return new Dish("Beef Chili Onion"); }
    public FriedItem prepareFried() { return new Dish("Fried Beef Bacon"); }
}
class SeaShantyFactory implements SetMenuFactory {
    public RiceItem prepareRice()   { return new Dish("Rice with Shrimp"); }
    public MainDish prepareMain()   { return new Dish("Crab Masala"); }
    public FriedItem prepareFried() { return new Dish("Fried Calamari"); }
}
class Restaurant {                 // client: assembles one family; cannot mix menus by mistake
    String deliver(SetMenuFactory f) {
        return f.prepareRice().name() + ", " + f.prepareMain().name() + ", " + f.prepareFried().name();
    }
}
public class SetMenuDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Restaurant r = new Restaurant();
        SetMenuFactory[] menus = { new VeggieHarvestFactory(), new ChickenDelightFactory(),
                                   new BeefFiestaFactory(), new SeaShantyFactory() };
        for (SetMenuFactory m : menus)
            System.out.println(m.getClass().getSimpleName().replace("Factory", "") + ": " + r.deliver(m));
    }
}

(c) Abstract Factory: families = companies (Uber, Pathao); products = CarFare and MotoFare. Each fare object holds its company's formula. (Strategy for the fare formula is also acceptable; Abstract Factory is the better answer because each company supplies a matching pair.)

// 2017-18 Q7(b) — Abstract Factory: each company supplies a matching (car, moto) fare family
interface CarFare  { double cost(int passengers, double d, int t); }
interface MotoFare { double cost(double d); }

class UberCar implements CarFare {
    public double cost(int n, double d, int t) {
        double f = (t == 1) ? 1.8 : (t == 2) ? 1.2 : 0.9;
        return n * d * 18 * f;
    }
}
class PathaoCar implements CarFare {
    public double cost(int n, double d, int t) {
        double f = (t == 1) ? 1.5 : (t == 2) ? 1.15 : 0.9;
        return n * d * 20 * f;
    }
}
class UberMoto   implements MotoFare { public double cost(double d) { return 25 + d * 12; } }
class PathaoMoto implements MotoFare { public double cost(double d) { return 30 + d * 11; } }

interface RideFactory { CarFare carFare(); MotoFare motoFare(); String name(); }
class UberFactory implements RideFactory {
    public CarFare carFare()   { return new UberCar(); }
    public MotoFare motoFare() { return new UberMoto(); }
    public String name()       { return "Uber"; }
}
class PathaoFactory implements RideFactory {
    public CarFare carFare()   { return new PathaoCar(); }
    public MotoFare motoFare() { return new PathaoMoto(); }
    public String name()       { return "Pathao"; }
}
public class RideDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double d = 10; int n = 2; int t = 1;   // in the exam read these with a Scanner
        for (RideFactory f : new RideFactory[]{ new UberFactory(), new PathaoFactory() })
            System.out.printf("%s car: %.2f   %s moto: %.2f%n",
                    f.name(), f.carFare().cost(n, d, t), f.name(), f.motoFare().cost(d));
    }
}

Check, d = 10 km, n = 2, t = 1: Uber car 2 × 10 × 18 × 1.8 = 648; Pathao car 2 × 10 × 20 × 1.5 = 600; Uber moto 25 + 120 = 145; Pathao moto 30 + 110 = 140 — matches the program output.

(d) Abstract Factory (sl. 17, 23–29). All platform-specific classes (WinButton, MacButton …) are created only inside one concrete factory. At start-up the configurator inspects the OS and creates WinFactory or MacFactory; the rest of the program talks to GUIFactory, Button and Checkbox interfaces. Porting to a new platform = writing one new factory and its products; no application code changes. (Bridge is a valid second answer: it separates the abstraction from a platform implementation hierarchy — IJ Mam's notes.)

sections.title: Lesson 7 — Singleton
sections.html:
Memorize

Singleton — Ensure a class has only one instance, and provide a global point of access to it. Encapsulated 'just-in-time initialisation' (initialisation on first use).

1. Structure (sl. 37) and implementation steps (sl. 39)

          Singleton
 ---------------------------------
 - instance: Singleton            (static)
 ---------------------------------
 - Singleton()                    (private constructor)
 + getInstance(): Singleton       (static)  { if (instance == null) instance = new Singleton(); return instance; }
  1. Add a private static field to hold the instance.
  2. Declare a public static creation method getInstance().
  3. Implement lazy initialisation inside it: create on the first call, return the same object afterwards.
  4. Make the constructor private so other code cannot use new.
  5. Replace direct constructor calls in client code with getInstance().

Slide example (sl. 38): DbConnection with private static instance and a private constructor that opens the SQL connection; DbConnection.getDbConnection() returns the shared connection.

2. Applicability and consequences (sl. 40–42)

  • Use it when a class must have exactly one instance available to all clients (database connection, configuration, logger).
  • Unlike a global variable, nothing except the class itself can replace the cached instance.
  • Consequences: controlled access to the sole instance; reduced name space (no globals); permits a variable number of instances — the same code can be changed to allow n instances (used in 2011-12 Q1(b) below).
  • Criticism: it violates SRP (it solves two problems at once) and makes unit testing harder.

3. Eager vs lazy initialisation (textbook — asked 2016-17, 2012-13)

EagerLazy
When createdWhen the class is loaded (static final field)On the first getInstance() call
Thread safetySafe automatically (class loading is thread-safe)Needs synchronized / double-checked locking / holder class
CostWastes memory/time if never usedPays only when used; small check on every call
Prefer whenObject is cheap and always neededObject is expensive (DB connection, large cache) or may never be used
// 2016-17 Q5(a), 2012-13 Q2(a), 2010-11 Q4(a) — eager, lazy, double-checked, holder
class EagerSingleton {
    private static final EagerSingleton INSTANCE = new EagerSingleton();  // made at class load
    private EagerSingleton() { }
    public static EagerSingleton getInstance() { return INSTANCE; }
}
class LazySingleton {
    private static LazySingleton instance;                                // made on first use
    private LazySingleton() { }
    public static synchronized LazySingleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) instance = new LazySingleton();
        return instance;
    }
}
class DclSingleton {
    private static volatile DclSingleton instance;
    private DclSingleton() { }
    public static DclSingleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (DclSingleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) instance = new DclSingleton();
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}
class HolderSingleton {                                // 2010-11 Q4(a)(ii): valid, lazy, thread-safe
    private HolderSingleton() { }
    private static class SingletonHolder {
        private static final HolderSingleton instance = new HolderSingleton();
    }
    public static HolderSingleton getInstance() { return SingletonHolder.instance; }
}
public class SingletonKinds {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(EagerSingleton.getInstance() == EagerSingleton.getInstance());
        System.out.println(LazySingleton.getInstance() == LazySingleton.getInstance());
        System.out.println(DclSingleton.getInstance() == DclSingleton.getInstance());
        System.out.println(HolderSingleton.getInstance() == HolderSingleton.getInstance());
    }
}

Practice — Lesson 7

(a) Actual — 2019-20 Q1(a). (b) Actual — 2016-17 Q5(a) / 2012-13 Q2(a). (c) Actual — 2010-11 Q4(a). (d) Actual — 2011-12 Q1(b).

(a) A web app creates userID, home-district, qualification and transaction (TxID) identifiers in the back end, each never duplicated and created serially from 1, used as primary keys. Demonstrate their creation with a suitable pattern. (15)

(b) Describe eager and lazy initialisation of a singleton; give an example where lazy should be preferred; draw the structure. (15)

(c) Which of the two implementations is a valid Singleton? (i) eager field but getInstance() is private; (ii) SingletonHolder nested class with public getInstance(). (5)

(d) Class Base is inherited by Derived1 and Derived2; at most 5 Derived1 and 10 Derived2 objects can exist. Write the Java code and a main that creates arrays of both. (18⅔)

Show solution

(a) Singleton (one generator object per identifier kind). If two generator objects existed, both would start at 1 and hand out duplicate primary keys; a single shared instance with a synchronized counter guarantees serial, unique values for the whole back end. In a real system the counter would be initialised from MAX(id) in the table at start-up.

// 2019-20 Q1(a) — one Singleton generator per identifier kind; serial ids from 1, never duplicated
class IdGenerator {
    private static IdGenerator userIds, districtIds, qualificationIds, txIds;
    private long next = 1;
    private IdGenerator() { }                                  // no outside construction

    public static synchronized IdGenerator forUser() {
        if (userIds == null) userIds = new IdGenerator();
        return userIds;
    }
    public static synchronized IdGenerator forDistrict() {
        if (districtIds == null) districtIds = new IdGenerator();
        return districtIds;
    }
    public static synchronized IdGenerator forQualification() {
        if (qualificationIds == null) qualificationIds = new IdGenerator();
        return qualificationIds;
    }
    public static synchronized IdGenerator forTransaction() {
        if (txIds == null) txIds = new IdGenerator();
        return txIds;
    }
    public synchronized long nextId() { return next++; }      // strictly serial
}
class RegistrationService {                // back end called by the UI
    long registerUser(String name)      { return IdGenerator.forUser().nextId(); }
    long createDistrict(String d)       { return IdGenerator.forDistrict().nextId(); }
    long createQualification(String q)  { return IdGenerator.forQualification().nextId(); }
    long recordTransaction()            { return IdGenerator.forTransaction().nextId(); }
}
public class IdDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        RegistrationService s = new RegistrationService();
        System.out.println("user " + s.registerUser("A") + ", user " + s.registerUser("B"));
        System.out.println("district " + s.createDistrict("Dhaka") + ", tx " + s.recordTransaction()
                + ", tx " + s.recordTransaction() + ", qualification " + s.createQualification("BSc"));
        System.out.println("same object? " + (IdGenerator.forUser() == IdGenerator.forUser()));
    }
}

Output: user 1, user 2 / district 1, tx 1, tx 2, qualification 1 / same object? true.

(b) Use the table in §3 and the code above. Lazy preferred example: a DatabaseConnectionPool or report generator that opens many connections — creating it at start-up slows launch and wastes resources if the user never opens a report. Structure: the box in §1.

(c) (i) is not usable: the eager field is fine, but getInstance() is private, so no other class can obtain the instance — there is no global access point. (ii) is valid (initialisation-on-demand holder): the private constructor stops new, the nested class is loaded only when getInstance() is first called (lazy), and the JVM's class loading makes it thread-safe without synchronized.

(d) Generalise the private constructor + static access method so the class counts its instances and refuses the (limit+1)-th one.

// 2011-12 Q1(b) — Base inherited by Derived1 (max 5) and Derived2 (max 10): Singleton generalised
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

abstract class Base {
    private static final Map<Class<?>, Integer> COUNT = new HashMap<>();
    protected Base(int limit) {                       // each subclass passes its own limit
        int c = COUNT.getOrDefault(getClass(), 0);
        if (c >= limit)
            throw new IllegalStateException(getClass().getSimpleName() + ": limit " + limit + " reached");
        COUNT.put(getClass(), c + 1);
    }
}
class Derived1 extends Base {
    private static final int MAX = 5;
    private Derived1() { super(MAX); }                // private: only getInstance() creates
    public static synchronized Derived1 getInstance() {
        try { return new Derived1(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { return null; }
    }
}
class Derived2 extends Base {
    private static final int MAX = 10;
    private Derived2() { super(MAX); }
    public static synchronized Derived2 getInstance() {
        try { return new Derived2(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { return null; }
    }
}
public class LimitedDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Derived1[] a = new Derived1[7];
        Derived2[] b = new Derived2[12];
        int ok1 = 0, ok2 = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) if ((a[i] = Derived1.getInstance()) != null) ok1++;
        for (int i = 0; i < b.length; i++) if ((b[i] = Derived2.getInstance()) != null) ok2++;
        System.out.println("Derived1 created: " + ok1 + " of " + a.length);
        System.out.println("Derived2 created: " + ok2 + " of " + b.length);
    }
}

Output: Derived1 created: 5 of 7 / Derived2 created: 10 of 12.

sections.title: Lesson 8 — Builder and Choosing a Creational Pattern
sections.html:
Memorize

Builder — Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation so that the same construction process can create different representations.

Problem (sl. 43): an application builds the parts of a complex aggregate; one construction specification must be able to produce several different representations.

1. Structure (sl. 44)

   Director                      «interface» Builder                 Product
 - builder: Builder  <>---------> + buildPartA()                  (complex object,
 + construct() {                    + buildPartB()                   assembled in parts)
     builder.buildPartA();          + getResult(): Product                ^
     builder.buildPartB(); }               ^          ^                   | creates
                                   ConcreteBuilder1  ConcreteBuilder2 ----+
ParticipantRole (kids-meal analogy, sl. 45)
DirectorFixes the order of the steps (the cashier tells the crew: burger, drink, toy)
BuilderInterface with one method per part
ConcreteBuilderBuilds and remembers one representation (the restaurant crew for one meal type)
ProductThe finished complex object (the bagged meal)
ClientPicks the concrete builder, gives it to the director, collects the product (the customer)

2. Slide examples (sl. 45–53)

  • Computer assembled from parts per order (500 GB disk + Intel vs 250 GB disk + AMD).
  • Vehicle (sl. 47–49): IBuilder (BuildBody, InsertWheels, AddHeadlights, GetVehicle); Car and MotorCycle builders; Product keeps a list of parts and Show(); Director.Construct(builder) calls the three steps in order.
  • CD packing (sl. 50–53): Packing (pack, price); CD → Company → Sony (20), Samsung (15); CDType holds items (addItem, getCost, showItems); CDBuilder.buildSonyCD() / buildSamsungCD(); BuilderDemo prints the costs.

3. Consequences (sl. 46)

  • Lets you vary a product's internal representation.
  • Isolates construction code from representation code.
  • Gives finer control over the construction process (step by step, under the director).

4. Choosing a creational pattern (2021-22 Q1(a))

PatternUse whenExample
Factory MethodOne product; the subclass (or a parameter) decides which concrete class; client must not call newLogistics.createTransport() → Truck / Ship; travel packages
Abstract FactoryA family of related products must be created together and stay consistent; swap the family as a wholeGUIFactory → WinButton + WinCheckbox; pizza ingredients per country
BuilderOne complex object built step by step; same steps give different representations; many optional partsHTML page; meals; forms per user type
SingletonExactly one shared instance with global accessDB connection, id generator
Bridge (structural)Two independent dimensions (abstraction × implementation) would explode into subclasses; connect two hierarchies by compositionShape × Color; Notification × Email/SMS/Push

Practice — Lesson 8

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q3(a). (b) Actual — 2018-19 Q3(b). (c) Actual — 2017-18 Q6(a). (d) Actual — 2020-21 Q1(a)–(b). (e) Actual — 2021-22 Q1(a).

(a) HTMLPageDirector tells the builder HTMLPageBuilder the pageTitle, pageHeading and several lines of text, then has it assemble the parts and return the page. Class diagram + code. (15)

(b) A grades application shows different forms (enabled/disabled buttons) to admin and student. Builder gives the form interface, concrete builders are the per-user forms, the product is the final form and the director is the application. Class diagram + code. (20)

(c) Lalbagh food shop: set meals with a main item (rice or bread); rice comes with gravy curries, bread with chicken or beef kebabs; drinks are ordered separately; the bill must be paid before eating. Class diagram + code. (7+15)

(d) Burger shop: Veggi/Beef/Chicken pizza, optional extra cheese, drinks (Coffee, Water, Coke — one or more), appetizers (Onion Rings, French Fries), and meals (appetizer + pizza with cheese + drinks). Construct the four orders (1 Beef pizza + French fry + cheese, 2 Chicken pizza + onion rings + water, 3 combo Veggi + French fry + two Cokes, 4 combo Veggi + Onion Rings + Coffee + Water) using three patterns, with price methods; then compare the patterns. (28+7)

(e) Differentiate the use cases of Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder and Bridge. (16)

Show solution

(a) Builder with the names given in the question.

HTMLPageDirector                  «interface» PageBuilder                 HTMLPage (product)
 - builder: PageBuilder <>-----> + setPageTitle(t)                      - title, heading, lines
 + construct(title, heading,       + setPageHeading(h)                    + render(): String
             lines...): HTMLPage   + addText(line)                              ^ creates
                                    + getPage(): HTMLPage                       |
                                            ^ HTMLPageBuilder ------------------+
// 2022-23 Q3(a) — Builder: HTMLPageDirector drives HTMLPageBuilder
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

class HTMLPage {                                       // product
    private String title = "", heading = "";
    private final List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    void setTitle(String t)   { title = t; }
    void setHeading(String h) { heading = h; }
    void addLine(String l)    { lines.add(l); }
    String render() {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("<html><head><title>" + title + "</title></head><body>\n");
        sb.append("<h1>").append(heading).append("</h1>\n");
        for (String l : lines) sb.append("<p>").append(l).append("</p>\n");
        return sb.append("</body></html>").toString();
    }
}
interface PageBuilder {                                // builder
    void setPageTitle(String t);
    void setPageHeading(String h);
    void addText(String line);
    HTMLPage getPage();                                // final assembly
}
class HTMLPageBuilder implements PageBuilder {         // concrete builder
    private final HTMLPage page = new HTMLPage();
    public void setPageTitle(String t)   { page.setTitle(t); }
    public void setPageHeading(String h) { page.setHeading(h); }
    public void addText(String line)     { page.addLine(line); }
    public HTMLPage getPage()            { return page; }
}
class HTMLPageDirector {                               // director
    private final PageBuilder builder;
    HTMLPageDirector(PageBuilder b) { builder = b; }
    HTMLPage construct(String title, String heading, String... lines) {
        builder.setPageTitle(title);
        builder.setPageHeading(heading);
        for (String l : lines) builder.addText(l);
        return builder.getPage();
    }
}
public class HtmlDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        HTMLPageDirector d = new HTMLPageDirector(new HTMLPageBuilder());
        System.out.println(d.construct("CSE 213", "Builder Pattern", "Line one.", "Line two.").render());
    }
}

(b) Builder exactly as the question maps it: FormBuilder (interface/abstract), AdminFormBuilder and StudentFormBuilder (concrete builders), Form (product), GradeApplication (director, chooses the builder from the login role and calls the steps in a fixed order).

// 2018-19 Q3(b) — Builder: a form per user type; Director = the application
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

class Form {                                                    // product
    private final List<String> parts = new ArrayList<>();
    void add(String p) { parts.add(p); }
    public String toString() { return String.join(" | ", parts); }
}
abstract class FormBuilder {                                    // builder
    protected Form form;
    void createNewForm() { form = new Form(); }
    abstract void buildHeader();
    abstract void buildGradeTable();
    abstract void buildButtons();
    Form getForm() { return form; }
}
class AdminFormBuilder extends FormBuilder {                    // concrete builders
    void buildHeader()     { form.add("Header: Admin panel"); }
    void buildGradeTable() { form.add("Grades: all students (editable)"); }
    void buildButtons()    { form.add("Edit[on] Publish[on] Delete[on]"); }
}
class StudentFormBuilder extends FormBuilder {
    void buildHeader()     { form.add("Header: My grades"); }
    void buildGradeTable() { form.add("Grades: own (read-only)"); }
    void buildButtons()    { form.add("Edit[off] Publish[off] Print[on]"); }
}
class GradeApplication {                                        // director
    Form formFor(String role) {
        FormBuilder b = role.equals("admin") ? new AdminFormBuilder() : new StudentFormBuilder();
        b.createNewForm();
        b.buildHeader();
        b.buildGradeTable();
        b.buildButtons();
        return b.getForm();
    }
}
public class FormDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        GradeApplication app = new GradeApplication();
        System.out.println("admin:   " + app.formFor("admin"));
        System.out.println("student: " + app.formFor("student"));
    }
}

(c) Builder: every set meal is built by the same steps (main item, sides, optional drink, bill) but each concrete builder gives a different representation. Waiter = director; the bill is computed from the product before it is served. Prices are assumed.

Waiter (director) <>--> SetMealBuilder {abstract}: addMainItem(), addSides(), addDrink(n,p), getMeal()
                              ^ RiceMealBuilder     (rice + gravy curry + dal)
                              ^ ChickenKebabMealBuilder (naan + chicken kebab)
                              ^ BeefKebabMealBuilder    (naan + beef kebab)
SetMeal (product) — list of Food; bill()
// 2017-18 Q6(a) — Builder: set meals (rice + curries, or bread + kebabs), optional drinks, bill first
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

class Food {
    final String name; final double price;
    Food(String name, double price) { this.name = name; this.price = price; }
}
class SetMeal {                                                // product
    private final List<Food> items = new ArrayList<>();
    void add(Food f) { items.add(f); }
    double bill() { double s = 0; for (Food f : items) s += f.price; return s; }
    void show() {
        for (Food f : items) System.out.printf("  %-20s %6.1f%n", f.name, f.price);
        System.out.printf("  %-20s %6.1f%n", "BILL (pay first)", bill());
    }
}
abstract class SetMealBuilder {                                // builder
    protected final SetMeal meal = new SetMeal();
    abstract void addMainItem();
    abstract void addSides();
    void addDrink(String name, double price) { meal.add(new Food(name, price)); }
    SetMeal getMeal() { return meal; }
}
class RiceMealBuilder extends SetMealBuilder {
    void addMainItem() { meal.add(new Food("Plain rice", 40)); }
    void addSides()    { meal.add(new Food("Chicken gravy curry", 90)); meal.add(new Food("Dal", 20)); }
}
class ChickenKebabMealBuilder extends SetMealBuilder {
    void addMainItem() { meal.add(new Food("Naan x2", 30)); }
    void addSides()    { meal.add(new Food("Chicken kebab", 110)); }
}
class BeefKebabMealBuilder extends SetMealBuilder {
    void addMainItem() { meal.add(new Food("Naan x2", 30)); }
    void addSides()    { meal.add(new Food("Beef kebab", 140)); }
}
class Waiter {                                                 // director
    SetMeal prepare(SetMealBuilder b, String drink, double drinkPrice) {
        b.addMainItem();
        b.addSides();
        if (drink != null) b.addDrink(drink, drinkPrice);       // drinks are optional extras
        return b.getMeal();
    }
}
public class LalbaghDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Waiter w = new Waiter();
        System.out.println("Rice set + lemonade:");
        w.prepare(new RiceMealBuilder(), "Lemonade", 35).show();
        System.out.println("Bread + beef kebab, no drink:");
        w.prepare(new BeefKebabMealBuilder(), null, 0).show();
    }
}

(d) Three patterns, each fitting one requirement (prices assumed: Veggi 300, Beef 400, Chicken 350, cheese +50, Coffee 80, Water 20, Coke 40, French Fry 100, Onion Rings 120): Decorator — extra cheese wraps a pizza and adds to price(); Composite — an order is a MenuItem containing MenuItems, so price() of an order = sum of its parts; Builder — a combo meal is assembled step by step (pizza, appetizer, drinks) by ComboBuilder.

// 2020-21 Q1(a) — the orders built with three patterns: Decorator (cheese), Composite (orders), Builder (combo meals)
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface MenuItem { String desc(); double price(); }          // common component interface
class ShopPizza implements MenuItem {
    private final String kind; private final double p;
    ShopPizza(String kind, double p) { this.kind = kind; this.p = p; }
    public String desc() { return kind + " pizza"; }
    public double price() { return p; }
}
class SimpleItem implements MenuItem {                         // drinks, appetizers
    private final String n; private final double p;
    SimpleItem(String n, double p) { this.n = n; this.p = p; }
    public String desc() { return n; }
    public double price() { return p; }
}
// assumed prices: Veggi 300, Beef 400, Chicken 350, cheese +50; Coffee 80, Water 20, Coke 40;
//                 French Fry 100, Onion Rings 120

// Pattern 1 — DECORATOR: extra cheese wraps any pizza
abstract class PizzaDecorator implements MenuItem {
    protected final MenuItem inner;
    PizzaDecorator(MenuItem i) { inner = i; }
}
class ExtraCheese extends PizzaDecorator {
    ExtraCheese(MenuItem i) { super(i); }
    public String desc() { return inner.desc() + " + cheese"; }
    public double price() { return inner.price() + 50; }
}

// Pattern 2 — COMPOSITE: an order is a MenuItem made of MenuItems
class Order implements MenuItem {
    private final String name;
    private final List<MenuItem> parts = new ArrayList<>();
    Order(String name) { this.name = name; }
    Order add(MenuItem m) { parts.add(m); return this; }
    public String desc() {
        List<String> d = new ArrayList<>();
        for (MenuItem m : parts) d.add(m.desc());
        return name + " [" + String.join(", ", d) + "]";
    }
    public double price() { double s = 0; for (MenuItem m : parts) s += m.price(); return s; }
}

// Pattern 3 — BUILDER: a combo meal is assembled step by step (appetizer, pizza, drinks)
class ComboMeal {
    final List<MenuItem> items = new ArrayList<>();
    double price() { double s = 0; for (MenuItem m : items) s += m.price(); return s; }
}
class ComboBuilder {
    private final ComboMeal meal = new ComboMeal();
    ComboBuilder pizza(String kind, double p, boolean cheese) {
        MenuItem pz = new ShopPizza(kind, p);
        meal.items.add(cheese ? new ExtraCheese(pz) : pz);
        return this;
    }
    ComboBuilder appetizer(String n, double p) { meal.items.add(new SimpleItem(n, p)); return this; }
    ComboBuilder drink(String n, double p)     { meal.items.add(new SimpleItem(n, p)); return this; }
    ComboMeal build() { return meal; }
}
public class BurgerShop {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MenuItem o1 = new Order("Order 1").add(new ExtraCheese(new ShopPizza("Beef", 400)))
                                          .add(new SimpleItem("French Fry", 100));
        MenuItem o2 = new Order("Order 2").add(new ShopPizza("Chicken", 350))
                                          .add(new SimpleItem("Onion Rings", 120)).add(new SimpleItem("Water", 20));
        ComboMeal o3 = new ComboBuilder().pizza("Veggi", 300, false).appetizer("French Fry", 100)
                                         .drink("Coke", 40).drink("Coke", 40).build();
        ComboMeal o4 = new ComboBuilder().pizza("Veggi", 300, false).appetizer("Onion Rings", 120)
                                         .drink("Coffee", 80).drink("Water", 20).build();
        System.out.println(o1.desc() + " = " + o1.price());
        System.out.println(o2.desc() + " = " + o2.price());
        System.out.println("Order 3 (combo) = " + o3.price());
        System.out.println("Order 4 (combo) = " + o4.price());
    }
}

Output: Order 1 = 400 + 50 + 100 = 550; Order 2 = 350 + 120 + 20 = 490; Order 3 = 300 + 100 + 2 × 40 = 480; Order 4 = 300 + 120 + 80 + 20 = 520.

PatternAdvantagesDisadvantages
DecoratorAdd any number of extras at run time (double cheese = two wrappers); no subclass explosion (BeefWithCheese …); OCPMany small objects; order of wrapping can matter; harder to debug
CompositeOrders and items are treated uniformly; nested combos; price() recursion is automaticHard to restrict what a composite may contain (e.g. 'exactly one pizza')
BuilderStep-by-step construction; fixed recipe for combos; validation before build()Extra builder classes; overkill for single items

(e) Use the table in §4. Key contrasts: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory — one product via subclass override vs a consistent family via a factory object; Builder — one complex product in steps, versus factories that return a product in one call; Bridge — structural, not creational: it avoids an abstraction × implementation class explosion by composition (Notification has a MessageSender). Draw one tiny diagram per pattern.

sections.title: Quick Notes — Creational Patterns
sections.html:
Revision points for Lessons 5–8.

L5 · Factory Method

  • Intent: interface for creating an object, subclasses decide the class.
  • Creator.factoryMethod() abstract; ConcreteCreator returns ConcreteProduct; client sees Product only.
  • Cues: client must not call new; centralised creation; add types without editing.
  • Slides: ShapeFactory, PaymentProcessor kiosk, electricity Plan (3.50/7.50/5.50), Logistics, Dialog.

L6 · Abstract Factory

  • Families of related products, consistent; one concrete factory per family.
  • Rows = families, columns = product kinds. Pizza (Italy/America), set menus, Uber/Pathao, GUI per OS.
  • Liability: adding a new product kind changes every factory.

L7 · Singleton

  • Private static instance + private constructor + public static getInstance().
  • Eager = at class load (thread-safe); lazy = on first call (needs synchronized / DCL / holder).
  • Variable number of instances: count in constructor (Derived1 ≤ 5, Derived2 ≤ 10).

L8 · Builder

  • Director fixes the steps; ConcreteBuilder makes one representation; getResult() returns the product.
  • Cues: 'complex object', 'step by step', 'same process, different representations', director named.
  • Burger shop: Decorator (cheese) + Composite (orders) + Builder (combos).

sections.title: Lesson 9 — Class Notation: Attributes, Operations, Kinds of Classes
sections.html:
1. What a class diagram shows (sl. 1–2)

A picture of the classes of an OO system: their fields and methods, and the connections between classes that interact or inherit. It does not show how classes interact over time (that is a sequence diagram) or algorithms.

Benefits: models data for complex information systems; overview of the structure before reading code (reduces maintenance time); better understanding of the application; detailed charts of the code to be written; helpful for developers and other stakeholders.

2. A single class (sl. 3)

+--------------------------+     +--------------------------+     +----------------------------+
|        Rectangle         |     |         Student          |     |       «interface»          |
+--------------------------+     +--------------------------+     |          Shape             |
| - width: int             |     | - name: String           |     +----------------------------+
| - height: int            |     | - id: int                |     | + calculateArea(): double  |
| / area: double           |     | - totalStudents: int     |     +----------------------------+
+--------------------------+     +--------------------------+     (abstract class: name in italics)
| # Rectangle(w:int,h:int) |     | # getID(): int           |
| + distance(r:Rectangle)  |     | ~ getEmail(): String     |
|   : double               |     +--------------------------+     totalStudents is static -> underline it
+--------------------------+
  • Name on top; «interface» above an interface name; italics for an abstract class.
  • Attributes in the middle (optional); operations at the bottom (optional).
  • Trivial get/set methods may be omitted, but never omit a method of an interface; do not repeat inherited methods.

3. Attribute and operation syntax (sl. 4–5)

visibility name : type [count] = default_value
visibility name(param: type, …) : return_type
SymbolMeaning
+public
#protected
-private
~package (default)
/derived (computed, e.g. / age from DOB)
underlinestatic (class-level)

Example (sl. 4–5): ~ courses[100]: Course; / Age: int; + Student(n: String, dob: String) — no return type for constructors or void methods; + calculateGPA(crs: Course[]): float.

4. Kinds of classes (2014-15 Q8(a) — textbook + slides)

KindNotationExample
Concrete classplain nameStudent
Abstract classname in italics (or {abstract})Security, Payment, RentalItem (sl. 12–13, 16)
Interface«interface» stereotype; realised with dashed line + hollow triangle«interface» Shape
Association classclass box joined to an association by a dashed lineJob between Company and Person (sl. 11)
Enumeration«enumeration» with literal valuesGender {male, female}, OrderStatus (sl. 19, 17)
Stereotyped analysis classes«entity», «boundary», «control»Invoice «entity», CreateInvoiceUI «boundary»
Data type / utility«datatype», «utility» (static members only)Address «datatype» (sl. 18)

Practice — Lesson 9

sections.title: Lesson 10 — Relationships, Multiplicity, Aggregation vs Composition
sections.html:
1. The relationship types (sl. 6–10)

RelationshipLine / arrowMeaning
Generalisation (class)solid line, triangle at the parentinheritance; hierarchies drawn top-down, arrows up
Realisation (interface)dashed line, hollow triangleclass implements interface
Associationsolid line, optional name ▶ and navigability arrowobjects are linked / use each other
Aggregationhollow diamond ◇ at the whole'is part of' — part can exist without the whole (Car ◇— Engine)
Compositionfilled diamond ◆ at the whole'is entirely made of' — parts live and die with the whole (Book ◆— Page)
Dependencydashed line, open arrow'uses temporarily' — implementation detail, not state (Lottery ⇢ Random)
Note

Slide 7 states: parent is a class → solid line with black arrow; interface → dashed line, white arrow; abstract class → solid line, white arrow. Standard UML uses a hollow triangle for every generalisation; either is accepted if you are consistent.

2. Multiplicity (sl. 8–9)

WrittenMeaning
1exactly one
0..1zero or one
or 0..zero or more
1..*one or more
2..4between 2 and 4
3..*three or more

Read each end from the opposite class: Book 1 ◆—— * Page = 'each book has many pages, each page belongs to exactly one book'. Car 1 —— 1 Engine = 'each car has one engine, each engine belongs to one car'.

3. Association class (sl. 11)

When the association itself has properties: Company * —— 1..* Person with a Job class (description, dateHired, salary) hanging on the association by a dashed line. Two separate associations Company–Job and Job–Person would be wrong — they would not tie one Job to one specific pair.

4. Slide examples (sl. 12–14)

Video rental store (sl. 12):
  Customer 1 ◇---- RentalInvoice ◆---- 1..* RentalItem {abstract}       RentalInvoice ---- 0..1 CheckoutScreen
                                               △
                                  +------------+-----------+
                                 DVD          VHS        Game
Inheritance (sl. 13): Security {abstract: presentValue(), history()} <- CashAccount, Stock, Bond, Property;
                      Stock <- SmallCapStock, LargeCapStock
Multiple inheritance (sl. 14): BankAccount <- InterestBearingItem, InsurableItem;  RealEstate <- InsurableItem, Asset
Trap

Aggregation vs composition is decided by lifetime and sharing, not by size. If deleting the whole must delete the part, and the part cannot be shared by two wholes → composition. If the part survives (an engine can be moved to another car; a player stays when the team is dissolved) → aggregation.

Practice — Lesson 10

(a) Actual — 2018-19 Q4(c). (b) Actual — 2017-18 Q8(c).

(a) Show example class diagrams of aggregation and composition in the context of a video rental store. (8)

(b) Show example diagrams of a real-world scenario to present aggregation and composition. (6)

Show solution

(a) Composition: a rental invoice is made of its rental line items; deleting the invoice deletes its lines. Aggregation: a customer has invoices / a video store has a catalogue of video titles — the titles exist even if the catalogue section is removed.

COMPOSITION                                   AGGREGATION
+---------------+ 1        1..* +-----------+  +-----------+ 1        0..* +---------------+
| RentalInvoice |◆-------------| RentalLine |  | Customer  |◇--------------| RentalInvoice |
+---------------+              +-----------+  +-----------+                +---------------+
| invoiceNo     |              | dueDate   |  | name      |                (an invoice record outlives
| date          |              | fee       |  | phone     |                 a deleted customer account)
+---------------+              +-----------+  +-----------+
                                    | * refers to 1                      +-----------+ 1     0..* +---------+
                                 +-----------+                           | Catalogue |◇----------| Video   |
                                 | Video     |                           +-----------+           +---------+

(b) Composition: House 1 ◆—— 1..* Room (rooms are destroyed with the house). Aggregation: Department 1 ◇—— * Professor (professors still exist if the department closes). Mark multiplicities at both ends and the diamond at the whole.

sections.title: Lesson 11 — Drawing a Class Diagram from a Scenario (worked TF diagrams)
sections.html:
1. Method (used for every solution below)

  1. Underline nouns → candidate classes; drop roles that are only attributes (name, date, rate).
  2. Find 'is a kind of' → generalisation; 'has / consists of' → aggregation or composition (check lifetime).
  3. Other verbs → named associations (treats ▶, teaches ▶, books ▶).
  4. Put a multiplicity at both ends; read every line aloud in both directions.
  5. Add key attributes and 1–3 operations per class; use enumerations for fixed sets (gender, status).
  6. Write any rule that UML lines cannot show as a {constraint} note.

2. Slide models to know (sl. 15–24)

  • sl. 15 Bank/ATM: Bank 1 ◇ * ATM, Bank 1 ◇ * Customer, Customer 1 — * Account (Current, Saving), ATM transactions.
  • sl. 16–17 Order system: Customer 1 — * Order ◆ 1..* OrderDetail * — 1 Item; Order 1 — * Payment {abstract} ← Cash, Check, Credit (and WireTransfer); «enumeration» OrderStatus.
  • sl. 18 Library domain: Library, Book, BookItem, Author, Account, Patron/Librarian, Catalog, «datatype» Address.
  • sl. 19 Hospital wards and teams (the TF question — solved below). sl. 20 Hospital organisation: Person ← Patient, Staff ← Operations/Administrative/Technical staff ← Doctor, Nurse, Front-desk, Technician …
