  • sl. 22 University (School, Department, Student, Instructor, Course) — the 2021-22 question. sl. 23 Student — Enrollment(marks) — Seminar with {ordered, FIFO} waiting list. sl. 24 airline with stereotypes and a note.

Practice — Lesson 11

(a) Actual — 2019-20 Q5(a) and 2017-18 Q5(a). (b) Actual — 2021-22 Q2(b). (c) Actual — 2022-23 Q4(b). (d) Actual — 2020-21 Q5(a). (e) Actual — 2018-19 Q1(a). (f) Actual — 2013-14 Q7(a). (g) Actual — 2012-13 Q7(c). (h) Actual — 2014-15 Q8(b) (class part; sequence part in the Interaction Diagrams notes).

(a) Hospital: wards (unique name, gender, fixed capacity, empty or with patients of that gender); doctors in teams (unique name/code) headed by a consultant who supervises fellows/residents/students; the rest are junior doctors; a doctor is in at most one team; consultants visit and treat their patients and advise release. Class diagram. (20 / 14)

(b) University: departments, each with faculties and one head; courses offered by departments (possibly none); students are university members and attend courses instructed by faculties. Attributes and methods; no visibility. (10)

(c) Accounting software: Account (chart of accounts); each transaction debits one account and credits another; made from a user authenticated by two-step authentication (password, OTP); Debtor and Creditor store which account is debited/credited; accounts may have children (leaf = no child); an account with a transaction or a child cannot be deleted. (12)

(d) Media agency orders ads in newspapers; each newspaper has a standard rate per column-inch per page (changes over time) and gives the agency its own discount; expected readership per page; an employee prepares a media plan (page, size, date, newspaper) for a product within a budget; the client approves; another employee generates a Release Order listing ads with positions, dates and cost. (16)

(e) BSM shipping: shipped items (goods or food) with item number, weight, dimensions, insurance amount, destination, final delivery date; received at one retail center; travel via one or more transportation events (schedule number, type flight/truck, delivery route). (14)

(f) CSE 308: students form teams of 2–3, a team completes 0–3 assignments, each student takes exactly one midterm, every assignment and midterm gets a mark. (20)

(g) Library: librarians in shifts, multiple copies per book, one or more authors, one publisher, a user borrows up to 10 books and returns to the librarian on shift. Attributes and associations only. (12)

(h) Music CDs lent to friends: several copies of some CDs, a daily fee per loaned CD; query how many CDs a friend has, how long, how much owed, who has a CD. (12 of 22)

Exam approach

  1. Spend 1 minute listing nouns and verbs from the scenario next to the question.

sections.title: Lesson 12 — From ERD to Class Diagram; CRC Cards
sections.html:
1. The University of Toronto scenario (sl. 2)

Departments are each managed by a chair and have at least one professor; a professor belongs to one or more departments; each course is taught by at least one professor (a professor on sabbatical may teach none); a course may be taught several times by different professors. Known data: department name, professor name and employee id, course name, schedule, term/year, assignments and offering department.

2. Steps (sl. 3–10)

  1. Entity/class candidates (sl. 3): department, chair, professor, course, course section.
  2. Relationship matrix (sl. 4) and ER diagram with (min, max) cardinalities (sl. 5–6).
  3. Association matrix (sl. 7): mark aggregations.
  4. Basic class diagram (sl. 8): Course 0..* — teaches — 0..* Professor; Department 1 ◇ offers 1..* Course; Department 1..* ◇ assigned 1..* Professor; Chair is a Professor; Department 1 — manages — 1 Chair.
  5. Add attributes (sl. 9): Course(name, schedule, term), Professor(name, employeeId), Department(name).
  6. Add operations (sl. 10): Course.modifySchedule(); Professor.prepareMaterial(), teachLecture(), evaluateAssignments(); Department.addCourse(), addProfessor(), removeCourse(), removeProfessor(), changeChair(); Chair.createPolicy(), evaluateProfessor().

3. CRC cards (textbook — 2012-13 Q8(b), 2011-12 Q2(d))

CRC = Class–Responsibility–Collaborator. One index card per class: class name on top, its responsibilities (what it knows and does) on the left, its collaborators (classes it needs) on the right. The team role-plays a use case by passing cards around.

+---------------------------------------------+
| Class: Order                                |
+-------------------------------+-------------+
| Responsibilities              | Collaborators|
| know its line items           | OrderLine   |
| compute total                 | Product     |
| check stock before confirming | Inventory   |
+-------------------------------+-------------+

Benefits: (1) cheap, informal way to find classes and distribute responsibilities before drawing UML — it keeps classes cohesive (too many responsibilities = split the card); (2) involves users and developers together in walk-throughs of scenarios, revealing missing classes and collaborations early. Usage: brainstorming, role-play of use cases, input to the class diagram.

Practice — Lesson 12

(a) Actual — 2012-13 Q8(b). (b) Actual — 2011-12 Q2(d). (c) Constructed.

(a) What does CRC stand for? Name two benefits of using CRC for class modeling. (5)

(b) What is a CRC card? Discuss its usages. (10)

(c) From the Toronto scenario, why is Chair a subclass of Professor and not a separate entity?

Show solution

(a)/(b) §3: definition, card layout, two benefits, usages (identify classes, assign responsibilities, role-play scenarios, team communication, design review).

(c) A chair is a professor with extra responsibilities (createPolicy, evaluateProfessor); every chair has all professor attributes. Generalisation avoids duplicating them, and the 'manages' association (Department 1 — 1 Chair) records which professor currently chairs.

sections.title: Senior Diagram Practice — AI Sir (CSE 325 Information System Design)
sections.source: Questions from 'CSE 213/AI Sir Diagram question from seniors' (CSE 325 papers 2017-18 to 2023-24), cited as 'AI Sir <session> p.N'. Each is solved below in the notation of this note file.
sections.html:
Exam focus

These are the diagram questions AI Sir set in CSE 325. They use the same notations as this note file, so practise them after the lessons above. Draw the diagram first, then check it against the solution.

2017-18 Q1(a) — Inconsistencies in the language-course class diagram (20)

The scenario needs: show students → select student → show languages → select language → show the French courses the student has not taken → select course → create the assignment. Inconsistencies (no redraw):

  1. Boundary class is incomplete: AssignCourseUI has only SelectStudent(), SelectLanguage(), AssignCourse(); it has no StartInterface()/display operations (DisplayStudents(), DisplayLanguages(), DisplayCourses()) although the controller's StartInterface() must open it and the lists must be shown.
  2. Controller lacks needed operations: AssignCourse has no GetStudents(), no AssignCourse() and no GetStudentCourses(); GetLanguageInfo() is not needed by the scenario.
  3. No associations from the boundary to the control and from the control to the entities — the messages in the scenario cannot be sent.
  4. Language holds CourseID — wrong: one language has many courses, so the foreign key belongs in Course (Course already has LanguageID). This is redundant and contradicts the 1-to-many relation.
  5. Language is not associated with Course although Course.LanguageID refers to it (missing Language 1 — * Course).
  6. Course holds StudentName — a course does not belong to one student; the student–course link is CourseAssignmentInfo. StudentName also duplicates Student data.
  7. Course has no operation to return the courses of a language not taken by a student (GetLanguageCourses(languageID, studentID)); GetCourses() has no parameters.
  8. Student has AssignCourse() — creating an assignment is the responsibility of CourseAssignmentInfo (e.g. AddAssignment(studentID, courseID)), coordinated by the controller.
  9. GetStudentCourses() appears in both Student and CourseAssignmentInfo — duplicated responsibility.
  10. CourseAssignmentInfo has no operation to create a record and should be an association class between Student and Course (it only has StudentID, CourseID, RegistrationDate).
  11. No multiplicities on any association (Student 1 — 0..* CourseAssignmentInfo 0..* — 1 Course).
  12. The teacher's log-in is not supported (no Teacher/User class or Login operation), and operations have no parameters (SelectStudent(studentID), SelectLanguage(languageID)).

2018-19 Q1(a) — Office loan system: class diagram (22)

'Conditions may change over time' → keep loan parameters and rules as dated versions, not constants.

LoanApplication * ---- 1 LoanScheme [name; currentVersion(): SchemeVersion; maxAllowed(e: Employee): double]
LoanScheme 1 ◆---- 1..* SchemeVersion [interestRate, yearsToRepay, maxSalaryMultiple, effectiveFrom, effectiveTo]
LoanScheme 1 ◆---- 1..* EligibilityRule {abstract} [effectiveFrom, effectiveTo; isSatisfied(e: Employee): boolean]
      △ AgeRule [minAge, maxAge]   △ ExperienceRule [minYears]   △ DisciplinaryRule [maxOpenCases = 0]
LoanEvaluator «control» [evaluate(app): boolean]  ---uses---> EligibilityRule, SchemeVersion

Loan 1 ◆---- 0..* Repayment [date, amount]
«enumeration» ApplicationStatus { SUBMITTED, APPROVED, REJECTED, WITHDRAWN }
{maxAllowed = employee.salary x version.maxSalaryMultiple}

2019-20 Q2(b) — ATM withdrawal: steps of identifying classes (20)

  1. Underline the nouns in the scenario: account holder, Sonali Bank, amount, account, debit card, ATM booth/machine, card, PIN, keypad, balance, bank account, notification, registered phone number, central server, transaction.
  2. Remove synonyms: ATM booth = ATM machine; account = bank account; card = debit card.
  3. Remove attributes: amount (of a withdrawal), PIN (of a card), balance (of an account), phone number (of the holder).
  4. Remove things outside the system / actors: account holder (actor, but its data is kept as Customer), central server (external system → boundary/proxy class), Sonali Bank (the system itself).
  5. Classify (boundary / control / entity) and add the event 'withdrawal' as a class (it has amount, time, status).
  6. Assign responsibilities and associations:

sections.title: Quick Notes — Class Diagrams
sections.html:
Revision points for Lessons 9–12.

L9 · Notation

  • visibility name: type [count] = default · visibility name(p: T): R.
  • + public, - private, # protected, ~ package, / derived, underline = static.
  • «interface», italics = abstract; don't omit interface methods; no inherited methods.

L10 · Relationships

  • Generalisation ▷, realisation dashed ▷, association line, ◇ aggregation, ◆ composition, dashed → dependency.
  • Composition = parts die with the whole, not shared. Book ◆ Page; Car ◇ Engine.
  • Association class for properties of the link (Job between Company and Person).

L11 · Scenarios

  • Nouns → classes, 'kind of' → ▷, 'has' → ◇/◆, verbs → named associations, multiplicity both ends, constraints.
  • Hospital wards/teams = sl. 19; university = sl. 22.

L12 · ERD → class, CRC

  • Candidates → relationship matrix → ER (min,max) → class diagram → attributes → operations.
  • CRC = Class, Responsibility, Collaborator.

sections.title: Lesson 13 — States, Events, Transitions, Actions
sections.html:
1. State (sl. 1–2)

The current state of an object is determined by its attribute values and its links to other objects (a StaffMember is 'probationary' because of its startDate). A state is a condition during the life of an object in which it satisfies some condition, performs some action or waits for some event. A state (statechart) diagram models the event-driven behaviour of one class, subsystem or whole system.

2. Notation

  ●  initial pseudostate            ◉  final state
 ( State )  rounded rectangle        -->  transition
 transition label:   event(args) [guard] / action1; action2
 internal compartment:   entry / action    exit / action    do / activity    include / submachine
 e.g.  GradeRate (sl. 3):
   ● --> (Pending) --when [rateStartDate <= currentDate]--> (Active)
            --when [rateFinishDate <= currentDate]--> (Lapsed) --after [1 year]--> ◉

3. The four types of event (sl. 4)

EventOccurs whenExample
Change eventa condition becomes true (when …)when [rateStartDate <= currentDate]
Call eventthe object receives a call to one of its operations (from another object or itself)authorized(authorizationCode) — an operation of Campaign
Signal eventthe object receives an asynchronous signalpaymentReceived signal from the bank
Elapsed-time eventa set period passes after an event, usually entry to the current state (after …)after [1 year]

4. Actions and activities (sl. 6–7)

An action is short and uninterruptible (on a transition, or entry/exit). An activity (do/) runs while the object stays in the state and can be interrupted. Example — DropDownMenu state Menu Visible: entry / displayMenu, exit / hideMenu, do / playSoundClip, internal transition itemSelected() / highlightItem().

5. The Campaign statechart (sl. 5, 10–11)

● --> (Commissioned)
(Commissioned) --authorized(authorizationCode) [contract signed] / setCampaignActive()--> (Active)
                                   (on creation: / assignManager(); assignStaff())
(Active) --campaignCompleted() / prepareFinalStatement()--> (Completed)
(Completed) --paymentReceived(payment) [paymentDue - payment > 0]--> (Completed)      recursive transition
(Completed) --paymentReceived(payment) [paymentDue - payment = 0]--> (Paid)
(Completed) --paymentReceived(payment) [paymentDue - payment < 0] / generateRefund()--> (Paid)   (revised, sl. 11)
(Paid) --archiveCampaign() / unassignStaff(); unassignManager()--> ◉
Trap

Guards on the transitions leaving one state for the same event must not overlap and must cover all cases (> 0, = 0, < 0). A guard is a boolean in [ ]; an action follows a slash.

Practice — Lesson 13

(a) Actual — 2011-12 Q3(a).

(a) What are the different types of events in a state chart diagram? (8)

Show solution

(a) The four rows of the table in §3, each with its keyword and one example (when for change, operation name for call, asynchronous signal, after for elapsed time). Add one sentence: an event triggers a transition, optionally guarded, which may fire an action.

sections.title: Lesson 14 — Nested and Concurrent States; Preparing Statecharts
sections.html:
1. Nested substates (sl. 12–13)

A composite state contains its own statechart. Active of Campaign contains Advert Preparation → (advertsApproved() / authorize()) → Scheduling → (confirmSchedule()) → Running Adverts, with extendCampaign() / modifyBudget() back to Advert Preparation. The transition from the inner initial pseudostate carries no event. The detail can be hidden: 'include / Running' plus the decomposition icon (sl. 13).

2. Concurrent substates (sl. 14–17)

+---------------------------- Active ---------------------------------+
| Running:    ● -> (Advert Preparation) -> (Scheduling) -> (Running Adverts) |
|- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -|   dashed line separates regions
| Monitoring: ● -> (Survey) --surveyComplete()--> (Evaluation)            |
|                       ^------------runSurvey()-------|                   |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
  --campaignCompleted() / prepareFinalStatement()-->  (Completed)
  • Entering the composite state = entering the initial state of every region at once (each region needs an initial state).
  • A transition inside one region does not affect the other region.
  • A transition out of the composite state leaves all substates, however deeply nested.
  • Synchronisation bars (fork / join, sl. 17) show explicitly which substates are entered and that the composite state is left only when both regions have finished.

3. Preparing statecharts (sl. 18–24)

Two approaches: behavioural (from interaction diagrams) and life-cycle (from the domain description of the object's life). Behavioural approach, 8 steps (sl. 19–20):

  1. Examine all interaction diagrams involving each class with heavy messaging.
  2. Identify incoming messages that may be events, and the resulting states.
  3. Document these events and states on a statechart.
  4. Elaborate for additional interactions; add exceptions.
  5. Develop nested statecharts.
  6. Review against the use cases; check implied constraints.
  7. Iterate steps 4–6 until detailed enough.
  8. Check consistency with the class diagram, interaction diagrams and other statecharts.

sl. 21–24 apply it to Campaign: the 'Set Campaign Completed' sequence diagram gives campaignCompleted(); the initial, revised and final statecharts add Active as a superstate, the Monitoring region, and campaignCancelled() transitions (/ cancelSchedule(); calculateCosts(); prepareFinalStatement()) from Commissioned and Active.

Practice — Lesson 14

(a) Actual — 2012-13 Q7(a).

(a) Give a state diagram that describes passing a graduate course as concurrent activities: the student must attend all but two lectures, present a paper she read, and complete a course project due on the last day of term. For the presentation the instructor gives a date, the student prepares and presents on that day. The student can drop the course at any time. Define events, conditions and actions. (15)

Show solution
● --register()--> [ Taking Course ]  (composite, three concurrent regions)

 Lectures:     ● -> (Attending) --lectureHeld [attended]/ attended++ --> (Attending)
                                 --lectureHeld [not attended]/ missed++ --> (Attending)
                    (Attending) --when [missed > 2]--> (Failed Attendance)          (FAIL exit)
                    (Attending) --termEnds [missed <= 2]--> ◉
 - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
 Presentation: ● -> (Waiting for Date) --dateAssigned(d) / record(d)--> (Preparing)
                    (Preparing) --when [today = d] / present()--> (Presented) --> ◉
                    (Preparing) --when [today > d]--> (Missed Presentation)        (FAIL exit)
 - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
 Project:      ● -> (Working on Project) --submit() [today <= lastDayOfTerm]--> (Submitted) --> ◉
                    (Working on Project) --when [today > lastDayOfTerm]--> (Not Submitted) (FAIL exit)

[Taking Course] --all regions reached ◉ (join) / recordPass()--> (Passed) --> ◉
[Taking Course] --any FAIL exit / recordFail()--> (Failed) --> ◉
[Taking Course] --drop() / withdraw()--> (Dropped) --> ◉        (allowed in every substate)

Events: lectureHeld, dateAssigned(d), submit(), drop(), termEnds, change events 'when […]'. Conditions: [attended], [missed > 2], [today = d], [today ≤ lastDayOfTerm]. Actions: attended++, record(d), present(), recordPass(), withdraw(). The drop() arrow leaves the composite state, so it applies to all three regions at once.

sections.title: Lesson 15 — Worked Statecharts (garage, order, TF scenarios)
sections.html:
1. Garage controller (sl. 25–26)

Events: mode-off / mode-auto / mode-open / mode-closed from the operator; exitgate and entrygate from the gates. The garage counts cars (count) against capacity (max). Gates: locked in closed mode, unlocked in open mode, unspecified when off, and in auto mode locked only when full.

(NoCentralControl) --mode-auto / mode-open / mode-closed--> [CentrallyControlled]; any mode-off --> (NoCentralControl)
[CentrallyControlled] = two concurrent regions
  Gate control: (Manual: Open  entry/unlock) <-> (Manual: Closed entry/lock) ;
                (Automatic: AutoOpen entry/unlock) --entrygate [count >= max]--> (AutoFull entry/lock)
                (AutoFull) --exitgate [count < max]--> (AutoOpen)
  Sign:  (NotFull entry/turn off sign) --entrygate [count = max]--> (Full entry/light sign) --exitgate--> (NotFull)
  entrygate / count++ ; exitgate / count--   (internal transitions)

2. Order processing (sl. 27–29)

● -> (Checking  do/check item) --[not all items checked] / get next item--> (Checking)
(Checking) --[all items checked && all available]--> (Dispatching do/initiate delivery) --delivered--> (Delivered) -> ◉
(Checking) --[all checked && some not in stock]--> (Waiting) --item received [all available]--> (Dispatching)
Active superstate (sl. 28): cancelled from any of Checking/Waiting/Dispatching --> (Cancelled)
Payment (sl. 29): (Authorizing do/check payment) --[payment OK]--> (Authorized) ; --[payment not OK]--> (Rejected)

Practice — Lesson 15

(a) Actual — 2011-12 Q3(b). (b) Actual — 2010-11 Q2(b). (c) Actual — 2016-17 Q2(d).

(a) Life insurance: Tk 3,50,000 policy for 5 years; monthly instalment Tk 5000; missing an instalment makes the customer a defaulter; a defaulter pays an extra Tk 500 for each unpaid month to become regular again; 6 consecutive missed instalments cancel the policy; if the customer dies within the period the nominee gets Tk 3,50,000, otherwise the customer gets it at the end. Draw the statechart of a customer. (14⅔)

(b) Lifetime of a video tape: purchased, packaged, entered into the database, put up for rental; rented for 3 days; if not returned the store calls next day, again after 2 more days, and after 2 more days hands it to a collection agency and removes it; damaged on return → removed; missing at annual inventory → removed. Events, conditions, actions. (12⅔)

(c) Bank (normal/foreign users; deposit, withdraw ≤ 1,00,000 per transaction, ≤ 3,00,000 and ≤ 5 withdrawals per day; quarterly interest; 2 % bonus per deposit once balance ≥ 20,00,000; foreign currency conversion): list the entity classes and draw the statechart of the most important one. (13)

Show solution

(a) State variable missed = consecutive unpaid months; paidMonths counts paid instalments (60 in 5 years).

● --purchasePolicy() / paidMonths := 0; missed := 0--> (Regular)
(Regular)   --payInstalment(5000) / paidMonths++--> (Regular)
(Regular)   --monthEnds [not paid] / missed := 1--> (Defaulter)
(Defaulter) --monthEnds [not paid && missed < 5] / missed++--> (Defaulter)
(Defaulter) --monthEnds [not paid && missed = 5] / missed := 6--> (Cancelled) --> ◉
(Defaulter) --payDues(missed x (5000 + 500)) / paidMonths += missed; missed := 0--> (Regular)
(Regular)   --when [paidMonths = 60] / payCustomer(350000)--> (Matured) --> ◉
(Regular), (Defaulter) --customerDies / payNominee(350000)--> (Claim Settled) --> ◉

(b) 

● --purchase() / package(); addToDatabase()--> (Available for Rent)
(Available) --checkOut(customer) / dueDate := today + 3--> (Rented)
(Rented)    --return() [not damaged]--> (Available)
(Rented)    --return() [damaged] / removeFromDatabase()--> (Removed)
(Rented)    --after [3 days] [not returned] / callCustomer()--> (Overdue 1)
(Overdue 1) --after [2 days] [not returned] / callCustomer()--> (Overdue 2)
(Overdue 2) --after [2 days] [not returned] / sendToCollectionAgency(); removeFromDatabase()--> (Removed)
(Overdue 1), (Overdue 2) --return() [not damaged]--> (Available) ; --return() [damaged] / remove--> (Removed)
(Available) --annualInventory [missing] / removeFromDatabase()--> (Removed) --> ◉

(c) Entity classes: User {abstract} ← NormalUser, ForeignUser; Account; Transaction ← Deposit, Withdrawal, CurrencyConversion; InterestPosting/BonusRule (or attributes of Account). The most important entity is Account (all rules change its state).

● --createAccount() / balance := 0; withdrawalsToday := 0; withdrawnToday := 0--> [Open]
[Open] has two concurrent regions:
 Balance tier: (Normal) --deposit(a) [balance + a >= 2,000,000]--> (Premium)   entry/ (none)
               (Premium) --deposit(a) / balance += 1.02 a  (2 % bonus)--> (Premium)
               (Premium) --withdraw(a) [balance - a < 2,000,000]--> (Normal)
               (Normal)  --deposit(a) [balance + a < 2,000,000] / balance += a--> (Normal)
 Daily limit:  (Can Withdraw) --withdraw(a) [a <= 100,000 && withdrawnToday + a <= 300,000 && balance >= a]
                    / balance -= a; withdrawnToday += a; withdrawalsToday++--> (Can Withdraw)
               (Can Withdraw) --when [withdrawalsToday = 5 || withdrawnToday = 300,000]--> (Daily Limit Reached)
               (Daily Limit Reached) --dayEnds / withdrawalsToday := 0; withdrawnToday := 0--> (Can Withdraw)
[Open]: internal transition  after [3 months] / balance += interest()
[Open] --closeAccount() [balance = 0]--> ◉

Exam approach

  1. Pick the object (customer, tape, account) — its life cycle is the diagram.
  2. List states as adjectives/conditions (Regular, Defaulter, Rented, Overdue).
  3. For each state ask: which events can happen here? where do they lead? write event [guard] / action.
  4. Use counters in guards for 'n times' rules; use after [t] for time rules; use concurrent regions for independent rules.
  5. Add initial and final states and check every state has a way out.

Exam focus

These are the diagram questions AI Sir set in CSE 325. They use the same notations as this note file, so practise them after the lessons above. Draw the diagram first, then check it against the solution.

2018-19 Q4(a) / 2020-21 Q4(a) — Inventory: states of a product (22 / 12)

Two concurrent views of a product: its stock level (one per product) and the life of an issued unit.

[Product] — region STOCK LEVEL

 (Reorder Requested) --goodsReceived(n) / stock += n [stock >= threshold]--> (In Stock)

[Product unit] — region ISSUED UNIT
 ● --> (Available) --requisitionApproved--> (Ready to Issue) --issue(employee)--> (Issued)

 (Return Pending) --returned / stock += 1--> (Available)

sections.html:
Revision points for Lessons 13–15.

L13 · Basics

  • Label: event(args) [guard] / action. entry/, exit/, do/, include/.
  • Events: change (when), call (operation), signal (async), elapsed-time (after).
  • Campaign: Commissioned → Active → Completed → Paid, guards on paymentDue − payment.

L14 · Nested & concurrent

  • Composite state, inner initial state; dashed line between concurrent regions.
  • Enter composite = enter all regions; leave composite = leave all; fork/join bars.
  • Behavioural approach (8 steps) vs life-cycle approach.

L15 · Worked

  • Garage: NoCentralControl / CentrallyControlled (Manual, Automatic) ‖ sign Full/NotFull.
  • Insurance: Regular ↔ Defaulter (missed counter) → Cancelled at 6; Matured; Claim Settled.

sections.title: Lesson 16 — Sequence Diagram Notation
sections.html:
A sequence diagram is an interaction diagram that models one scenario of a use case: which messages are sent, between which objects, and in what order (sl. 1). Horizontal axis = participants; vertical axis = time, downward (sl. 2). The scenario usually starts with an unattached 'found message' from the actor.

ElementNotationSlide
Object / participantbox with underlined name:Class (name optional: :Client)sl. 4
Lifelinedashed vertical line under the box — the object's life during the scenariosl. 4
Synchronous messagesolid line, filled arrowhead; caller waitssl. 5
Asynchronous messagesolid line, open (stick) arrowhead; caller continuessl. 5
Return messagedashed line, open arrowheadsl. 5
Activationthin rectangle on the lifeline while the method is on the stack; nest it for self-callssl. 6
Creationarrow labelled new / «create» to a box drawn lower downsl. 7
DeletionX at the end of the lifelinesl. 7
Framesopt [cond] (if), alt [cond] / [else] separated by a dashed line (if/else), loop [cond]sl. 8

Worked example — check email (sl. 3)

Actor  :Client                      :Server
 |-- checkEmail -->|                            (found message)
 |                 |-- sendUnsentEmail -------->|
 |                 |<-- response (ack) ---------|
 |                 |-- newEmail --------------->|
 |                 |<-- response ---------------|
 |                 |-- [newEmail] getEmail ---->|          (guarded message)
 |                 |-- deleteOldEmail --------->|

Practice — Lesson 16

(a) Actual — 2011-12 Q2(c).

(a) What are the different types of messages in a sequence diagram? Discuss them briefly with examples. (12)

Show solution

(a) Six message kinds, each with arrow and example:

MessageArrowExample
Synchronous (call)solid line, filled head; sender blocks until return:ATM → :Bank : verifyPIN(pin)
Asynchronous (signal)solid line, open head; sender continues:WordProcessor →> :PrintSpooler : print(file)
Return / replydashed line, open head:Bank - -> :ATM : ok
Createdashed/solid arrow «create» / new to the new object's box:Handler → :Query : new
Destroymessage ending in X on the target lifeline:Session → :Cart : «destroy»
Self (reflexive)arrow back to the same lifeline, nested activation:Order → :Order : computeTotal()
Found / lostfound: from a filled dot (unknown sender); lost: to a dot (never arrives)found: checkEmail from the user

sections.title: Lesson 17 — From a Use Case to a Sequence Diagram
sections.html:
1. The Register use case (sl. 1–3)

Typical course of events (17 steps): student opens the registration interface, the system asks for id and password, shows unfinished courses, the student selects courses, the system checks prerequisites (deselecting failed ones), checks total credit hours, notifies the adviser, who views details and authorises; the system updates the registration and prints the course card.

The sequence diagrams use boundary objects (:MainMenuUI, :RegisterUI), a control object (:Register) and entity objects (:Student, :Course, :RegInfo). Diagram 1 (sl. 2): itemSelected() → [selectedItem = register] Register() creates the control, RegisterUI(), showLogin(), login(id, pw) → verifyLogin(id, pw) → Student() / getStudentInfo(id); [pwAccepted = false] showLogin(). Diagram 2 (sl. 3): [pwAccepted = true] getCourseList(), getRegInfo(id), prepareUnfinishedCourseList(), showCourseList(*Courses); loop selectCourse(Cid) → checkPreRequisite() → [PRcompleted = true] / addToList(RegInfo) or showError(type); showConfirmation(type).

sl. 4 (printer): CustomerP → PrinterP : PrintFile; PrinterP → Printer : GetStatus; branching [Ready] Print, [Busy] PutInQueue, [OutOfService] CallRepair; asynchronous Ready(file) / GetNext from the queue. sl. 5: 'Add a new advert to a campaign' with loop frames and creation of newAd:Advert.

Exam approach

  1. Number the narrative into steps; each verb between two parties becomes one message.
  2. Choose participants left to right: actor, boundary (UI), control, entities, external systems.
  3. Use alt for if/else (e.g. limit exceeded), opt for optional steps, loop for repetition.
  4. Show activations, returns of important values and creations (new).

sections.title: Lesson 18 — Collaboration (Communication) Diagrams
sections.html:
1. What they are (Lec 9 sl. 6)

  • Hold the same information as sequence diagrams, but show the links between the objects.
  • There is no time axis; order is given by sequence numbers on the messages.
  • Numbers are nested (3, 3.1, 3.1.1) to show which message is sent while handling which.

Register collaboration diagram (sl. 7): RegisterUI, AuthorizeRegistrationUI (boundaries), Register (control), Student, RegistrationInfo, Result, Course (entities); messages 2 showLogin(), 3 login(), 4 verifyLogin(), 7 showCourseList(), 8 selectCourse(), 9 verifyPreReq(), 10 getResult(), 11 showPRError(), 12–13 finalize(), 14a/14b showRegInfo()/showTCError(), 15–16 authorize(), 18 updateRegInfo()/showConfirmation(). Concurrent alternatives use letters (14a, 14b).

2. Model consistency (sl. 8)

Every operation in a message must exist in the receiver's class with the same signature, and the sender must hold a reference to the receiver — through an association, or because another object passed it.

3. Additional examples (Lec 10, scanned)

  • Add a new campaign: 1 *getClient(), 2 startInterface(), 3 selectClient(), 4 showClientCampaigns(), 5 getClientCampaigns(), 6–7 createNewCampaign(), 8 createCampaign(), 9 addNewCampaign().
  • Assign staff contact: getClient(), getStaffDetails(), selectClient(), assignStaffContact() forwarded to Client.
  • Check campaign budget: nested numbering 3.1, 3.1.1, 3.1.2, 4.1, 4.1.1, 4.1.1.1 *getCost(), 4.1.1.2 getOverheads().
  • Record completion: 4.1.2 printCompletionForm() on :CompleteCampaignPI; Add a new advert: 5.1.1.1 creates the Advert. Slide 7 gives the equivalent sequence diagram.

Practice — Lesson 18

(a) Actual — 2014-15 Q7(c). (b) Actual — 2012-13 Q6(a). (c) Actual — 2012-13 Q5(c). (d) Actual — 2010-11 Q1(a).

(a) Explain two different types of interaction diagrams with example. (9⅔)

(b) Grocery sales system collaboration diagram for creating an invoice: 1: InvoiceNo := NewInvoice(); 2: SearchProduct(query); 2.1: searchProduct(query); 3: SelectProduct(pcode, qty); 3.1: GetPrice(pcode); 3.2: [product available] CalcAmount(qty, price); 4: SaveInvoice(); 4.1: SaveInvoice(); 4.1.1: UpdateQuantity(pcode, qty) among :Cashier, :CreateInvoice, :Invoice, :Product. (i) Draw the sequence diagram (ii) add stereotypes (iii) give the UML class Invoice with everything the diagram implies. (10+2+4)

(c) A word processor (active object) creates a print file and asynchronously asks a print spooler (active object) to print it; the spooler repeatedly reads a block and sends it to the printer (active object) by procedure call. Draw the collaboration diagram and an activity diagram of the print-file operation. (9)

(d) Check Out Books use case (worker, patron, books, due date by faculty/student, non-circulating books): draw a relatively complete collaboration diagram and class diagram with associations. (24⅔)

Show solution

(a) Sequence diagram — time-ordered, lifelines and activations; best for showing the order and timing of messages (e.g. check email, sl. 3 of Lec 8). Collaboration (communication) diagram — objects and links in space, messages numbered 1, 1.1, 2 …; best for showing which objects are connected (e.g. Register, Lec 9 sl. 7). Both are semantically equivalent; tools can convert one into the other.

(b)(i) From the numbers: 2.1 is sent by :CreateInvoice to :Product while handling 2, etc.

:Cashier            :CreateInvoice «control»       :Invoice «entity»        :Product «entity»
 |--1: NewInvoice()-------->|
 |<--InvoiceNo--------------|
 |--2: SearchProduct(query)->|--2.1: searchProduct(query)------------------------>|
 |--3: SelectProduct(pcode,qty)->|--3.1: GetPrice(pcode)----------------------------->|
 |                          |<--price--------------------------------------------|
 |                          |--3.2: [product available] CalcAmount(qty, price)-->|  (on :Invoice)
 |--4: SaveInvoice()------->|--4.1: SaveInvoice()------>|
 |                          |                           |--4.1.1: UpdateQuantity(pcode, qty)-->|

(ii) :Cashier is the actor (or «boundary» if it is the cashier's screen); :CreateInvoice «control»; :Invoice «entity»; :Product «entity».

(iii) Only what the diagram shows: Invoice receives CalcAmount(qty, price) and SaveInvoice(), and sends UpdateQuantity to Product (so Invoice is associated with Product); NewInvoice() returns an InvoiceNo.

+-------------------------------------------+
|              Invoice «entity»             |
+-------------------------------------------+
| invoiceNo                                 |
| amount (computed by CalcAmount)           |
+-------------------------------------------+
| + CalcAmount(qty, price)                  |
| + SaveInvoice()                           |
+-------------------------------------------+
Invoice * ---- * Product   (Invoice sends UpdateQuantity(pcode, qty) to Product)

(c) Active objects are drawn with a thick border; the asynchronous message has a half (stick) arrowhead.

COLLABORATION DIAGRAM
 [:WordProcessor] (active) ---1: «create»---> [:PrintFile]
 [:WordProcessor] ---2: print(file)  (asynchronous)---> [:PrintSpooler] (active)
 [:PrintSpooler]  ---2.1 *[until end of file]: readBlock()---> [:PrintFile]
 [:PrintSpooler]  ---2.2 *[for each block]: printBlock(block)  (procedure call)---> [:Printer] (active)

ACTIVITY DIAGRAM — print file operation
 ● -> (Create print file) -> (Request spooler to print) -> (Read next block) -> <block read?>
      [yes] -> (Send block to printer) -> back to (Read next block)
      [end of file] -> (Close print file) -> ◉

Worker --1: identifyPatron(patronId)--> [:CheckOutUI] --1.1: checkOutStart(patronId)--> [:CheckOutController]
[:CheckOutController] --1.2: p := findPatron(patronId)--> [:PatronCatalog] ; --1.3: allowed := canBorrow()--> [p:Patron]
   1.4a [not allowed]: showProhibition(reason) --> [:CheckOutUI]
*[for each book]  2: enterBook(bookId) --> [:CheckOutController]
   2.1: c := findCopy(bookId) --> [:BookCatalog] ;  2.2: circ := canCirculate() --> [c:Copy]
   2.3a [not circ]: showNonCirculating() --> [:CheckOutUI]
   2.3b [circ]: due := calcDueDate(p.type) (self) ; 2.4: new Loan(p, c, due) --> [l:Loan]
   2.5: markCheckedOut() --> [c:Copy]  ;  2.6: showDueDate(due) --> [:CheckOutUI]
3: done() --> [:CheckOutController]
Class diagram

sections.title: Lesson 19 — UML Overview, Actors, Use Cases and Their Relationships
sections.html:
1. UML (sl. 1–2)

UML = Unified Modeling Language: an international industry-standard graphical notation for describing software analysis and design — pictures (views) of an OO system. Diagrams listed: use case, class, sequence, collaboration, statechart, object, activity, component, deployment.

Static (structure)Dynamic (behaviour)
Class, Object, Component, Deployment, Package, Composite structureUse case, Activity, State machine (statechart), Sequence, Communication (collaboration), Timing, Interaction overview
Note

Textbook background for older questions. Four kinds of things in UML: structural things (class, interface, use case, component, node), behavioural things (interaction, state machine), grouping things (package), annotational things (note). Extensibility mechanisms: stereotypes («entity», «include»), tagged values ({version = 2.1}) and constraints ({ordered}, {balance ≥ 0}). Behavioural diagrams: use case (functions from the user's view), activity (workflow), state machine (life of one object), and the interaction diagrams sequence / communication / timing / interaction overview (message exchange).

2. Use cases, actors, stakeholders (sl. 3–7)

  • A use case is a sequence of actions a system performs that yields a valuable result for a particular actor — a scenario-based description of how the system interacts with its environment.
  • Actor: anything with behaviour outside the system that acts on it — a human role, a hardware device, an external system, or time. Drawn as a stick figure with its name. A single actor may represent many people.
  • Primary actor initiates the interaction to achieve a goal; supporting actor performs sub-goals; a stakeholder is anyone interested in the system and may never act in a scenario.
  • Finding actors (sl. 5): who is interested, where is it used, who benefits, who supplies/uses/removes information, does one person play several roles (one actor per role), do several people play the same role (one actor).

3. Diagram elements and relationships (sl. 8–15)

ElementNotationRule / example
Use caseellipse with a verb–noun nameone function, may contain several scenarios (paths): Make appointment
Associationplain line (or double-headed arrow) actor — use casecommunication; Patient — Make appointment
System boundaryrectangle around the use cases, actors outsidedefines scope; may be one module of an ERP
Generalisationline with hollow triangle from child to parentNew Patient, Old Patient → Patient; Make new/old patient appt → Make appointment
«extend»dashed arrow from the extension to the baseoptional behaviour: Update patient information ··> Make appointment
«include»dashed arrow from the base to the included use casemandatory reused behaviour: Manage schedule ··> Record availability
Trap

Directions: «include» points to the use case that is always executed as part of the base; «extend» points to the base it may optionally extend. (Slide 14's picture draws the include arrow from Record availability to Manage schedule; slide 14's text and standard UML say base → included. Follow the text and say so.) Old papers call «include» 'uses'.

Practice — Lesson 19

(a) Actual — 2013-14 Q1(c). (b) Actual — 2014-15 Q5(c). (c) Actual — 2013-14 Q5(b) / 2012-13 Q7(d). (d) Actual — 2016-17 Q1(a). (e) Actual — 2010-11 Q1(b).

(a) Define extends and uses relationships in use case diagrams with real-life examples. (7⅔)

(b) What types of UML diagrams exist? Name each, give its purpose, classify as static or dynamic. (10)

(c) What are the (four) kinds of things in UML? (12 / 4⅔)

(d) Discuss some extensibility mechanisms of UML. (12)

(e) List all behavioral UML diagrams and describe the purpose of each. (8)

Show solution

(a) «extend» (extends): optional or conditional behaviour inserted into a base use case at an extension point; the base is complete without it; arrow from extension to base. Example (ATM): (Print receipt) ··«extend»··> (Withdraw cash) — only if the customer asks. «include» (uses): behaviour common to several use cases factored out and always executed; arrow from base to included. Example: (Withdraw cash) ··«include»··> (Authenticate user) and (Transfer funds) ··«include»··> (Authenticate user).

(b) Table in §1 plus one-line purpose each: class — static structure; object — snapshot of instances; component — physical modules; deployment — hardware nodes and artifacts; package — grouping; use case — functionality from the users' view; activity — workflow/business process; state machine — life cycle of one object; sequence — time-ordered messages; communication — messages over links; timing — state changes over time.

(c) Structural, behavioural, grouping, annotational things (NOTE above), each with two examples.

(d) Stereotypes — new model element kinds derived from existing ones, shown «name» or with an icon («interface», «entity», «include»); tagged values — name=value properties attached to elements ({author = Rahim}, {version = 1.2}); constraints — conditions in braces, possibly in OCL ({ordered}, {ward.gender = patient.gender}). Profiles bundle them for a domain.

(e) Use case, activity, state machine, sequence, communication (collaboration), timing, interaction overview — purpose of each as in (b).

sections.title: Lesson 21 — BPMN Core: Events, Activities, Gateways
sections.html:
1. Core elements (sl. 1, 8)

ElementSymbolMeaning
Activity (task)rounded rectanglework done: verb + noun ('Check stock availability')
Start eventthin circle ○trigger; creates a token (token source)
End eventthick circle ◎outcome; consumes the token (token sink)
Gatewaydiamond ◇split or join of the flow
Sequence flowsolid arroworder of activities

2. Worked example — order-to-cash (sl. 2–7, 13)

Narrative: triggered by receipt of a purchase order; check stock; confirm or reject; if confirmed, emit invoice and ship goods; finish by archiving the order (or when rejected).

○ Purchase order received -> [Check stock availability] -> <X>
     <X> [items not in stock] -> [Reject order] -> ◎ Order rejected
     <X> [items in stock]     -> [Confirm order] -> <+> -> [Emit invoice] ---> <+> -> [Archive order] -> ◎ Order fulfilled
                                                  <+> -> [Ship goods]  ---> <+>

3. Gateways (sl. 9–18)

GatewaySplitJoinExample
XOR ◇ with ×takes exactly one branch (labelled conditions; optional default flow)proceeds when one incoming branch completesinvoice checking: post / re-send / block (sl. 10)
AND ◇ with +takes all branches (parallel)waits for all incoming branchesairport: security screening ‖ luggage screening (sl. 12)
OR ◇ with ○takes one or more branches by conditionwaits for all active branchesorder distribution: Amsterdam and/or Hamburg (sl. 17–18)

Order distribution without OR (sl. 14–16): Solution 1 = XOR with three branches (only Amsterdam, only Hamburg, both → AND split/join); Solution 2 = AND split with an XOR 'skip' on each branch. The OR gateway (sl. 18) expresses it in one split/join pair.

Trap

Beginner's mistake (sl. 19): pairing an XOR split with an AND join deadlocks — the AND join waits forever for the branch that was not taken. Also, two activities on parallel branches need not run at the same time; they are only independent.

4. Naming guidelines (sl. 20)

  1. Name every event and task.
  2. Task = verb + business object (+ complement): Issue driver licence.
  3. Message event = object + past participle: Invoice received, Claim settled.
  4. Avoid generic verbs: Handle, Record …
  5. Label every XOR-split branch with a condition: Policy is invalid.

sections.title: Lesson 22 — BPMN Pools, Lanes, Message Flows and Artifacts
sections.html:
• Pool (sl. 21): a resource class — usually a business party (a whole company). Lane: a sub-class inside a pool — department (Sales, Warehouse), role (Manager), or software system (ERP). Lanes can be nested.
  • Message flow (sl. 23): dashed line with open arrowhead between pools; to the pool boundary = informative message, to an activity/event = message that triggers it.
  • Syntactic rules (sl. 25): sequence flow cannot cross pool boundaries (message flow can); both may cross lanes; a message flow cannot connect two elements in the same pool.
  • Data object (sl. 28): artifact required or produced by an activity, with state in brackets (Purchase order [approved]). Data store: persistent storage (Warehouse DB, Orders DB). Text annotation (sl. 29): open bracket joined by a dotted line; does not affect token flow.

Practice — Lesson 22

(a) Constructed (likely TF form). (b) Constructed.

(a) Model in BPMN: a student submits an online course-drop request; the advisor reviews it; if rejected the student is notified; if approved, the accounts office computes the refund while the registrar updates the record, then the student is notified. Use pools/lanes and gateways.

(b) Why must an XOR-split not be closed by an AND-join? Give the fix.

Show solution
Pool Student (black box)  ··drop request··> Pool University
Pool University, lanes: Advisor | Accounts | Registrar | System
 Advisor:   ○ Drop request received -> [Review drop request] -> <X>
            <X> [request rejected] -> [Notify rejection] -> ◎ Request rejected   ··rejection··> Student pool
            <X> [request approved] -> <+>
 Accounts:  <+> -> [Compute refund] ------------> <+>
 Registrar: <+> -> [Update academic record] ----> <+>
 System:    <+> (join) -> [Notify student of drop] -> ◎ Course dropped          ··confirmation··> Student pool
 Data: Drop request [submitted] -> Review ; Student record (data store) <- Update academic record

(b) The XOR split passes the token to only one branch; an AND join waits for a token on every incoming branch, so it never fires — deadlock. Close an XOR split with an XOR join (or use AND split + AND join if both branches must run).

sections.title: Quick Notes — Use Cases and BPMN
sections.html:
Revision points for Lessons 19–22.

L19 · Use case basics

  • Actor = role outside the system (human, device, system, time); stakeholder may never act.
  • Association line; boundary box; generalisation ▷; «include» base → included (always); «extend» extension → base (optional).
  • UML things: structural, behavioural, grouping, annotational; extensibility: stereotypes, tagged values, constraints.

L20 · Worked

  • Narrative: actor, precondition, main flow, alternate flows (2a…), postcondition.
  • Mentcare: criminal as misuser actor; Guess password extends Log on.

L21 · BPMN core

  • ○ start, ◎ end, rounded task, ◇ gateway, arrow sequence flow.
  • XOR = one branch; AND = all; OR = some, join waits for active ones. XOR split + AND join = deadlock.

L22 · Pools

  • Pool = party; lane = department/role/system; message flow only between pools.
  • Data object [state], data store, annotation.

sections.title: Lesson 23 — Testing Basics: V&V, Fault Terms, Black Box vs White Box
sections.html:
1. Quality-control techniques (sl. 1)

Fault avoidance prevents errors before release (reviews, inspections, walkthroughs, methodologies, testing, verification). Fault tolerance lets the system recover by itself (rollbacks, redundancy, mirroring).

2. Verification and validation (sl. 2)

VerificationValidation
QuestionAre we building the product right?Are we building the right product?
Checksproducts of a phase satisfy the conditions set at the start of that phasethe system satisfies the specified requirements (user needs)
Howtesting, reviews, inspectionscomparison against requirements, acceptance testing

3. Mistake, fault, failure, error (sl. 3–4)

TermMeaningfactorial(int a) example
Mistakehuman action producing an incorrect resultprogrammer did not consider a < 1
Fault / defectincorrect step, process or data definition in the programmissing input validation
Failureinability to perform the required function within the performance requirementoverflow / crash / infinite recursion
Errordifference between computed and correct valueexception or wrong output instead of an error message
int factorial(int a) {
    if (a == 1) return 1;          // a = 0 or a < 0 recurses forever -> stack overflow
    return a * factorial(a - 1);
}

4. Goals (sl. 5–7)

Testing = analysing a software item to detect differences between existing and required conditions (bugs) and to evaluate its features. Test throughout development. Goal: write test cases that cause failures — as few as possible, without two tests causing the same failure. Testing cannot guarantee all faults are found.

5. Black box vs white box (sl. 8–13)

Black boxWhite box
Basisspecification only: inputs → outputs; internals unknowninternal structure: paths, conditions, loops, branches
Advantagesnot influenced by the code; robust to implementation changes; independent testers; good for validationfinds boundaries inside the code; yields useful tests; examines data structures; good for verification
Disadvantagesmisses bugs not covered by the spec (control-flow details, optimisations, alternate algorithms)tests can share the implementation's bugs; impossible to exercise all paths (exhaustive testing explodes)
Exam-ready answer

Exhaustive testing is nearly impossible (2014-15 Q2(a)): a function with two 32-bit int inputs has 264 ≈ 1.8 × 1019 input pairs; at 109 tests per second that is about 585 years. A loop that runs up to 20 times with 5 paths per iteration has Σ 5k (k = 1…20) ≈ 1014 paths. Hence we choose representative tests (EP, BVA, coverage).

Practice — Lesson 23

(a) Actual — 2017-18 Q8(a). (b) Actual — 2012-13 Q4(d) / 2010-11 Q6(c). (c) Actual — 2021-22 Q3(c). (d) Actual — 2013-14 Q3(b).

(a) Advantages and disadvantages of black-box testing; discuss performance and regression testing. (4+8)

(b) Differentiate verification and validation; defect testing and debugging. What I/O faults would you check in a banking transaction module? (6 / 7)

(c) 'It costs less to fix a bug found in the later stages of the SDLC' — agree? (5)

(d) Explain the debugging process with a diagram. (8)

Show solution

(a) Table §5 for black box. Performance (load) testing checks compliance with performance requirements (response time, throughput under expected load); regression testing re-runs a selected subset of tests after a change to make sure nothing that worked is broken (Lesson 24).

(b) V&V — table §2. Defect testing aims to reveal that a defect exists (a failing test); debugging locates and removes the fault that caused the failure, then re-tests. Banking I/O faults: negative or zero amount, amount with too many decimals, non-numeric input, account number of wrong length / nonexistent, withdrawal above balance or limit, wrong currency, output rounding errors, balance not updated or updated twice.

(c) Disagree. The later a bug is found, the more work products depend on it: a requirement error found in maintenance forces changes to design, code, tests and documentation and re-deployment. Studies (Boehm) give relative costs of roughly 1 (requirements) : 5 (design) : 10 (coding) : 20–50 (testing) : 100+ (after release). That is why reviews and testing start early (shift-left).

(d) Execute test cases → results compared with expected → failure observed → suspected causes → additional tests / instrumentation → identified cause → correction → regression tests. Approaches: brute force (print/dump), backtracking (from symptom back through the code), cause elimination (binary partition of the input or code).

sections.title: Lesson 24 — Six Types of Testing, Integration Order, Performance Tests
sections.html:
TypeWhatWho / box
Unitindividual units or small groups; code does what it is intended to at a low structural levelprogrammer; white box; automated
Integrationcombined components tested for their interaction — units that work alone may fail togetherprogrammers while integrating; mostly white box
Non-functional (system)complete system vs specified requirements: stress (beyond limits), performance/load (meets performance requirements), usability (learn, input, interpret outputs)external test group; mostly black box
Acceptanceformal test against acceptance criteria so the customer can accept or rejectcustomer, in their environment; black box
Regressionselective re-testing after modification: representative sample + tests most likely affected. Smoke test = small subset showing the system is stable and major functions workany; re-run often
Betafree advance version to real users who report errors. + unexpected errors, low cost, wide environments; − not systematic, low-quality reportsexternal users

Test plan (sl. 22): document of scope, approach, resources and schedule — test items, features, tasks, who tests, risks needing contingency. Write it early.

1. Integration strategies (textbook)

StrategyOrderNeeds
Big bangall at oncenothing — but faults are hard to locate
Top-downfrom the main module downward (depth-first or breadth-first)stubs for lower modules not yet integrated
Bottom-upfrom leaf modules upward in clustersdrivers to call the cluster
Sandwichtop-down for upper levels, bottom-up for lowerboth

Stub = dummy called module that returns canned answers. Driver = dummy calling program that feeds inputs and checks outputs. Unit-test environment (2014-15 Q2(d)) = driver + module under test + stubs, plus test cases and results.

Internal vs external integration (2022-23 Q1(c)): internal = between components of our own system; external = between our system and third-party systems/APIs.

Practice — Lesson 24

(a) Actual — 2021-22 Q3(b). (b) Actual — 2022-23 Q1(c). (c) Actual — 2024-25 Q6(c). (d) Actual — 2013-14 Q3(a) / 2011-12 Q8(d). (e) Actual — 2019-20 Q8(b) / 2017-18 Q7(a). (f) Actual — 2024-25 Q7(a). (g) Actual — 2020-21 Q8(c). (h) Actual — 2011-12 Q7(a). (i) Actual — 2019-20 Q5(b).

(a) Briefly discuss the six types of testing. (10)

(b) Construct an example of internal and of external integration testing for a ride-sharing app. (10)

(c) Smart temperature system: Display Panel (top), Temperature Controller (middle, still under development), Sensor (low). Display and Sensor are ready. How do you integration-test? (10)

(d) Show the order of module tests for top-down integration (stubs and drivers) of a tree ROOT → M1, M2, M3; M1 → M4 → M8, M9; M2 → M5, M6; M3 → M7 (depth-first). (9⅔ / 10)

(e) Spec: 100 simultaneous users. The app failed at 90 users, then crashed at 150. Which two tests would have caught these? Also: load vs stress testing for BIIS; is code review black-box testing? (6 / 15)

(f) Course registration risks: burst to 10,000 students when registration opens; collapse when load exceeds capacity; slowdown after 8 h. For each give the performance-test type, its goal, and a JMeter configuration (threads, loop count, ramp-up, duration). (15)

(g) Smoke vs regression testing with an example. (8)

(h) Online stock-trading tests — unit, integration or system: (i) quotes within 3 s for 200 simultaneous users (ii) server accepts an order only with sufficient funds (iii) client refuses non-existent stocks (iv) order with sufficient funds is eventually executed (v) removed account cannot order. (10)

(i) ERP HRM (employment record, promotion, payroll & loan, disciplinary action, pension) interacting with Accounts; a suspended employee gets half salary, refunded if proved innocent. Give 4 inter-component and 2 inter-module integration requirements. (15)

Show solution

(a) One line per row of the table: purpose, who, black/white box.

(b) Internal: Ride-request module → Matching service → Fare calculator: a request from Gulshan to Banani must produce a matched driver and a fare computed with the right distance. External: our Payment module ↔ bKash/card gateway (payment success/failure callbacks), Maps API (route and ETA returned for the given coordinates), SMS gateway (OTP delivered).

(c) The missing module is in the middle, so use a sandwich approach with a stub and a driver: (1) Display + stub of the Controller that returns canned processed values ('25 °C', 'warning: 45 °C') — checks display and warnings. (2) Sensor + driver that plays the Controller's role: calls readTemperature() and checks the raw values/format. (3) When the Controller is ready, replace stub and driver: Sensor → Controller → Display, and re-run both sets as regression tests.

(d) Depth-first top-down: test ROOT with stubs S1, S2, S3; replace S1 by M1 (stub S4); M4 (stubs S8, S9); M8; M9; then M2 (stubs S5, S6); M5; M6; then M3 (stub S7); M7. Order of integration: ROOT, M1, M4, M8, M9, M2, M5, M6, M3, M7 — after each step re-run the earlier tests. Drivers are not needed in top-down (the real parent calls the module); they are needed only in bottom-up.

(e) Failure at 90 (< 100 users): load (performance) testing at the specified 100 users would have revealed it. Crash at 150: stress testing beyond the specified limit would show how it fails and whether it recovers gracefully. BIIS: load = 2,000 students checking results at the expected peak; stress = 10,000 at once until it breaks. Code review is not black-box testing — it is a static white-box technique: reviewers read the source code; nothing is executed.

RiskTest typeGoalJMeter (threads · ramp-up · loop · duration)
Burst to 10,000 at openingSpike testsudden jump in users: response time, errors, recovery10,000 threads · ramp-up 10 s · loop 1 (or 5) · 5 min
Collapse beyond capacityStress testfind the breaking point and failure mode beyond capacitystep 2,000 → 20,000 threads (Stepping/Ultimate Thread Group) · ramp-up 10 min · loop forever · 30 min
Slowdown after 8 hEndurance (soak) testmemory leaks, resource exhaustion under steady load1,500 threads · ramp-up 5 min · loop forever · 8–10 h

(g) Smoke: a small, fast subset run on every new build to decide whether it is stable enough to test (login, search, add to cart, checkout open). Regression: a larger selection re-run after a change to make sure existing features still work (after changing the discount code, re-run all cart, pricing and checkout tests). Smoke is wide and shallow; regression is deep on what the change may affect.

(h) (i) system (performance with the whole system) · (ii) unit test of the ordering server's validation, then integration with the account database · (iii) unit test of the client (input validation), and integration if the stock list comes from the server · (iv) integration (order server + accounts + external price server) and system · (v) integration (account DB ↔ ordering server) and system.

(i) Inter-component: (1) Disciplinary Action → Payroll: suspension sets salary to 50 % from the suspension date; (2) Disciplinary Action → Payroll: proved innocent → withheld 50 % paid back as arrears; (3) Promotion → Employment Record & Payroll: new grade updates the record and the salary scale; (4) Payroll ↔ Loan: monthly loan instalment deducted from salary, loan balance updated; (also Employment Record → Pension: service length). Inter-module: (1) Payroll → Accounts: monthly salary journal posted (expense, bank) including half-salary during suspension and later arrears; (2) Pension / Loan → Accounts: pension and loan disbursements and recoveries posted to the right ledgers.

sections.title: Lesson 25 — Code Coverage Criteria
sections.html:
Code coverage = degree to which the source code is executed by a test suite. High coverage → more thoroughly tested → lower chance of hidden bugs (sl. 1).

CriterionQuestion (sl. 2)
Method coverageHave all methods been called?
Statement coverageHave all statements been executed?
Decision / branch coverageHas every decision taken both its true and false outcome?
Condition coverageHas every individual condition (atomic boolean) been both true and false?

Worked example — getTriangle (sl. 3–6)

String getTriangle(int a, int b, int c) {
  D1: if (a == b && b == c) { success(); return "Equilateral"; }     // conditions C1: a==b, C2: b==c
  D2: if (a == b || b == c || c == a) return "Isosceles";           // C3: a==b, C4: b==c, C5: c==a
      return "Scalene";
}
Test (a,b,c)C1C2D1C3C4C5D2Result
(1,1,2)TFFT––TIsosceles
(2,2,2)TTTEquilateral
(2,2,3)TFFT––TIsosceles
(1,2,2)F–FFT–TIsosceles
(2,1,2)F–FFFTTIsosceles
(2,3,4)F–FFFFFScalene
  • Method (sl. 3): (1,1,2) and (2,2,2) — getTriangle and success() both called.
  • Condition (sl. 4): (2,2,3), (2,2,2), (1,2,2), (2,1,2) — every C1…C5 is T at least once and F at least once (C5 is never F here under short-circuit; the slide counts C3–C5 by whether each was T/F when evaluated).
  • Branch (sl. 5) and statement (sl. 6): add (2,3,4) so that D2 is false and 'return "Scalene"' runs.
  • Hierarchy: branch coverage ⇒ statement coverage; condition coverage does not imply branch coverage (combine them: condition/decision coverage).

Benefits, limitations, tools (sl. 7–8)

Benefit: measures completeness of tests and shows missed paths. Limits: high coverage ≠ correctness; tools only see the code that exists, not missing requirements; do not write tests just to please the tool. Tools: djUnit, EclEmma (instruction, block, line, method, type coverage), Clover.

Practice — Lesson 25

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q4(c). (b) Actual — 2020-21 Q6(b) / 2018-19 Q2(b). (c) Actual — 2023-24 Q5(c).

(a) something(int x) { if (x < 0 || y < x) { y := -y; x := -x; } z := x; } — show a minimal-length data set that achieves condition coverage. (8)

(b) Give an example test execution ensuring method, branch and condition coverage. What are the characteristics of good unit testing? (15)

(c) Why is high test coverage important? What risks arise if coverage is too low? (8)

Show solution

(a) Conditions: A = (x < 0), B = (y < x); y is an outer (global) variable, so it is part of the test data. Condition coverage: A and B must each be true once and false once.

TestxyA: x<0B: y<xDecision
T1-10TF (0 < -1 false)T
T210FT (0 < 1)T

Two tests achieve condition coverage if both operands are evaluated. Under short-circuit '||', B is not evaluated in T1, so add T3: x = 1, y = 5 (A = F, B = F, decision F) — 3 tests, which also give decision coverage. Minimal answer: {(−1, 0), (1, 0)} without short-circuit; {(−1, 0), (1, 0), (1, 5)} with it.

(b) Use getTriangle: method coverage {(1,1,2), (2,2,2)}; condition coverage {(2,2,3), (2,2,2), (1,2,2), (2,1,2)}; branch coverage = those + (2,3,4). Good unit tests (IJ Mam's Unit Testing deck): Automatic (no human input), Atomic (decides pass/fail itself), Single responsibility (one feature), Independent (runs in isolation), Repeatable (same result every run); also fast and with descriptive names.

(c) Importance: shows how much of the code the tests exercise; reveals untested paths, dead code and missing tests; gives confidence for refactoring and regression. Low coverage risks: bugs hidden in unexecuted branches (error handling, rare conditions) reach production; changes break untested code silently; security holes in unchecked input paths; poor estimate of quality. But 100 % coverage still cannot find missing requirements.

sections.title: Lesson 26 — White-Box Test Design: Basis Paths and Loop Testing
sections.html:
1. Basis path testing

  1. Draw the flow graph: nodes = statements/decision points, edges = control flow; a compound condition becomes one node per simple condition.
  2. Cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E − N + 2 = P + 1 (P = number of simple decisions) = number of regions.
  3. List V(G) linearly independent paths (each adds at least one new edge).
  4. Design one test case per path (input + expected output).
V(G) = E − N + 2 = P + 1

2. Loop testing

Loop typeTests (n = max passes)
Simple loopskip the loop; 1 pass; 2 passes; m passes (m < n); n − 1, n, n + 1 passes
Nested loopsstart at the innermost loop with outer loops at minimum; test it as a simple loop; work outward
Concatenatedindependent → as simple loops; dependent → as nested

Practice — Lesson 26

(a) Actual — 2023-24 Q3(b). (b) Actual — 2011-12 Q7(b). (c) Actual — 2012-13 Q4(c). (d) Actual — 2014-15 Q2(b) / 2013-14 Q3(d).

sections.title: Lesson 27 — Equivalence Partitioning, BVA, Positive and Negative Testing
sections.html:
1. Equivalence partitioning (sl. 1–4)

Divide the input domain into partitions whose values the software treats the same way; test one value per partition. If one value works, assume all in the partition work; if it fails, assume all fail.

PartitionBalanceInterest
1 invalid< 0undefined → exception
20 ≤ B < 10000.5 %
31000 ≤ B < 100000.75 %
410000 ≤ B1.0 %
// sl. 3 — how NOT to test: 0, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000 ... many values, only partitions 2 and 3 covered
// sl. 4 — one value per partition
try { calculateSavingsInterest(-1.0); fail("Exception expected"); } catch (Exception ex) { }
assertEquals(0.50,  calculateSavingsInterest(100.0));     // 100 x 0.5 %
assertEquals(15.0,  calculateSavingsInterest(2000.0));    // 2000 x 0.75 %
assertEquals(200.0, calculateSavingsInterest(20000.0));   // 20000 x 1 %

2. Boundary value analysis (sl. 5)

Most errors occur at partition boundaries, so test on and next to each boundary: −0.01 | 0, 0.01, 999.99 | 1000, 9999.99 | 10000.

Memorize

BVA for a closed range [a, b] of integers: a − 1, a, a + 1, (nominal), b − 1, b, b + 1. Weak ECT = enough tests that every class of every input appears once → max(classes per input). Strong ECT = every combination → product of the class counts.

3. Positive and negative testing (sl. 6–14)

Positive testing: valid input, the application must work and must not show an error (phone number 6184536032). Negative testing: invalid input, the application must handle it gracefully (xyZ#53()032). Typical negative scenarios:

  • required fields left empty (sl. 8)
  • data of the wrong type for the field (sl. 9)
  • more characters than allowed (sl. 10)
  • values outside the allowed bounds — day −1, month 13 (sl. 11)
  • values beyond the data type range — int −32,768…32,767 (2 bytes), ±2,147,483,647 (4 bytes), float ±3.4E+38 (sl. 12)
  • unreasonable data — 300-character name, age 200 (sl. 13)
  • web session — open URLs recorded while logged in after logging out (sl. 14)

Practice — Lesson 27

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q1(b). (b) Actual — 2024-25 Q7(b). (c) Actual — 2024-25 Q5(a). (d) Actual — 2023-24 Q1(c). (e) Actual — 2023-24 Q3(c) / 2013-14 Q3(e). (f) Actual — 2020-21 Q7(a) / 2018-19 Q3(a). (g) Actual — 2021-22 Q4(c). (h) Actual — 2020-21 Q5(b). (i) Actual — 2018-19 Q1(b).

(a) Test cases for income tax: 0 % below 4 lac, 10 % for 4–10 lac, 20 % above 10 lac. (10)

(b) Irrigation pump: OFF if M < 30, LOW if 30 ≤ M ≤ 70, HIGH if M > 70 (M integer). All BVA tests for the LOW partition. (10)

(c) Lab-section registration with independent inputs: credits C1 < 60, C2 60–99, C3 > 99, C4 invalid; CGPA G1 < 2.50, G2 2.50–3.49, G3 ≥ 3.50, G4 invalid; status S1 not approved, S2 approved, S3 invalid/missing. (i) minimal weak ECT suite (ii) number of strong ECT cases (iii) a defect the weak suite may miss. (15)

(d) Design test cases for your password policy (Mentcare). (10)

(e) Explain the principle of equivalence-partition testing. Why is it used in real software? (8 / 6⅔)

(f) GM entitled to one laptop (and two mobile phones) per year via a requisition app: positive and negative tests. (10 / 7)

(g) Five negative-testing ideas for a web application, with examples. (5)

(h) EP: test input set for whether the Release Order cost (size × rate × (1 − discount)) is computed properly. (12)

(i) EP: test input set for different user roles of BIIS. (12)

Show solution

(b) LOW partition 30 ≤ M ≤ 70. Boundary tests: 29 → OFF, 30 → LOW, 31 → LOW, 50 → LOW (nominal), 69 → LOW, 70 → LOW, 71 → HIGH. The two outside values check the neighbouring partitions; a robust set adds non-integer / missing reading → error.

Weak tests use C2 only with G2, so the C2 + G3 + S2 combination is never run and the bug escapes; similarly an invalid CGPA (G4) together with S1 might crash instead of reporting an error.

sections.title: Quick Notes — Software Testing
sections.html:
Revision points for Lessons 23–27.

L23 · Basics

  • Verification = built right; validation = right product.
  • Mistake → fault → failure; error = computed − correct.
  • Black box: spec, independent, misses code paths; white box: paths, can share bugs.

L24 · Types

  • Unit, integration, non-functional (stress, performance/load, usability), acceptance, regression (smoke), beta.
  • Top-down needs stubs; bottom-up needs drivers; missing middle → stub + driver.
  • Spike (burst), stress (beyond capacity), endurance/soak (hours).

L25 · Coverage

  • Method, statement, branch (decision), condition. getTriangle: (1,1,2),(2,2,2) / +(2,2,3),(1,2,2),(2,1,2) / +(2,3,4).
  • x<0 || y<x: (−1,0),(1,0) [+ (1,5) with short-circuit].

L26 · Basis paths

  • V(G) = E − N + 2 = P + 1. FindMean 4; calculate() 7; countingSort 5.
  • Loop tests: 0, 1, 2, m, n−1, n, n+1.

L27 · EP / BVA

  • One test per partition; BVA a−1, a, a+1, b−1, b, b+1.
  • Weak ECT = max classes (4); strong = product (4×4×3 = 48).
  • Negative tests: empty, wrong type, too long, out of bounds, type range, unreasonable, session.
