sections.title: Lesson 1 — Decorator
sections.html:
Structural patterns explain how to assemble objects and classes into larger structures while keeping these structures flexible and efficient (pp. 2–4).

1. The Starbuzz problem (pp. 5–21)

  • Beverage (description, getDescription(), abstract cost()) with HouseBlend, DarkRoast, Decaf, Espresso; customers add condiments — steamed milk, soy, mocha, whip — or not.
  • Subclass per combination (DarkRoastWithMochaAndWhip …) → class explosion (pp. 11–13).
  • Boolean flags in Beverage (hasMilk(), setMocha() …) and cost() adds them (pp. 14–21). Problems: a new condiment changes the superclass; iced tea inherits condiments it cannot take; no double mocha.

2. Decorate instead (pp. 22–46)

Start with a beverage and wrap it: DarkRoast inside Mocha inside Whip. cost() is delegated inward and each wrapper adds its own price: Whip.cost() = .10 + Mocha.cost() = .10 + .20 + DarkRoast.cost() (.99) = $1.29.

// Slides 33-46 — Decorator: Starbuzz beverages and condiments (Head First)
abstract class Beverage {
    String description = "Unknown Beverage";
    public String getDescription() { return description; }
    public abstract double cost();
}
abstract class CondimentDecorator extends Beverage {
    Beverage beverage;                                   // the wrapped component
    public abstract String getDescription();
}
class Espresso extends Beverage {
    Espresso() { description = "Espresso"; }
    public double cost() { return 1.99; }
}
class DarkRoast extends Beverage {
    DarkRoast() { description = "Dark Roast Coffee"; }
    public double cost() { return .99; }
}
class HouseBlend extends Beverage {
    HouseBlend() { description = "House Blend Coffee"; }
    public double cost() { return .89; }
}
class Mocha extends CondimentDecorator {
    Mocha(Beverage b) { beverage = b; }
    public String getDescription() { return beverage.getDescription() + ", Mocha"; }
    public double cost() { return .20 + beverage.cost(); }
}
class Whip extends CondimentDecorator {
    Whip(Beverage b) { beverage = b; }
    public String getDescription() { return beverage.getDescription() + ", Whip"; }
    public double cost() { return .10 + beverage.cost(); }
}
class Soy extends CondimentDecorator {
    Soy(Beverage b) { beverage = b; }
    public String getDescription() { return beverage.getDescription() + ", Soy"; }
    public double cost() { return .15 + beverage.cost(); }
}
public class StarbuzzCoffee {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Beverage b1 = new Espresso();
        System.out.printf("%s $%.2f%n", b1.getDescription(), b1.cost());
        Beverage b2 = new Whip(new Mocha(new Mocha(new DarkRoast())));
        System.out.printf("%s $%.2f%n", b2.getDescription(), b2.cost());
        Beverage b3 = new Whip(new Mocha(new Soy(new HouseBlend())));
        System.out.printf("%s $%.2f%n", b3.getDescription(), b3.cost());
    }
}

Output (as on p. 46): Espresso $1.99 · Dark Roast Coffee, Mocha, Mocha, Whip $1.49 · House Blend Coffee, Soy, Mocha, Whip $1.34.

3. Definition and structure (pp. 47–50)

Memorize

Decorator lets you attach new behaviours to objects by placing them inside special wrapper objects that contain the behaviours. (GoF: attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically; a flexible alternative to subclassing.)

        «interface» Component  <------------------------------+
        + execute()                                           | wraps (has-a)
           ^                    ^                             |
   ConcreteComponent       BaseDecorator {abstract} ----------+
   + execute()             - wrappee: Component
                           + BaseDecorator(c: Component)
                           + execute() { wrappee.execute(); }
                                   ^                 ^
                     ConcreteDecoratorA     ConcreteDecoratorB
                     + execute() { super.execute(); extra(); }
Client:  a = new ConcreteComponent();  b = new ConcreteDecoratorA(a);  c = new ConcreteDecoratorB(b);  c.execute();
ParticipantRole
Componentcommon interface of wrappers and wrapped objects
ConcreteComponentthe object being wrapped; basic behaviour
BaseDecoratorholds a reference of the Component type and delegates all work to it
ConcreteDecoratorsadd behaviour before/after calling the wrapped object
Clientwraps components in as many layers as needed, working through the Component interface

Real-world: java.io (Misc p. 2) — new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream("data.txt"))): FileInputStream reads bytes (core), InputStreamReader adds byte→char conversion, BufferedReader adds buffering and readLine(). Open for extension, closed for modification.

Use Decorator whenPrefer instead
extras are optional, combinable, repeatable, chosen at run timeStrategy — to swap the whole algorithm, not stack layers
subclassing would explode or is impossible (final class)Adapter — when the interface must change, not be kept
each layer adds one responsibility and keeps the interfaceComposite — when objects form a part–whole tree

Practice — Lesson 1

(a) Actual — 2021-22 Q2(a).

(a) A five-layer network model: the user creates Packet(message, length) e.g. ('hello', 5); the Application layer adds APPHEADER_ (length 15), Transport TRHEADER_ (24), Network NETHEADER_ (34), Data-link DHEADER_ and _DTRAILER (51), Physical PHEADER_ (59) and returns the final Packet. Identify the pattern, implement it and give the UML class diagram. (20)

Show solution

(a) Decorator. Every layer has the same interface (send a packet), wraps the layer above it, and adds one header (data-link: header and trailer) without changing the others. Layers can be added, removed or re-ordered by changing the wrapping only.

«interface» Layer + send(msg): Packet  <----------------------------+
   ^ RawPacket (creates Packet(msg))                                   | inner
   ^ LayerDecorator {abstract} - inner: Layer ---------------------------+
        ^ ApplicationLayer  ^ TransportLayer  ^ NetworkLayer  ^ DataLinkLayer  ^ PhysicalLayer
Packet - message: String  + length(): int
// 2021-22 Q2(a) — Decorator: each layer wraps the packet and adds its header (data-link also a trailer)
class Packet {
    final String message;
    Packet(String m) { message = m; }
    int length() { return message.length(); }
    public String toString() { return "message: " + message + ", length: " + length(); }
}
interface Layer { Packet send(String msg); }                 // component

class RawPacket implements Layer {                            // concrete component: user's Packet
    public Packet send(String msg) { return new Packet(msg); }
}
abstract class LayerDecorator implements Layer {              // base decorator
    protected final Layer inner;
    LayerDecorator(Layer inner) { this.inner = inner; }
}
class ApplicationLayer extends LayerDecorator {
    ApplicationLayer(Layer l) { super(l); }
    public Packet send(String m) { return new Packet("APPHEADER_" + inner.send(m).message); }
}
class TransportLayer extends LayerDecorator {
    TransportLayer(Layer l) { super(l); }
    public Packet send(String m) { return new Packet("TRHEADER_" + inner.send(m).message); }
}
class NetworkLayer extends LayerDecorator {
    NetworkLayer(Layer l) { super(l); }
    public Packet send(String m) { return new Packet("NETHEADER_" + inner.send(m).message); }
}
class DataLinkLayer extends LayerDecorator {
    DataLinkLayer(Layer l) { super(l); }
    public Packet send(String m) { return new Packet("DHEADER_" + inner.send(m).message + "_DTRAILER"); }
}
class PhysicalLayer extends LayerDecorator {
    PhysicalLayer(Layer l) { super(l); }
    public Packet send(String m) { return new Packet("PHEADER_" + inner.send(m).message); }
}
public class NetworkStack {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Layer stack = new PhysicalLayer(new DataLinkLayer(new NetworkLayer(
                      new TransportLayer(new ApplicationLayer(new RawPacket())))));
        System.out.println(new RawPacket().send("hello"));
        System.out.println(new ApplicationLayer(new RawPacket()).send("hello"));
        System.out.println(stack.send("hello"));
    }
}

Output: message: PHEADER_DHEADER_NETHEADER_TRHEADER_APPHEADER_hello_DTRAILER, length: 59 — the lengths 5, 15, 24, 34, 51, 59 match the question.

sections.title: Lesson 2 — Composite
sections.html:
Pancake House and Diner menus are merged; the Waitress must print all menus, a submenu (desserts inside the diner menu) or the whole hierarchy (pp. 51–55). Menus contain menu items and other menus → a tree of nodes (Menu) and leaves (MenuItem) (p. 56).

Waitress --> «abstract» MenuComponent: getName(), getDescription(), getPrice(), isVegetarian(), print(),
                                       add(c), remove(c), getChild(i)      (default: throw UnsupportedOperation)
              ^ MenuItem (leaf): name, description, vegetarian, price; print()
              ^ Menu (composite): menuComponents: List<MenuComponent>; add, remove, getChild,
                                  print() { print own name; for each child: child.print(); }
Memorize

Composite lets you compose objects into tree structures and then work with these structures as if they were individual objects (p. 58).

Client --> «interface» Component + execute()  <-----------+
             ^ Leaf + execute()  (does the real work)      | children (0..*)
             ^ Composite - children: Component[] ----------+
                         + add(c), remove(c), getChildren()
                         + execute() { for each child: child.execute(); combine results }

Implementation issues and consequences (2011-12 Q1(a) — GoF background)

IssueChoice
Where to declare add/removein Component (transparency: client treats all alike, but a leaf must reject add) or only in Composite (safety: compile-time check, but client must know the type)
Parent referenceskeep a parent link for upward navigation / deletion; maintain it in add/remove
Child ordering & storageList if order matters (menus, layers); cache aggregated values if expensive
Who deletes childrenthe composite, when it is deleted (unless children are shared)
Sharing componentspossible (Flyweight) but complicates parent references

Consequences: uniform treatment of leaves and composites; easy to add new component kinds; simple client code with recursion. Liability: the design can become overly general — hard to restrict which components a composite may hold.

Practice — Lesson 2

(a) Actual — 2019-20 Q2(a) / 2020-21 Q3(a). (b) Actual — 2024-25 Q2(a). (c) Actual — 2010-11 Q4(d). (d) Actual — 2011-12 Q1(a).

(a) A Managing Director heads Technical, Administration and Finance divisions, each with a Manager; five developers under the technical manager, three executives under admin, two officers under finance. Implement the hierarchy with Composite; any employee must be able to show all employees under him/her (direct and indirect). (20 / 15)

(b) FinCorp: offices in cities within states within countries; state, country and global reports aggregate their subordinates and attach level-specific analysis; optional sections (tax, investment, compliance) may be added in any combination without changing the core report. Identify the pattern(s) and implement minimally. (20)

(c) Extend the Facebook-group design (Observer) so a group page can itself be a member of another group ('CSE BUET 08' joins 'BUETIANS'). Which pattern, and how? (12⅔)

(d) Discuss the implementation issues and consequences of the Composite pattern. (14)

Show solution

(a) Component = Employee; leaf = Worker (developer, executive, officer); composite = Manager (MD and the three managers). showAll() prints the employee and recursively everyone below; countAll() counts direct + indirect.

// 2019-20 Q2(a), 2020-21 Q3(a) — Composite: employees and their (direct + indirect) subordinates
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

abstract class Employee {                                     // component
    protected final String name, designation;
    Employee(String n, String d) { name = n; designation = d; }
    void add(Employee e)    { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    void remove(Employee e) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
    List<Employee> getSubordinates() { return new ArrayList<>(); }
    abstract void showAll(String indent);                     // shows this employee and everyone below
    public String toString() { return designation + ": " + name; }
}
class Worker extends Employee {                               // leaf
    Worker(String n, String d) { super(n, d); }
    void showAll(String indent) { System.out.println(indent + this); }
}
class Manager extends Employee {                              // composite
    private final List<Employee> subordinates = new ArrayList<>();
    Manager(String n, String d) { super(n, d); }
    void add(Employee e)    { subordinates.add(e); }
    void remove(Employee e) { subordinates.remove(e); }
    List<Employee> getSubordinates() { return subordinates; }
    void showAll(String indent) {
        System.out.println(indent + this);
        for (Employee e : subordinates) e.showAll(indent + "   ");
    }
    int countAll() {                                         // direct + indirect
        int c = 0;
        for (Employee e : subordinates) c += 1 + (e instanceof Manager ? ((Manager) e).countAll() : 0);
        return c;
    }
}
public class CompanyHierarchy {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Manager md = new Manager("Karim", "Managing Director");
        Manager tech = new Manager("Rahim", "Technical Manager");
        Manager admin = new Manager("Salma", "Admin Manager");
        Manager fin = new Manager("Nabil", "Finance Manager");
        md.add(tech); md.add(admin); md.add(fin);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) tech.add(new Worker("Dev" + i, "Developer"));
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) admin.add(new Worker("Exec" + i, "Executive"));
        for (int i = 1; i <= 2; i++) fin.add(new Worker("Officer" + i, "Officer"));
        md.showAll("");
        System.out.println("Under MD: " + md.countAll() + ", under Technical Manager: " + tech.countAll());
    }
}

Output: the tree with MD at the top and 'Under MD: 13, under Technical Manager: 5'.

(b) Composite for requirement (i): CityOffice is a leaf; State, Country and Global are composites that sum their children's expenditure and run their own analysis(); all share the ReportUnit interface, so every stakeholder calls report() the same way. Decorator for requirement (ii): TaxSection, InvestmentSection and ComplianceSection wrap any ReportUnit and append their section, in any combination, without touching the core classes.

«interface» ReportUnit: name(), expenditure(), report()
   ^ CityOffice (leaf)
   ^ Region {abstract} (composite) - children: List<ReportUnit>; add(u); expenditure() = own + Σ children; analysis()
        ^ State   ^ Country   ^ Global
   ^ ReportSection {abstract} (decorator) - inner: ReportUnit
        ^ TaxSection   ^ InvestmentSection   ^ ComplianceSection
// 2024-25 Q2(a) — Composite (city/state/country/global) + Decorator (optional report sections)
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface ReportUnit {                                 // the one consistent reporting interface
    String name();
    double expenditure();
    String report();
}
class CityOffice implements ReportUnit {               // leaf
    private final String name; private final double exp;
    CityOffice(String n, double e) { name = n; exp = e; }
    public String name() { return name; }
    public double expenditure() { return exp; }
    public String report() { return name + " expenditure = " + exp; }
}
abstract class Region implements ReportUnit {          // composite
    private final String name; private final double ownExpenditure;
    protected final List<ReportUnit> children = new ArrayList<>();
    Region(String n, double own) { name = n; ownExpenditure = own; }
    Region add(ReportUnit u) { children.add(u); return this; }
    public String name() { return name; }
    public double expenditure() {                      // aggregates subordinate units
        double s = ownExpenditure;
        for (ReportUnit u : children) s += u.expenditure();
        return s;
    }
    protected abstract String analysis();              // varies by level
    public String report() {
        return name + " total = " + expenditure() + " [" + analysis() + "]";
    }
}
class State extends Region {
    State(String n, double own) { super(n, own); }
    protected String analysis() {
        double max = 0; String top = "";
        for (ReportUnit u : children) if (u.expenditure() > max) { max = u.expenditure(); top = u.name(); }
        return "highest-spending city: " + top;
    }
}
class Country extends Region {
    Country(String n, double own) { super(n, own); }
    protected String analysis() { return "average per state: " + expenditure() / Math.max(1, children.size()); }
}
class Global extends Region {
    Global(String n) { super(n, 0); }
    protected String analysis() {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("share:");
        for (ReportUnit u : children) sb.append(String.format(" %s %.0f%%", u.name(), 100 * u.expenditure() / expenditure()));
        return sb.toString();
    }
}
abstract class ReportSection implements ReportUnit {   // decorator: same interface, wraps any unit
    protected final ReportUnit inner;
    ReportSection(ReportUnit u) { inner = u; }
    public String name() { return inner.name(); }
    public double expenditure() { return inner.expenditure(); }
}
class TaxSection extends ReportSection {
    TaxSection(ReportUnit u) { super(u); }
    public String report() { return inner.report() + "\n  + Tax details: 15% = " + 0.15 * expenditure(); }
}
class InvestmentSection extends ReportSection {
    InvestmentSection(ReportUnit u) { super(u); }
    public String report() { return inner.report() + "\n  + Investment summary attached"; }
}
class ComplianceSection extends ReportSection {
    ComplianceSection(ReportUnit u) { super(u); }
    public String report() { return inner.report() + "\n  + Government compliance report attached"; }
}
public class FinCorpReports {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        State ny = (State) new State("New York", 0).add(new CityOffice("NYC", 500)).add(new CityOffice("Buffalo", 200));
        State ca = (State) new State("California", 50).add(new CityOffice("LA", 400));
        Country usa = (Country) new Country("USA", 100).add(ny).add(ca);
        Country de = (Country) new Country("Germany", 0).add(new State("Bavaria", 0).add(new CityOffice("Munich", 300)));
        Global world = (Global) new Global("FinCorp Global").add(usa).add(de);
        System.out.println(ny.report());                                   // State Director
        System.out.println(new TaxSection(usa).report());                  // Country Head + tax
        System.out.println(new ComplianceSection(new InvestmentSection(world)).report());  // CFO + 2 sections
    }
}

Output: New York total = 700 [highest-spending city: NYC] · USA total = 1250 + tax 187.5 · FinCorp Global total = 1550 [USA 81 %, Germany 19 %] + investment + compliance sections.

(c) Composite. Make the group itself a member: introduce GroupMember (Component) with receive(update); User is a leaf, Group is a composite that holds members (users or groups). When a post is published in BUETIANS, it calls receive() on each member; the 'CSE BUET 08' group forwards to all its own members, so they automatically become members of BUETIANS. Group keeps its Observer role (subject) and now also implements the observer/member interface.

«interface» GroupMember + receive(post: String)              (Observer + Component)
   ^ User (leaf): receive(p) { newsFeed.add(p); }
   ^ Group (composite + subject): members: List<GroupMember>; join(m); leave(m);
                                  publish(p) { for m in members: m.receive(p); }
                                  receive(p) { publish(p); }      // a member group re-broadcasts

(d) The issues table and consequences above.

sections.title: Lesson 3 — Adapter (object vs class)
sections.html:
An adapter sits between your existing system and a vendor class with a different interface, like a plug adapter (pp. 61–65). Duck simulator (pp. 66–79): Duck (quack, fly), MallardDuck; vendor Turkey (gobble, fly — short distance), WildTurkey. TurkeyAdapter implements Duck: quack() → turkey.gobble(); fly() → five turkey.fly() calls.

public class TurkeyAdapter implements Duck {
    Turkey turkey;
    public TurkeyAdapter(Turkey turkey) { this.turkey = turkey; }
    public void quack() { turkey.gobble(); }
    public void fly() { for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) turkey.fly(); }
}
Memorize

Adapter — Convert the interface of a class into another interface clients expect. Adapter lets classes work together that couldn't otherwise because of incompatible interfaces (p. 83).

OBJECT ADAPTER (composition, p. 86-88)             CLASS ADAPTER (inheritance, p. 89-90)
Client --> «interface» Target + request()           Client --> «interface» Target + request()
                ^                                                  ^
             Adapter - adaptee: Adaptee ---->  Adaptee          Adapter ------------|>  Adaptee
             + request() {                     + specificRequest()  + request() { specificRequest(); }
                 adaptee.specificRequest(); }                   (extends Adaptee AND implements Target)
Object adapterClass adapter
Mechanismcomposition: holds an Adapteeinheritance: subclasses Adaptee and implements Target
Languageworks in every OO languageneeds multiple inheritance (C++); in Java only if Target is an interface
Prosadapts the Adaptee and all its subclasses; can be swapped at run time; keeps Adaptee hiddenno extra object; can override Adaptee behaviour; no need to re-implement the whole Adaptee
Conscannot override Adaptee methods easily; one more object/indirectiontied to one concrete Adaptee class; exposes Adaptee's public methods; inflexible

XML → JSON example (p. 85): a stock app downloads XML data but the analytics library wants JSON; an XML-to-JSON adapter converts the data before calling the library. Decorator vs Adapter (pp. 94–95): a decorator adds responsibilities and keeps the interface; an adapter converts the interface.

Practice — Lesson 3

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q1(a). (b) Actual — 2018-19 Q4(b). (c) Actual — 2016-17 Q5(d). (d) Actual — 2010-11 Q4(e).

(a) A service returns the temperature for a city name; the client wants to pass a zip code. Class diagram + code. (15)

(b) Bird (fly(), makeSound()) and ToyDuck (squeak()): use Bird objects in place of ToyDucks. Class diagram + code. (18)

(c) Draw the class-adapter UML; pros and cons of object adapter vs class adapter. (6⅔)

(d) The application uses LibX (vendor out of business); LibY offers the same functionality with different interfaces; no source code for either. Which pattern? Class diagram. (7)

Show solution

(a) Object Adapter. Target = ZipWeatherService.getTemperature(int zip); Adaptee = existing CityWeatherService.getTemperature(String city); Adapter maps the zip code to a city and delegates.

Client --> «interface» ZipWeatherService + getTemperature(zip: int): double
                 ^
          ZipToCityAdapter - service: CityWeatherService - zipToCity: Map<int,String> ---> CityWeatherService
          + getTemperature(zip) { return service.getTemperature(zipToCity.get(zip)); }   + getTemperature(city: String)
// 2022-23 Q1(a) — Object Adapter: clients pass a zip code; the existing service needs a city name
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

class CityWeatherService {                                     // adaptee (existing, unchanged)
    double getTemperature(String city) {
        switch (city) { case "Dhaka": return 31.5; case "Chittagong": return 29.0; default: return Double.NaN; }
    }
}
interface ZipWeatherService { double getTemperature(int zipCode); }   // target expected by the client

class ZipToCityAdapter implements ZipWeatherService {           // adapter
    private final CityWeatherService service;
    private final Map<Integer, String> zipToCity = new HashMap<>();
    ZipToCityAdapter(CityWeatherService s) {
        service = s;
        zipToCity.put(1000, "Dhaka");
        zipToCity.put(4000, "Chittagong");
    }
    public double getTemperature(int zipCode) {
        String city = zipToCity.get(zipCode);
        if (city == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown zip " + zipCode);
        return service.getTemperature(city);                    // translate, then delegate
    }
}
public class WeatherAdapter {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ZipWeatherService ws = new ZipToCityAdapter(new CityWeatherService());
        System.out.println("1000 -> " + ws.getTemperature(1000) + " C");
        System.out.println("4000 -> " + ws.getTemperature(4000) + " C");
    }
}

(b) Target = ToyDuck; Adaptee = Bird; BirdAdapter implements ToyDuck and holds a Bird; squeak() → makeSound().

// 2018-19 Q4(b) — Adapter: use Bird objects where ToyDuck objects are expected
interface Bird { void fly(); void makeSound(); }
class Sparrow implements Bird {
    public void fly() { System.out.println("Flying"); }
    public void makeSound() { System.out.println("Chirp Chirp"); }
}
interface ToyDuck { void squeak(); }                         // target
class PlasticToyDuck implements ToyDuck {
    public void squeak() { System.out.println("Squeak"); }
}
class BirdAdapter implements ToyDuck {                       // adapter
    private final Bird bird;                                 // adaptee
    BirdAdapter(Bird bird) { this.bird = bird; }
    public void squeak() { bird.makeSound(); }               // translate the call
}
public class BirdAdapterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ToyDuck[] ducks = { new PlasticToyDuck(), new BirdAdapter(new Sparrow()) };
        for (ToyDuck d : ducks) d.squeak();                  // client sees only ToyDuck
    }
}

(c) Class-adapter diagram in the box above (Adapter extends Adaptee, implements Target); pros/cons table.

(d) Adapter. Keep the application's code written against LibX's interface (extract it as an interface LibXApi if needed); write LibXToLibYAdapter classes that implement those interfaces and delegate each call to the corresponding LibY classes (object adapters, since we cannot modify either library).

Application --> «interface» LibXApi (the old method signatures)
                      ^
               LibXToLibYAdapter - y: LibYClass  ---> LibYClass (new, different interface)
               + oldMethod(args) { convert args; return y.newMethod(converted); }

sections.title: Lesson 4 — Bridge
sections.html:
Shapes (Circle, Square) × colours (Red, Blue): subclassing every combination (RedCircle, BlueSquare …) grows as shapes × colours (pp. 96–103). Split into two hierarchies — form and colour — and let Shape contain a Color: inheritance becomes composition (p. 104).

Memorize

Bridge lets you split a large class or a set of closely related classes into two separate hierarchies — abstraction and implementation — which can be developed independently of each other (p. 108).

Client --> Abstraction  - i: Implementation  <>--------------> «interface» Implementation
           + feature1() { i.method1(); }                            + method1(), method2(), method3()
           + feature2()                                                ^                 ^
              ^                                               ConcreteImplA     ConcreteImplB
        RefinedAbstraction + featureN()

Abstraction = high-level control layer (GUI); it delegates the real work to the implementation layer (platform APIs: Linux, Windows, macOS) (pp. 105–107). Implementations are interchangeable; the same GUI works under different OSs.

Notification example (Misc pp. 7–8)

Abstractions: Alert, Promotion, OTP notifications; implementations: Email, SMS, Push. Without Bridge 3 × 3 = 9 classes; with Bridge 3 + 3 classes and any combination at run time.

// IJ Misc deck p7-8 — Bridge: notification kind x sending channel
interface MessageSender { void send(String msg); }                    // implementation hierarchy
class EmailSender implements MessageSender { public void send(String m) { System.out.println("Email: " + m); } }
class SmsSender   implements MessageSender { public void send(String m) { System.out.println("SMS: " + m); } }
class PushSender  implements MessageSender { public void send(String m) { System.out.println("Push: " + m); } }

abstract class Notification {                                         // abstraction
    protected final MessageSender sender;                             // the bridge
    Notification(MessageSender s) { sender = s; }
    abstract void notifyUser();
}
class AlertNotification extends Notification {
    AlertNotification(MessageSender s) { super(s); }
    void notifyUser() { sender.send("Server is down!"); }
}
class OtpNotification extends Notification {
    OtpNotification(MessageSender s) { super(s); }
    void notifyUser() { sender.send("Your OTP is 482913"); }
}
class PromotionNotification extends Notification {
    PromotionNotification(MessageSender s) { super(s); }
    void notifyUser() { sender.send("50% off this weekend"); }
}
public class NotificationBridge {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new AlertNotification(new SmsSender()).notifyUser();
        new OtpNotification(new EmailSender()).notifyUser();
        new PromotionNotification(new PushSender()).notifyUser();
    }
}
PatternIntent in one lineCue words
Decoratoradd responsibilities by wrapping; same interfaceoptional add-ons, layers, extra cheese, headers
Compositepart–whole trees treated uniformlyhierarchy, sub-menu, subordinates, group in a group, aggregate totals
Adapterconvert one interface to the one clients expectexisting/vendor class, incompatible, zip vs city, LibX → LibY
Bridgeabstraction and implementation vary independentlytwo dimensions, platform, channel, colour × shape

Practice — Lesson 4

(a) Constructed (Bridge vs Adapter). (b) Constructed.

(a) Bridge and Adapter both delegate to another object. What is the difference in intent and timing?

(b) A drawing app draws Circle and Rectangle using either a vector or a raster renderer. Give the Bridge diagram.

Show solution

(a) Bridge is designed up front to let two dimensions vary independently (abstraction ↔ implementation chosen at run time). Adapter is applied after the fact to make an existing, incompatible class fit an expected interface.

Shape {abstract} - renderer: Renderer ------> «interface» Renderer + drawCircle(x,y,r), drawRect(x,y,w,h)
  + draw()                                         ^ VectorRenderer     ^ RasterRenderer
  ^ Circle  draw() { renderer.drawCircle(...) }
  ^ Rectangle draw() { renderer.drawRect(...) }

sections.title: Quick Notes — Structural Patterns
sections.html:
Revision points for Lessons 1–4.

L1 · Decorator

  • Wrapper with the same interface; cost/behaviour delegated inward + own addition.
  • Starbuzz: DarkRoast + Mocha + Mocha + Whip = $1.49. java.io BufferedReader.
  • Network packet layers = Decorator (each always adds a header).

L2 · Composite

  • Component, Leaf, Composite(children); operation recurses over children.
  • Transparency vs safety of add/remove; parent links; ordering.
  • Employee hierarchy, FinCorp (Composite + Decorator), group inside group.

L3 · Adapter

  • Target, Adapter, Adaptee; object (composition) vs class (inheritance).
  • Zip → city, Bird → ToyDuck, Turkey → Duck, LibX → LibY.
  • Decorator keeps the interface; Adapter converts it.

L4 · Bridge

  • Abstraction has an Implementation; both hierarchies vary independently.
  • Shapes × colours; notifications × channels (9 → 6 classes).

sections.title: Lesson 5 — Strategy
sections.html:
Behavioral patterns deal with how objects behave and interact: communication, flow of responsibility and how tasks are carried out between objects (pp. 2–3).

1. SimUDuck (pp. 4–39)

  • Duck superclass with quack(), swim(), display(), and later fly() → RubberDuck inherits fly() and flies (p. 8).
  • Override fly() to do nothing in RubberDuck, DecoyDuck … → every new duck must be checked (pp. 9–12).
  • Flyable / Quackable interfaces → duplicated fly code in every class; a change touches all (pp. 13–18).
  • Principle (p. 19): identify the aspects that vary and separate them from what stays the same.
  • Duck has FlyBehavior and QuackBehavior (FlyWithWings, FlyNoWay; Quack, Squeak, MuteQuack); performFly() delegates; setFlyBehavior() changes it at run time — ModelDuck gets FlyRocketPowered (pp. 20–39).
Memorize

Strategy — Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from the clients that use it (p. 45).

Client --creates strategy--> Context - strategy: Strategy ---------> «interface» Strategy + execute(data)
                              + setStrategy(s)                          ^            ^
                              + doSomething() { strategy.execute(data); }  ConcreteStrategyA  ConcreteStrategyB

Navigator example (pp. 42–44): routeStrategy = Road / PublicTransport / Walking, each buildRoute(A, B). Payment (p. 47): Credit card vs PayPal.

Use Strategy whenNot when
several variants of one algorithm/behaviour; choose or switch at run timethe variants are steps of one fixed skeleton → Template Method
a class has a big conditional choosing the behaviourbehaviour depends on the object's own state and changes itself → State

Practice — Lesson 5

(a) Actual — 2018-19 Q2(a). (b) Actual — 2020-21 Q2(b). (c) Actual — 2020-21 Q2(a). (d) Actual — 2020-21 Q2(c).

(a) Robots: interface IBehaviour, AggressiveBehaviour, DefensiveBehaviour, NormalBehaviour; Robot passes sensor data (position, close obstacles) to its behaviour; Big Robot is aggressive, George v.2.1 defensive, R2 normal; later the behaviours change. Class diagram + code. (20)

(b) Three sorting routines (selection, insertion, quicksort): demonstrate Strategy. (10)

(c) A web system shows mobile talk-time schemes and their cost; new schemes are added often. Decouple the UI programmers from the scheme classes. (10)

(d) Student IDs with marks: find grades and prepare the merit list of the students with the highest grade, using a pattern; any grading scheme. (15)

Show solution

(a) Strategy: Robot = context, Behaviour = strategy interface, three concrete behaviours; setBehaviour() switches at run time.

Robot - name, position, behaviour: Behaviour --------> «interface» Behaviour + moveCommand(name, pos, obstacle): int
  + setBehaviour(b)  + move(obstacleClose)                   ^ AggressiveBehaviour ^ DefensiveBehaviour ^ NormalBehaviour
// 2018-19 Q2(a) — Strategy: robot behaviours changed at run time
interface Behaviour { int moveCommand(String robot, int position, boolean obstacleClose); }
class AggressiveBehaviour implements Behaviour {
    public int moveCommand(String r, int pos, boolean obs) {
        System.out.println(r + ": aggressive - attack the robot found"); return obs ? 1 : 0; }
}
class DefensiveBehaviour implements Behaviour {
    public int moveCommand(String r, int pos, boolean obs) {
        System.out.println(r + ": defensive - run away in the opposite direction"); return obs ? -1 : 0; }
}
class NormalBehaviour implements Behaviour {
    public int moveCommand(String r, int pos, boolean obs) {
        System.out.println(r + ": normal - ignore other robots"); return 0; }
}
class Robot {                                         // context
    private final String name; private Behaviour behaviour; private int position;
    Robot(String name) { this.name = name; }
    void setBehaviour(Behaviour b) { behaviour = b; }
    void move(boolean obstacleClose) {                // passes sensor info to the strategy
        position += behaviour.moveCommand(name, position, obstacleClose);
    }
}
public class RobotSim {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Robot r1 = new Robot("Big Robot"), r2 = new Robot("George v.2.1"), r3 = new Robot("R2");
        r1.setBehaviour(new AggressiveBehaviour());
        r2.setBehaviour(new DefensiveBehaviour());
        r3.setBehaviour(new NormalBehaviour());
        r1.move(true); r2.move(true); r3.move(true);
        System.out.println("-- behaviours changed --");
        r1.setBehaviour(new DefensiveBehaviour());
        r2.setBehaviour(new NormalBehaviour());
        r3.setBehaviour(new AggressiveBehaviour());
        r1.move(true); r2.move(true); r3.move(true);
    }
}

(b) Sorter (context) holds a SortStrategy; three concrete strategies.

// 2020-21 Q2(b) — Strategy: selection / insertion / quick sort
import java.util.Arrays;

interface SortStrategy { void sort(int[] a); }
class SelectionSort implements SortStrategy {
    public void sort(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) {
            int m = i;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) if (a[j] < a[m]) m = j;
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[m]; a[m] = t;
        }
    }
}
class InsertionSort implements SortStrategy {
    public void sort(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            int k = a[i], j = i - 1;
            while (j >= 0 && a[j] > k) { a[j + 1] = a[j]; j--; }
            a[j + 1] = k;
        }
    }
}
class QuickSort implements SortStrategy {
    public void sort(int[] a) { qs(a, 0, a.length - 1); }
    private void qs(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return;
        int p = a[hi], i = lo;
        for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) if (a[j] < p) { int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t; i++; }
        int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[hi]; a[hi] = t;
        qs(a, lo, i - 1); qs(a, i + 1, hi);
    }
}
class Sorter {                                          // context
    private SortStrategy strategy;
    Sorter(SortStrategy s) { strategy = s; }
    void setStrategy(SortStrategy s) { strategy = s; }
    int[] sort(int[] data) { int[] c = data.clone(); strategy.sort(c); return c; }
}
public class SortStrategyDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] d = {5, 2, 9, 1, 7, 3};
        Sorter s = new Sorter(new SelectionSort());
        System.out.println("selection " + Arrays.toString(s.sort(d)));
        s.setStrategy(new InsertionSort());
        System.out.println("insertion " + Arrays.toString(s.sort(d)));
        s.setStrategy(new QuickSort());
        System.out.println("quick     " + Arrays.toString(s.sort(d)));
    }
}

(c) Strategy: every scheme implements TalkTimeScheme (name(), cost(minutes)); the UI page depends only on that interface and receives the list from a registry/factory. Adding a scheme = one new class + one registry line; the UI code never changes.

// 2020-21 Q2(a) — Strategy: UI depends only on the TalkTimeScheme interface; new schemes are plug-ins
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface TalkTimeScheme { String name(); double cost(int minutes); }
class PerMinuteScheme implements TalkTimeScheme {
    public String name() { return "Per minute (Tk 1.0/min)"; }
    public double cost(int m) { return m * 1.0; }
}
class BundleScheme implements TalkTimeScheme {
    public String name() { return "Bundle 300 min for Tk 199, then Tk 0.8/min"; }
    public double cost(int m) { return 199 + Math.max(0, m - 300) * 0.8; }
}
class NightScheme implements TalkTimeScheme {          // added later: no UI change
    public String name() { return "Night owl (Tk 0.5/min)"; }
    public double cost(int m) { return m * 0.5; }
}
class SchemeRegistry {                                 // the only place that knows concrete schemes
    static List<TalkTimeScheme> all() {
        List<TalkTimeScheme> l = new ArrayList<>();
        l.add(new PerMinuteScheme()); l.add(new BundleScheme()); l.add(new NightScheme());
        return l;
    }
}
class SchemePage {                                     // UI team codes against the interface only
    void show(TalkTimeScheme s, int minutes) {
        System.out.printf("%-45s %4d min -> Tk %.2f%n", s.name(), minutes, s.cost(minutes));
    }
}
public class TalkTimeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SchemePage ui = new SchemePage();
        for (TalkTimeScheme s : SchemeRegistry.all()) ui.show(s, 400);
    }
}

(d) Strategy for the grading scheme (BUET letter grades or pass/fail chosen at run time); ResultProcessor computes grades and the merit list (students with the top grade, sorted by marks).

// 2020-21 Q2(c) — Strategy: grading scheme chosen at run time; merit list of the top grade
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

interface GradingStrategy { String grade(int marks); String topGrade(); }
class BuetGrading implements GradingStrategy {
    public String grade(int m) {
        if (m >= 80) return "A+"; if (m >= 75) return "A"; if (m >= 70) return "A-";
        if (m >= 65) return "B+"; if (m >= 60) return "B"; if (m >= 55) return "B-";
        if (m >= 50) return "C+"; if (m >= 45) return "C"; if (m >= 40) return "D"; return "F";
    }
    public String topGrade() { return "A+"; }
}
class PassFailGrading implements GradingStrategy {
    public String grade(int m) { return m >= 50 ? "P" : "F"; }
    public String topGrade() { return "P"; }
}
class ResultProcessor {                                // context
    private GradingStrategy strategy;
    ResultProcessor(GradingStrategy s) { strategy = s; }
    void setStrategy(GradingStrategy s) { strategy = s; }
    Map<String, String> grades(Map<String, Integer> marks) {
        Map<String, String> g = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : marks.entrySet()) g.put(e.getKey(), strategy.grade(e.getValue()));
        return g;
    }
    List<String> meritList(Map<String, Integer> marks) {   // students with the highest grade, by marks
        List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : marks.entrySet())
            if (strategy.grade(e.getValue()).equals(strategy.topGrade())) ids.add(e.getKey());
        ids.sort((a, b) -> marks.get(b) - marks.get(a));
        return ids;
    }
}
public class MeritListDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Integer> marks = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        marks.put("2205001", 86); marks.put("2205002", 74); marks.put("2205003", 91); marks.put("2205004", 38);
        ResultProcessor rp = new ResultProcessor(new BuetGrading());
        System.out.println(rp.grades(marks));
        System.out.println("Merit list: " + rp.meritList(marks));
    }
}

sections.title: Lesson 6 — Template Method
sections.html:
Coffee: boil water, brew coffee grinds, pour in cup, add sugar and milk. Tea: boil water, steep tea bag, pour in cup, add lemon. Same skeleton (pp. 49–63) → CaffeineBeverage.prepareRecipe() is final: boilWater(); brew(); pourInCup(); addCondiments(); — brew() and addCondiments() are abstract; Coffee and Tea implement them.

Hook (p. 72): if (customerWantsCondiments()) addCondiments(); — customerWantsCondiments() returns true by default and subclasses may override it.

Memorize

Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in the superclass but lets subclasses override specific steps of the algorithm without changing its structure (p. 73).

AbstractClass
 + templateMethod() {final}  { step1(); step2(); if (hook()) step3(); step4(); }
 # step1(), step4()          (implemented: common)
 # step2(), step3()          {abstract}
 # hook(): boolean           (default implementation, may be overridden)
        ^                         ^
 ConcreteClass1             ConcreteClass2   (override step2, step3, optionally hook)

Data mining (pp. 75–77): DocDataMiner, CSVDataMiner, PDFDataMiner repeat openFile, extractData, parseData, analyzeData, sendReport, closeFile → DataMiner.mine(path) template; format-specific steps abstract; analyzeData and sendReport shared.

Template MethodStrategy
Based oninheritance — alter parts by extending them in subclassescomposition — alter behaviour by supplying a different strategy object
Level / timeclass level, static (fixed at compile time)object level, can switch at run time
Controlssuperclass controls the order of stepscontext delegates the whole algorithm

Practice — Lesson 6

(a) Actual — 2024-25 Q8(a).

(a) A DataParser reads data files in different formats (CSV, JSON …) through the same steps (open, extract, parse, analyse, report, close) but the analysis algorithm must be selectable. Redesign it using Template Method and Strategy together, in Java. (15)

Show solution

(a) Template Method fixes the pipeline in a final process() method; format-specific steps (extractData, parseData) are abstract and implemented by CsvParser and JsonParser; wantsReport() is a hook. The analysis step varies independently of the format, so it is a Strategy object injected into the parser — any format can be combined with any analysis without new subclasses.

DataParser {abstract} - analysis: AnalysisStrategy -------> «interface» AnalysisStrategy + analyze(values)
 + process(raw) {final}  (template)                             ^ AverageAnalysis   ^ MaxAnalysis
 # openFile(), extractData(){abstract}, parseData(){abstract}, wantsReport() (hook), sendReport(), closeFile()
     ^ CsvParser    ^ JsonParser
// 2024-25 Q8(a) — Template Method (fixed parsing pipeline) + Strategy (pluggable analysis)
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

interface AnalysisStrategy { String analyze(List<Double> values); }     // strategy
class AverageAnalysis implements AnalysisStrategy {
    public String analyze(List<Double> v) {
        return "average = " + v.stream().mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).average().orElse(0); }
}
class MaxAnalysis implements AnalysisStrategy {
    public String analyze(List<Double> v) {
        return "max = " + v.stream().mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).max().orElse(0); }
}
abstract class DataParser {                                             // template
    private final AnalysisStrategy analysis;
    DataParser(AnalysisStrategy a) { analysis = a; }
    public final String process(String raw) {                          // the template method
        String content = openFile(raw);
        List<Double> data = parseData(extractData(content));
        String result = analysis.analyze(data);                        // varying algorithm = strategy
        if (wantsReport()) sendReport(result);                         // hook
        closeFile();
        return result;
    }
    protected String openFile(String raw) { return raw.trim(); }       // common steps
    protected abstract String extractData(String content);             // format-specific steps
    protected abstract List<Double> parseData(String data);
    protected boolean wantsReport() { return true; }                   // hook with default
    protected void sendReport(String r) { System.out.println("Report: " + r); }
    protected void closeFile() { }
}
class CsvParser extends DataParser {
    CsvParser(AnalysisStrategy a) { super(a); }
    protected String extractData(String c) { return c; }
    protected List<Double> parseData(String d) {
        return Arrays.stream(d.split(",")).map(String::trim).map(Double::valueOf).toList(); }
}
class JsonParser extends DataParser {
    JsonParser(AnalysisStrategy a) { super(a); }
    protected String extractData(String c) { return c.substring(c.indexOf('[') + 1, c.indexOf(']')); }
    protected List<Double> parseData(String d) {
        return Arrays.stream(d.split(",")).map(String::trim).map(Double::valueOf).toList(); }
    protected boolean wantsReport() { return false; }
}
public class DataMinerDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(new CsvParser(new AverageAnalysis()).process("3, 5, 10"));
        System.out.println(new JsonParser(new MaxAnalysis()).process("{\"v\": [4, 9, 2]}"));
    }
}

sections.title: Lesson 7 — Observer
sections.html:
Weather-O-Rama (pp. 82–94): WeatherData has getTemperature(), getHumidity(), getPressure() and measurementsChanged(); three displays (current conditions, statistics, forecast) must update, and more may be added. Coding the displays into measurementsChanged() couples WeatherData to concrete classes. Newspaper subscription (pp. 95–107): publisher + subscribers who can subscribe and unsubscribe.

Memorize

Observer — Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically (p. 121).

«interface» Subject                                «interface» Observer
 + registerObserver(o)  + removeObserver(o)          + update(temp, humidity, pressure)
 + notifyObservers()                                   ^            ^              ^
        ^                                      CurrentConditions  StatisticsDisplay  ForecastDisplay
   WeatherData - observers: List<Observer>     (each has display(); its constructor calls
   + measurementsChanged() { notifyObservers(); }  weatherData.registerObserver(this))

General form (p. 121–127): Publisher (subscribers[], mainState; subscribe(s), unsubscribe(s), notifySubscribers() { for each s: s.update(this) }) and «interface» Subscriber update(context). Push = subject sends the data in update(); pull = subject sends itself and observers read what they need. Observer = event listener (p. 128).

Practice — Lesson 7

(a) Actual — 2023-24 Q2(a). (b) Actual — 2022-23 Q4(a) / 2017-18 Q8(b). (c) Actual — 2020-21 Q3(b). (d) Actual — 2024-25 Q8(b). (e) Actual — 2010-11 Q4(c).

(a) StockMarket: StockGrabber holds the prices; StockObserver objects must be updated when any price changes. (i) UML with the pattern (6) (ii) code StockGrabber and StockObserver (8×2).

(b) BUET alumni register to a blog; when a new article is posted the blog notifies them; they then open the blog and read it. Class diagram + code. (15 / 5+12)

(c) A dashboard shows the max and average temperature, updated at the end of each day. Pattern + design. (10)

(d) Breaking-news items must appear on several displays (TV ticker, mobile app, website) as soon as they arrive. (10)

(e) Facebook group: users join and leave; every wall post is broadcast to all members' news feeds. Pattern, class diagram and code fragments. (12)

Show solution

(a) 

«interface» Subject + register(o), unregister(o), notifyObservers()      «interface» Observer + update(ibm, aapl, goog)
        ^                                                                       ^
StockGrabber - observers: List<Observer>                                 StockObserver - id, stockGrabber: Subject
  - ibmPrice, aaplPrice, googPrice                                        + update(...)  (prints the prices)
  + setIBMPrice(p) / setAAPLPrice(p) / setGOOGPrice(p) -> notifyObservers()
StockObserver ----registers with----> StockGrabber (1 subject, 0..* observers)
// 2023-24 Q2(a) — Observer: StockGrabber (subject) and StockObserver (observer)
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface Subject {
    void register(Observer o);
    void unregister(Observer o);
    void notifyObservers();
}
interface Observer { void update(double ibmPrice, double aaplPrice, double googPrice); }

class StockGrabber implements Subject {
    private final List<Observer> observers = new ArrayList<>();
    private double ibmPrice, aaplPrice, googPrice;
    public void register(Observer o)   { observers.add(o); }
    public void unregister(Observer o) { observers.remove(o); }
    public void notifyObservers() {
        for (Observer o : observers) o.update(ibmPrice, aaplPrice, googPrice);
    }
    public void setIBMPrice(double p)  { ibmPrice = p;  notifyObservers(); }
    public void setAAPLPrice(double p) { aaplPrice = p; notifyObservers(); }
    public void setGOOGPrice(double p) { googPrice = p; notifyObservers(); }
}
class StockObserver implements Observer {
    private static int count = 0;
    private final int id;
    private final Subject stockGrabber;
    StockObserver(Subject s) {
        stockGrabber = s;
        id = ++count;
        s.register(this);                                // subscribes itself
        System.out.println("New observer " + id);
    }
    public void update(double ibm, double aapl, double goog) {
        System.out.printf("Observer %d: IBM %.2f AAPL %.2f GOOG %.2f%n", id, ibm, aapl, goog);
    }
    void stop() { stockGrabber.unregister(this); }
}
public class StockDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        StockGrabber g = new StockGrabber();
        StockObserver o1 = new StockObserver(g);
        g.setIBMPrice(197.00);
        StockObserver o2 = new StockObserver(g);
        g.setAAPLPrice(677.60);
        o1.stop();
        g.setGOOGPrice(676.40);                          // only observer 2 is told
    }
}

(b) Pull model: update(blog) tells the user that a new article is posted; the user then calls blog.getLatestArticle() — exactly 'then the user will access the blog and read'.

// 2022-23 Q4(a), 2017-18 Q8(b) — Observer: alumni blog notifies registered users; they pull the new article
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface BlogObserver { void update(Blog blog); }
class Blog {                                               // subject (publisher)
    private final List<BlogObserver> subscribers = new ArrayList<>();
    private final List<String> articles = new ArrayList<>();
    void register(BlogObserver o)   { subscribers.add(o); }
    void unregister(BlogObserver o) { subscribers.remove(o); }
    void postArticle(String title) {
        articles.add(title);
        for (BlogObserver o : subscribers) o.update(this);  // 'a new article is posted'
    }
    String getLatestArticle() { return articles.get(articles.size() - 1); }
}
class AlumniUser implements BlogObserver {               // concrete observer
    private final String name;
    AlumniUser(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public void update(Blog blog) {
        System.out.println(name + " notified: a new article is posted");
        System.out.println(name + " reads: " + blog.getLatestArticle());   // pull model
    }
}
public class BlogDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Blog blog = new Blog();
        AlumniUser a = new AlumniUser("Asef"), b = new AlumniUser("Nadia");
        blog.register(a); blog.register(b);
        blog.postArticle("Life after BUET");
        blog.unregister(a);
        blog.postArticle("Alumni reunion 2026");
    }
}

(c) Observer: TemperatureLog (subject) collects readings and at endOfDay() pushes (max, avg) to every attached widget; new widgets just attach.

// 2020-21 Q3(b) — Observer: end-of-day temperature summary pushed to dashboards
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface DayObserver { void update(double max, double avg); }
class TemperatureLog {                                    // subject
    private final List<Double> readings = new ArrayList<>();
    private final List<DayObserver> observers = new ArrayList<>();
    void attach(DayObserver o) { observers.add(o); }
    void record(double t) { readings.add(t); }
    void endOfDay() {
        double max = readings.stream().mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).max().orElse(0);
        double avg = readings.stream().mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).average().orElse(0);
        for (DayObserver o : observers) o.update(max, avg);
        readings.clear();
    }
}
class MaxTempWidget implements DayObserver {
    public void update(double max, double avg) { System.out.println("Max today: " + max); }
}
class AvgTempWidget implements DayObserver {
    public void update(double max, double avg) { System.out.printf("Average today: %.2f%n", avg); }
}
public class TempDashboard {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TemperatureLog log = new TemperatureLog();
        log.attach(new MaxTempWidget()); log.attach(new AvgTempWidget());
        for (double t : new double[]{24.5, 31.0, 29.5, 27.0}) log.record(t);
        log.endOfDay();
    }
}

(d) Observer: NewsAgency (subject) keeps a list of NewsDisplay observers (TvTicker, MobileApp, Website); publish(news) calls display.update(news) on each. Displays subscribe/unsubscribe at run time; the agency does not know their concrete classes. Same code shape as (a).

(e) Observer: Group = subject with join(user) = register, leave(user) = remove, postOnWall(msg) → notifyMembers() → user.update(group, msg) adds it to the user's news feed. Group also has title, admins, type (open/closed) and related groups. For groups inside groups see the Composite extension in the Structural notes (2010-11 Q4(d)).

sections.title: Lesson 8 — Mediator
sections.html:
Air-traffic control (p. 129): pilots do not talk to each other; all communication goes through the tower. Customer profile dialog (pp. 131–150): checkboxes, text fields and buttons that react to each other create a web of dependencies; instead the Dialog is the mediator — components only notify it.

Memorize

Mediator restricts direct communications between objects and forces them to collaborate only via a mediator object; it reduces chaotic dependencies (p. 157).

ComponentA - m: Mediator   ComponentB - m: Mediator  ...   (each calls m.notify(this, event))
        \                     |                      /
         +--------> «interface» Mediator + notify(sender, event) <-------+
                              ^
                   ConcreteMediator - componentA, componentB, ...
                   + notify(sender, event) { if (sender == componentA) reactOnA(); ... }
MediatorObserver
Goaleliminate mutual dependencies among a set of components; all depend on one mediatorestablish dynamic one-way connections: subscribers follow a publisher
Directionmany ↔ one ↔ many (two-way coordination logic in the mediator)one → many notifications
Notea mediator is often implemented with observer-style notify()observers can come and go at run time

Practice — Lesson 8

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q2(a). (b) Actual — 2019-20 Q1(b). (c) Actual — 2024-25 Q5(b)(i).

(a) ATC coordinates landing and take-off; flights must not depend on each other. Class diagram + code. (15)

(b) Three servers sort with selection, insertion and quicksort; a central broker receives (algorithm, data), forwards to the right server, returns the sorted array, and queues requests that arrive together. Demonstrate Mediator. (20)

(c) A Smart Home Hub coordinates motion sensors, lights, alarms and other devices. A motion event may trigger one or more coordinated actions (light on, alarm, notify the hub): show why Mediator is preferable to letting the motion sensor talk to the devices directly. (Part (ii) of this question — record/queue/replay — needs Command, which is not in this term's syllabus.)

Show solution
«interface» ATCMediator + register(f), requestLanding(f): boolean, landed(f)
        ^ ControlTower - flights: List<Flight> - runwayFree: boolean
Flight - id - atc: ATCMediator + land() + receive(msg)       Flight 0..* ---- 1 ControlTower
// 2022-23 Q2(a) — Mediator: flights talk only to the ATC tower
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface ATCMediator {
    void register(Flight f);
    boolean requestLanding(Flight f);
    void landed(Flight f);
}
class ControlTower implements ATCMediator {
    private final List<Flight> flights = new ArrayList<>();
    private boolean runwayFree = true;
    public void register(Flight f) { flights.add(f); }
    public boolean requestLanding(Flight f) {
        if (runwayFree) {
            runwayFree = false;
            for (Flight o : flights) if (o != f) o.receive(f.id + " is landing, hold your position");
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
    public void landed(Flight f) {
        runwayFree = true;
        for (Flight o : flights) if (o != f) o.receive("runway free after " + f.id);
    }
}
class Flight {                                         // colleague: knows only the mediator
    final String id; private final ATCMediator atc;
    Flight(String id, ATCMediator atc) { this.id = id; this.atc = atc; atc.register(this); }
    void land() {
        if (atc.requestLanding(this)) { System.out.println(id + ": landing"); atc.landed(this); }
        else System.out.println(id + ": waiting - runway busy");
    }
    void receive(String msg) { System.out.println(id + " <- ATC: " + msg); }
}
public class AtcDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ATCMediator tower = new ControlTower();
        Flight bg = new Flight("BG-147", tower), ek = new Flight("EK-585", tower);
        bg.land();
        ek.land();
    }
}

(b) CentralBroker is the concrete mediator; clients and servers are colleagues that never reference each other. A FIFO queue holds simultaneous requests.

Client - broker: Broker + requestSort(alg, data) + receive(sorted)
«interface» Broker + submit(client, alg, data) + processAll()
   ^ CentralBroker - servers: Map<String, SortServer> - queue: Queue<Request>
SortServer {abstract} + algorithm() + sort(a)   ^ SelectionServer ^ InsertionServer ^ QuickServer
// 2019-20 Q1(b) — Mediator: central broker forwards sorting requests to servers, queueing them
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Queue;

interface Broker { void submit(Client c, String algorithm, int[] data); void processAll(); }

abstract class SortServer {                                  // colleague
    abstract String algorithm();
    abstract int[] sort(int[] a);
}
class SelectionServer extends SortServer {
    String algorithm() { return "selection"; }
    int[] sort(int[] a) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        for (int i = 0; i < c.length - 1; i++) { int m = i;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < c.length; j++) if (c[j] < c[m]) m = j;
            int t = c[i]; c[i] = c[m]; c[m] = t; }
        return c;
    }
}
class InsertionServer extends SortServer {
    String algorithm() { return "insertion"; }
    int[] sort(int[] a) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        for (int i = 1; i < c.length; i++) { int k = c[i], j = i - 1;
            while (j >= 0 && c[j] > k) { c[j + 1] = c[j]; j--; } c[j + 1] = k; }
        return c;
    }
}
class QuickServer extends SortServer {
    String algorithm() { return "quick"; }
    int[] sort(int[] a) { int[] c = a.clone(); Arrays.sort(c); return c; }   // library quicksort for primitives
}
class Client {                                               // colleague
    private final String name; private final Broker broker;
    Client(String name, Broker b) { this.name = name; broker = b; }
    void requestSort(String alg, int[] data) { broker.submit(this, alg, data); }
    void receive(int[] sorted) { System.out.println(name + " got " + Arrays.toString(sorted)); }
}
class CentralBroker implements Broker {                      // concrete mediator
    private record Request(Client c, String alg, int[] data) { }
    private final Map<String, SortServer> servers = new HashMap<>();
    private final Queue<Request> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void addServer(SortServer s) { servers.put(s.algorithm(), s); }
    public void submit(Client c, String alg, int[] data) { queue.add(new Request(c, alg, data)); }
    public void processAll() {                               // FIFO when several requests arrive together
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            Request r = queue.poll();
            r.c().receive(servers.get(r.alg()).sort(r.data()));
        }
    }
}
public class SortBroker {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CentralBroker b = new CentralBroker();
        b.addServer(new SelectionServer()); b.addServer(new InsertionServer()); b.addServer(new QuickServer());
        Client c1 = new Client("C1", b), c2 = new Client("C2", b);
        c1.requestSort("quick", new int[]{4, 1, 3});
        c2.requestSort("selection", new int[]{9, 7, 8});
        c1.requestSort("insertion", new int[]{2, 0, 1});
        b.processAll();
    }
}

(c) Direct links: MotionSensor would hold references to Light, Alarm, Notifier and contain the rules → N sensors × M devices dependencies; adding a device or changing a rule edits every sensor. With Mediator the sensor only calls hub.notify(this, "motion"); the hub owns the coordination rules, devices and sensors stay independent and reusable, and rules change in one place.

// 2024-25 Q5(b)(i) — Mediator: sensors talk only to the hub; the hub owns the coordination rules
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

interface HubMediator { void notify(Device sender, String event); }

abstract class Device {                                  // colleague: knows only the mediator
    protected final HubMediator hub; final String name;
    Device(String name, HubMediator hub) { this.name = name; this.hub = hub; }
}
class MotionSensor extends Device {
    MotionSensor(HubMediator h) { super("MotionSensor", h); }
    void detect() { hub.notify(this, "motion"); }
}
class DoorSensor extends Device {
    DoorSensor(HubMediator h) { super("DoorSensor", h); }
    void forced() { hub.notify(this, "forced"); }
}
class Light extends Device {
    Light(HubMediator h) { super("Light", h); }
    void on() { System.out.println("Light ON"); }
}
class Alarm extends Device {
    Alarm(HubMediator h) { super("Alarm", h); }
    void activate() { System.out.println("Alarm ACTIVATED"); }
}
class SmartHomeHub implements HubMediator {             // concrete mediator
    Light light; Alarm alarm;
    final List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
    public void notify(Device sender, String event) {
        log.add(sender.name + ":" + event);
        if (sender instanceof MotionSensor && event.equals("motion")) {
            light.on();
            System.out.println("Hub notified: motion in hallway");
        } else if (sender instanceof DoorSensor && event.equals("forced")) {
            alarm.activate();
            light.on();
        }
    }
}
public class SmartHomeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SmartHomeHub hub = new SmartHomeHub();
        hub.light = new Light(hub);
        hub.alarm = new Alarm(hub);
        new MotionSensor(hub).detect();
        new DoorSensor(hub).forced();
        System.out.println("events: " + hub.log);
    }
}

sections.title: Lesson 9 — State (and State vs Strategy)
sections.html:
Mighty Gumball (pp. 203–216): states No Quarter, Has Quarter, Gumball Sold, Out of Gumballs; actions insertQuarter, ejectQuarter, turnCrank, dispense. Coding it with int constants and an if-else on the state in every action works, but the new 'winner' rule (10 % of the time two gumballs) forces changes in every method — the nightmare of change.

New design (pp. 217–240): a State interface with the four actions; one class per state (NoQuarterState, HasQuarterState, SoldState, SoldOutState, WinnerState); GumballMachine holds the state objects and the current state and delegates every action to it; states call machine.setState(next).

Memorize

State — Allow an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object will appear to change its class (p. 241).

Context - state: State                         «interface» State + doThis() + doThat()
 + Context(initialState)                               ^                    ^
 + changeState(s) { state = s; }                ConcreteStateA        ConcreteStateB
 + doThis() { state.doThis(); }                 - context: Context    (may call context.changeState(new B()))
// IJ slides p203-240 — State pattern: gumball machine
interface State { void insertQuarter(); void ejectQuarter(); void turnCrank(); void dispense(); }

class GumballMachine {                                          // context
    final State soldOut, noQuarter, hasQuarter, sold;
    private State state;
    int count;
    GumballMachine(int n) {
        soldOut = new SoldOutState(this); noQuarter = new NoQuarterState(this);
        hasQuarter = new HasQuarterState(this); sold = new SoldState(this);
        count = n; state = n > 0 ? noQuarter : soldOut;
    }
    void setState(State s) { state = s; }
    void insertQuarter() { state.insertQuarter(); }
    void ejectQuarter() { state.ejectQuarter(); }
    void turnCrank() { state.turnCrank(); state.dispense(); }
    void releaseBall() { System.out.println("A gumball comes rolling out"); if (count > 0) count--; }
}
class NoQuarterState implements State {
    private final GumballMachine m; NoQuarterState(GumballMachine m) { this.m = m; }
    public void insertQuarter() { System.out.println("You inserted a quarter"); m.setState(m.hasQuarter); }
    public void ejectQuarter() { System.out.println("You haven't inserted a quarter"); }
    public void turnCrank() { System.out.println("You turned, but there's no quarter"); }
    public void dispense() { System.out.println("You need to pay first"); }
}
class HasQuarterState implements State {
    private final GumballMachine m; HasQuarterState(GumballMachine m) { this.m = m; }
    public void insertQuarter() { System.out.println("You can't insert another quarter"); }
    public void ejectQuarter() { System.out.println("Quarter returned"); m.setState(m.noQuarter); }
    public void turnCrank() { System.out.println("You turned..."); m.setState(m.sold); }
    public void dispense() { System.out.println("No gumball dispensed"); }
}
class SoldState implements State {
    private final GumballMachine m; SoldState(GumballMachine m) { this.m = m; }
    public void insertQuarter() { System.out.println("Please wait, we're already giving you a gumball"); }
    public void ejectQuarter() { System.out.println("Sorry, you already turned the crank"); }
    public void turnCrank() { System.out.println("Turning twice doesn't get you another gumball!"); }
    public void dispense() {
        m.releaseBall();
        if (m.count > 0) m.setState(m.noQuarter);
        else { System.out.println("Oops, out of gumballs!"); m.setState(m.soldOut); }
    }
}
class SoldOutState implements State {
    private final GumballMachine m; SoldOutState(GumballMachine m) { this.m = m; }
    public void insertQuarter() { System.out.println("Machine is sold out"); }
    public void ejectQuarter() { System.out.println("You haven't inserted a quarter"); }
    public void turnCrank() { System.out.println("No gumballs"); }
    public void dispense() { System.out.println("No gumball dispensed"); }
}
public class GumballDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        GumballMachine g = new GumballMachine(1);
        g.insertQuarter(); g.turnCrank();
        g.insertQuarter();                              // sold out now
    }
}

Document example (pp. 252–253): publish() behaves differently in Draft (→ Moderation, or Published if admin), Moderation (→ Published if approved) and Published (do nothing).

StateStrategy
Commonboth use composition and delegate to a helper object ('twins separated at birth', p. 254)
Who changes the helperthe context or the states themselves, as a result of actionsthe client chooses/sets it
Knowledgestates may know each other and the contextstrategies are independent and unaware of each other
Modelsbehaviour that depends on the object's current state (life cycle)interchangeable algorithms for one task
Examplegumball machine, document workflow, TCP connectionsorting algorithms, payment methods, routes

(a) Actual — 2024-25 Q8(c).

(a) State vs Strategy. (10)

Show solution

(a) The comparison table above with one diagram each (Context → State with transitions between ConcreteStates; Context → Strategy set by the client) and the gumball vs sorting examples.
