sections.title: Lesson 11 — Generic Process Model: Framework Activities and Process Flows
sections.html:
Software is embodied knowledge that is initially scattered and incomplete; a step-by-step process brings that knowledge into the software (p. 3). A process model divides software-development work into distinct phases and gives a road map (p. 4).

Framework activityWhat happens (pp. 6–8)
1 Communicationproject team communicates with the client; requirements gathered
2 Planningschedule the development and estimate the cost
3 Modelinganalyse requirements; design algorithms, flowcharts, components
4 Constructionimplement and test the components
5 Deploymentdeliver to the client; feedback used to improve quality
Process flowMeaning (pp. 9–14)
Linearthe five activities once, in sequence
Iterativerepeat one or more activities before moving on
Evolutionaryactivities in a circle; each cycle (incremental release) gives a more complete version
Parallelone or more activities run in parallel with others (e.g. modeling of one part with construction of another)
Note

Textbook background: umbrella activities run across all framework activities — project tracking and control, risk management, quality assurance, technical reviews, measurement, configuration management, reusability management, work-product preparation. PSP framework activities: planning, high-level design, high-level design review, development, postmortem.

Practice — Lesson 11

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q6(a). (b) Actual — 2013-14 Q4(c). (c) Actual — 2018-19 Q5(c). (d) Actual — 2014-15 Q4(a).

(a) Core activities of the generic process model; describe waterfall with advantages and disadvantages. (10)

(b) Framework and umbrella activities. (8)

(c) What does framework activity mean? Name five PSP framework activities. (3+10)

(d) Why are framework activities not applicable to every project in the same way? (6⅔)

Show solution

(a) Five activities from the first table, then waterfall (Lesson 12 §1) — the five activities run once in order; advantages: simple, understandable, manageable; disadvantages: all requirements up front, testing and client evaluation at the end (high risk), no iteration.

(b) Framework activities = the five phases that produce the product. Umbrella activities = NOTE list; they support every phase and manage progress, quality, change and risk.

(c) A framework activity is one of the generic steps applicable to all software projects regardless of size. PSP: planning, high-level design, high-level design review, development, postmortem.

(d) The activities are always present but their depth, order and repetition depend on the project: a small web page needs light planning, a safety-critical system heavy modeling and reviews; agile projects interleave them in short iterations. The process flow (linear/iterative/evolutionary/parallel) adapts them.

sections.title: Lesson 12 — Prescriptive Models: Waterfall, Incremental, Prototyping, Spiral (+ V, RAD, UP)
sections.html:
ModelHow it worksAdvantagesDisadvantagesUse when
Waterfall (pp. 17–22)communication → planning → modeling → construction → deployment, once, sequentiallysimple to use; understandable workflow; easily manageable as requirements are knownclient must give all requirements up front; testing and client evaluation only at the end → high risk; no iterationsmall projects, well-defined stable requirements
Incremental (pp. 23–28)core product first, then increments adding features; feedback after eachflexible to change; modifications throughout; errors mitigated by client review; early working product; easy testing; low initial costhard to split into increments; total cost high; complete planning needed up front; refining requirements may hurt architectureclient wants primitive functionality quickly
Prototyping (pp. 31–35)build prototypes from known requirements; client evaluates; repeat until acceptableactive client involvement; early error detection; detailed requirements not needed to startcan slow the process; frequent change adds complexity; prototypes may be scrappedvague requirements, unclear module behaviour
Spiral (pp. 36–40)series of versions; each loop includes risk analysis (planning, risk analysis, engineering, evaluation)rigorous risk handling; changes possible latecostly and complicated; needs risk-assessment expertiselarge, high-risk, uncertain projects

Evolutionary (pp. 29–30): suits changing requirements when a complete product cannot be delivered by the deadline but a limited version can; unlike incremental (requirements fixed up front, refined per increment), requirements evolve. Food for thought (pp. 41–42): prescriptive models bring order, but some chaos aids creativity — leads to agile.

Note

Textbook models for older questions. V model: waterfall with a test level paired to each phase — requirements ↔ acceptance test, system design ↔ system test, architecture ↔ integration test, module design ↔ unit test, coding at the bottom. RAD: 60–90-day cycles, component reuse and parallel teams; a 'high-speed waterfall' because the same phases are compressed with automation and reuse. Unified Process (RUP): phases inception, elaboration, construction, transition (+ production); use-case driven, architecture-centric, iterative and incremental; disciplines (workflows) run concurrently in each phase, so the product evolves.

Practice — Lesson 12

(a) Actual — 2024-25 Q1(c). (b) Actual — 2021-22 Q6(a) / 2017-18 Q2(a). (c) Actual — 2016-17 Q5(b). (d) Actual — 2013-14 Q4(d) / 2011-12 Q8(a). (e) Actual — 2012-13 Q1(b). (f) Actual — 2011-12 Q8(b) / 2012-13 Q1(d). (g) Actual — 2018-19 Q8(a)–(b).

(a) 'Personalized Mental Health Companion' app (track mental states, AI exercises, virtual companion); only high-level requirements; the team chooses incremental development to get feedback after each part. Is incremental suitable? Propose alternatives if more appropriate. (10)

(b) How do incremental and evolutionary models address waterfall's shortcomings? / Problems of waterfall and models that solve them. (10 / 7)

(c) Describe the spiral model; arguments for and against it. (15)

(d) Suitable process model: (i) innovative scientific software with unknown issues (ii) quick stock-brokerage solution for a new instrument (iii) large software with very unstable users; impatient, result-oriented client who keeps changing requirements. (9 / 10)

(e) 'Waterfall may lead to blocking states' — agree? (7)

(f) Four phases of RUP and four differences from waterfall. (12 / 15)

(g) V model; when to use incremental; four problems of evolutionary models. (7, 2+8)

Show solution

(a) Partly suitable. For: early working core (mood tracking) gives feedback; requirements are high-level so increments let them be refined; the client sees progress. Against: AI exercises and a virtual companion are uncertain and high-risk (clinical safety, data privacy, model behaviour); incremental needs a fairly complete plan and architecture up front and refining requirements each increment can break the architecture. Better: Spiral (risk analysis each loop — privacy, safety, AI accuracy) combined with prototyping of the companion UI, or an agile (Scrum) process with short sprints, user testing and a risk backlog. Recommended: spiral/agile hybrid — build a prototype of the AI companion in early loops, then deliver features in sprints.

(b) Waterfall shortcomings: requirements fixed early, late testing, late client feedback, no iteration, nothing usable until the end. Incremental: a working core early, feedback after each increment, changes accommodated in later increments, errors found earlier, lower initial cost. Evolutionary (prototyping/spiral): requirements can evolve; prototypes clarify vague needs; spiral adds explicit risk analysis per loop.

(c) Description from the table and figure; for: risk-driven, accommodates change, early prototypes, suits large projects; against: costly and complex, depends on risk-assessment expertise, hard to convince clients the evolution is controllable, not for small projects.

(d) (i) Spiral (or prototyping) — innovation and unknown issues need risk analysis and experiments. (ii) RAD / incremental or Scrum — quick delivery of core functionality, requirements fairly clear. (iii) Prototyping / agile — unstable users need to see and react to working versions. Impatient client who keeps changing requirements: an agile model (Scrum or XP) — fixed-length sprints keep control (changes go into the backlog and are prioritised for the next sprint), the client sees working software every 2–4 weeks.

(e) Agree. In waterfall each phase waits for the previous one to be completed and signed off; team members who finish early (e.g. testers) sit idle until construction ends, and a question in one phase blocks the next — 'blocking states'. Iterative/agile models avoid this by overlapping activities.

(f) Inception (business case, scope, key use cases), elaboration (architecture baseline, most use cases, risks), construction (build and test increments), transition (beta, deployment, training). Differences: RUP is iterative and incremental (waterfall single pass); disciplines overlap in every phase (waterfall: one activity per phase); risks attacked early through architecture; working executable at the end of each iteration; use-case driven; changes accommodated between iterations.

(g) V model — NOTE above. Incremental when the client needs core functionality quickly, requirements are mostly known, staffing is limited, or technical risks can be deferred. Evolutionary problems: process not visible (no regular deliverables); systems poorly structured by continual change; hard to plan cost/time (unknown number of cycles); special skills needed; prototype may be mistaken for the product.

sections.title: Lesson 13 — Agile Principles and Extreme Programming
sections.html:
Why agile (p. 44): earlier models are slow, business is fast and changing. Agile = 'moving quickly' — rapid, incremental delivery; delivery over analysis and design; continuous communication with the client (pp. 46–49). Agile processes discourage detailed analysis, planning and documentation and are flexible to change in team and product. Plans are short-lived: some features persist, some change, some are dropped; focus is on construction (pp. 50–51).

The 12 agile principles (Agile Manifesto 2001, pp. 52–55)

  1. Satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.
  2. Welcome changing requirements, even late, for the client's competitive advantage.
  3. Deliver working software frequently — weeks to a couple of months, prefer shorter.
  4. Client and developers work together regularly throughout the project.
  5. Build projects around motivated individuals; give them environment, support and trust.
  6. Face-to-face conversation is the most efficient way to convey information.
  7. Working software is the primary measure of progress.
  8. Sustainable development: a constant pace indefinitely.
  9. Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility.
  10. Simplicity — the art of maximising the amount of work not done — is essential.
  11. The best architectures, requirements and designs emerge from self-organising teams.
  12. At regular intervals the team reflects on how to become more effective and adjusts.

Human factors (p. 56): competent, skilful, knowledgeable, committed, collaborative, decisive, faithful, respectful, self-organised people.

Extreme Programming (pp. 58–63)

  • Kent Beck: take good practices to extreme levels from day one; lightweight — the simplest thing that works.
  • Values: communication with clients, simplicity, feedback, respect (and courage); customer satisfaction first.
  • Whole-team problem solving; pair programming — two developers at one computer design, code and test user stories.
  • Advantages: simple code easy to modify; testing from day one; energising environment. Disadvantages: design may be neglected; little documentation and monitoring → repeated errors.
  • Planning/feedback loops (p. 63): release plan (months) → iteration plan (weeks) → acceptance test (days) → stand-up (one day) → pair negotiation (hours) → unit test (minutes) → pair programming (seconds).
Note

Textbook XP activities: planning (user stories, story points, project velocity = stories (points) completed per iteration, used to plan the next release), design (KISS, CRC cards, spike solutions = quick prototypes for a hard problem), coding (unit tests first, pair programming, continuous integration), testing (daily unit tests, customer acceptance tests). ASD phases: speculation, collaboration, learning.

Practice — Lesson 13

(a) Actual — 2021-22 Q7(a). (b) Actual — 2023-24 Q8(a). (c) Actual — 2016-17 Q6(b). (d) Actual — 2018-19 Q5(b). (e) Actual — 2017-18 Q2(d). (f) Actual — 2012-13 Q2(d).

(a) Reasons to shift from traditional to agile development. (10)

(b) A scenario chooses between incremental and agile development — justify the better choice. (8)

(c) Explain how XP follows the agility principles. (15)

(d) Draw development cost vs schedule progress for agile development. (10)

(e) Is pair programming more efficient? (7)

(f) Project velocity in XP with an example. (6⅔)

Show solution

(a) Requirements change fast and cannot be frozen; markets need early releases; waterfall gives late feedback and high risk; heavy documentation slows teams; agile delivers working software every few weeks, welcomes change, involves the client continuously, reduces risk through frequent feedback, and motivates self-organising teams (cite principles 1, 2, 3, 4, 7).

(b) Choose agile when requirements are unclear or changing and the client can be involved continuously; choose incremental when requirements are known and stable, a complete plan/architecture is possible, and contracts need fixed scope. State the scenario's facts against these two lists.

(c) Map XP practices to principles: small releases (1, 3); on-site customer and user stories (4, 6); welcome change via short iterations and refactoring (2); test-first and continuous integration (7, 9); simple design, YAGNI (10); 40-hour week (8); pair programming and collective ownership (5, 11); iteration retrospective (12).

(d) In agile the cost of change stays almost flat as the schedule progresses, while in conventional development it rises steeply:

cost of change
   ^                                   / conventional (waterfall)
   |                                 /
   |                              /
   |                          /
   |                    _ _ /_ _ _ _ _ _ _ _  agile (flat, low)
   |            _ _ - -/
   |  _ _ - - -      /
   +-----------------------------------------> development schedule progress

(e) Usually yes for quality: continuous review catches defects early, knowledge spreads, design is better, less rework; studies show about 15 % more effort but ~15 % fewer defects. Less efficient for trivial tasks or mismatched pairs. Overall efficient when rework and maintenance are counted.

(f) Velocity = story points completed in an iteration. Example: iterations completed 20, 24, 22 points → average 22; the release backlog has 132 points → about 6 iterations; if velocity drops, re-plan or reduce scope.

sections.title: Lesson 14 — Scrum and Kanban
sections.html:
Scrum (pp. 64–72)

Named after the rugby formation; a lightweight, iterative, incremental agile process — simple, gradual, frequent delivery; widely used.

TermMeaning
Sprintunit cycle of development, 2 weeks to 1 month
Product backlogall client requirements of the product
Sprint backlogrequirements selected for the current sprint
Daily scrumdaily synchronisation meeting on plans and progress
Scrum masterusually the project manager (facilitator)
Product ownerthe client (owns and prioritises the product backlog)
Tickets / scrum boardsubtasks and the board that tracks them
Product backlog --(sprint planning: choose items)--> Sprint backlog
      ^                                                    |
      |  unfinished items go back                          v
      +------------------------------------------  SPRINT (2-4 weeks)
                                                  planning -> implementation (daily scrum) ->
                                                  product review -> process review (retrospective)
                                                           |
                                                           v
                                          Potentially shippable increment -> client feedback

Advantages: less hierarchy, freedom; adaptability; products deliverable sooner; more client involvement; retrospective reduces mistakes. Disadvantage: works best with small teams.

Kanban (pp. 73–83)

看板 = signboard. Heavy visualisation so everyone is always up to date. Tasks split into subtasks, each on a Kanban card with the user story; cards move on a board (To-Do → In Progress → Done). Pull system: a free member pulls the next card. Agile coach, daily stand-ups and retrospectives exist, but there are no sprints — continuous flow. Advantages: leadership from everyone, adapts to the team, workload per card adjusted to keep a decent lead time. Disadvantage: no fixed time-frame → possible delay.

Practice — Lesson 14

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q6(c) / 2021-22 Q5(b). (b) Actual — 2022-23 Q6(b) / 2021-22 Q8(b). (c) Actual — 2016-17 Q6(a). (d) Actual — 2017-18 Q2(e). (e) Actual — 2014-15 Q4(d) / 2011-12 Q5(c).

(a) Activities in a Scrum sprint; the two kinds of backlog. (15 / 20)

(b) Kanban: how workload per card affects lead time; visualisation with cards and board. (10 / 15)

(c) Short notes: sprint, backlog, pair programming, code refactoring, spike solution. (3×5)

(d) Write Scrum meeting minutes for a digital library project. (7)

(e) Distinguishing features of Scrum; Scrum vs plan-based management (people allocation, cost estimation, team cohesion, membership changes). (10 / 18)

Show solution

(a) Product owner orders the product backlog → sprint planning selects items into the sprint backlog and breaks them into tickets → implementation with daily scrums (what I did, what I will do, blockers) → product review (demo to the client) → retrospective (process review) → increment delivered; unfinished items return to the product backlog for the next sprint. Product backlog = all requirements; sprint backlog = this sprint's subset.

(b) Lead time = time for a card from To-Do to Done. If cards pile up in In Progress, each card is too big — reduce the work per card (split it) so cards flow and lead time falls; if cards fly through with idle capacity, increase the work per card (p. 81). Board: columns To-Do / In Progress / Done (often with WIP limits), cards show the subtask, the user story, owner and due date; everyone sees status at a glance.

(c) Sprint and backlog — table. Pair programming — two developers, one computer: driver types, navigator reviews; roles swap. Refactoring — improving internal structure without changing behaviour (Refactoring notes). Spike solution — a small throw-away prototype to explore a risky technical problem and estimate it.

(d) Daily scrum, Digital Library, Sprint 3, Day 4 — Present: PO Rahim (observer), SM Nadia, devs A, B, C. A: done 'search by author'; today 'search by ISBN'; blocker: none. B: done borrow API; today due-date reminder; blocker: SMS gateway key pending (SM to follow up). C: done catalogue UI; today pagination; blocker: none. Burndown: 18 of 30 points left, on track. Action items: SM gets SMS key by 2 pm. Next scrum: 10 am tomorrow.

(e) Features: sprints, roles (PO, SM, team), backlogs, daily scrum, review, retrospective, time-boxing, self-organisation. vs plan-based: people allocation — team self-assigns tasks per sprint vs manager assigns from a full plan; cost estimation — per sprint from velocity and story points, refined continuously vs up-front estimate of the whole project; team cohesion — stable small cross-functional team with daily contact vs functional silos; membership change — knowledge shared through daily scrum and collective ownership makes replacement easier, while plan-based relies on documentation.

sections.title: Lesson 15 — Unit Testing, JUnit, Fixtures and Test-Driven Development
sections.html:
Unit tests are white-box tests written by developers to verify small units of program functionality, written concurrently with the implementation (pp. 1–2).

Property of a good unit test (p. 3)Meaning
Automaticruns completely by itself, no human input
Atomicdecides pass/fail by itself, no human interpretation
Single responsibilitytests exactly one feature
Independentruns in isolation from other tests (even of the same function)
Repeatablesame result on every run

JUnit (pp. 4–17)

public class MathTest {                      // pp. 7-11 (Math.add / Math.sub)
    private Math calc;
    @Before public void setUp()    { calc = new Math(); }   // fixture, before EACH test
    @After  public void tearDown() { calc = null; }        // clean-up after each test
    @Test public void testAdd() {
        assertEquals(11, calc.add(5, 6));  assertEquals(0, calc.add(0, 0));
        assertEquals(-10, calc.add(-5, -5)); assertEquals(1, calc.add(-5, 6));
    }
    @Test public void testSub() {
        assertEquals(-1, calc.sub(5, 6));  assertEquals(0, calc.sub(0, 0));
        assertEquals(0, calc.sub(-5, -5)); assertEquals(-11, calc.sub(-5, 6));
    }
}
Assertion (p. 12)Fails if
assertTrue(test) / assertFalse(test)test is false / true
assertEquals(expected, actual)values not equal (equals)
assertSame / assertNotSamenot the same object / the same object (==)
assertNull(v) / assertNotNull(v)v not null / v null
fail()always — e.g. after a call that should have thrown

Every assertion may take a message first: assertEquals("message", expected, actual). Framework features (p. 13): fixtures (fixed baseline state so results are repeatable — @Before, @Test, @After), test suites (@RunWith + @Suite bundle test classes), test runners, JUnit classes.

Trap

Write the expected value first (pp. 19–20); give tests long descriptive names (test_addDays_wrapToNextMonth_2, p. 22); use expected-answer objects (assertEquals(new Date(2050,3,1), d), p. 21); messages should say what is being checked, not repeat the values JUnit already prints (pp. 23–24).

Test-driven development (textbook)

  1. Add a test for the next small piece of functionality.
  2. Run all tests — the new one fails (red).
  3. Write the minimum code to make it pass.
  4. Run all tests — all pass (green).
  5. Refactor the code (and tests), re-run — still green; repeat.

Benefits: every line is covered by a test (safety net for refactoring); forces small, decoupled, testable design; requirements clarified before coding; fewer defects and less debugging; tests document the behaviour; quick feedback.

Practice — Lesson 15

(a) Actual — 2024-25 Q6(a). (b) Actual — 2019-20 Q7(a). (c) Actual — 2023-24 Q3(a) / 2016-17 Q7(a). (d) Actual — 2014-15 Q2(c) / 2013-14 Q3(c). (e) Actual — 2010-11 Q6(e).

(a) isLeapYear(int year) returns true for leap years, false otherwise, and throws IllegalArgumentException if year ≤ 0. Write a complete JUnit test class covering all logically distinct input classes including invalid input; meaningful names and assertions. (15)

(b) What are fixtures in unit testing? Give 3 examples. Write a unit-test method for the partitions of a grading system A > 80, B 70–80, C 60–70, with boundary value analysis. (20)

(c) Describe TDD and its benefits / five steps of TDD demonstrated on an example. (12 / 15)

(d) Write an automated tester (driver) for a module that sorts floating-point data, checking the order and that output and input are the same data set; generate different sizes. (13 / 12)

(e) Design test cases for a Queue class. (15)

Show solution

(a) Input classes: divisible by 4 not by 100 (leap); not divisible by 4 (not leap); divisible by 100 not by 400 (not leap); divisible by 400 (leap); boundary 1 and 4; invalid 0 and negative (exception).

// 2024-25 Q6(a) — one test per logically distinct input class
import static org.junit.Assert.*;
import org.junit.Test;

public class LeapYearTest {
    @Test
    public void divisibleBy4NotBy100_isLeap() {
        assertTrue("2024 is divisible by 4 but not by 100", LeapYear.isLeapYear(2024));
    }
    @Test
    public void notDivisibleBy4_isNotLeap() {
        assertFalse("2023 is not divisible by 4", LeapYear.isLeapYear(2023));
    }
    @Test
    public void divisibleBy100NotBy400_isNotLeap() {
        assertFalse("1900 is a century year not divisible by 400", LeapYear.isLeapYear(1900));
    }
    @Test
    public void divisibleBy400_isLeap() {
        assertTrue("2000 is divisible by 400", LeapYear.isLeapYear(2000));
    }
    @Test
    public void smallestValidYear_isNotLeap() {
        assertFalse("year 1 (boundary)", LeapYear.isLeapYear(1));
    }
    @Test
    public void firstLeapYear_isLeap() {
        assertTrue("year 4", LeapYear.isLeapYear(4));
    }
    @Test(expected = IllegalArgumentException.class)
    public void zero_throws() {
        LeapYear.isLeapYear(0);
    }
    @Test(expected = IllegalArgumentException.class)
    public void negativeYear_throws() {
        LeapYear.isLeapYear(-4);
    }
}

(b) Fixture = fixed, known state created before each test so results are repeatable. Examples: an object under test created in @Before (new Grader / new Math); a set of test data arrays; a temporary file or in-memory database prepared and removed in @After. Partitions and boundaries: A {81, 90, 100}, B {71, 75, 80}, C {61, 65, 70}, below C {60}, invalid {−1, 101}.

public class Grader {
    // A: mark > 80, B: 70 < mark <= 80, C: 60 < mark <= 70, otherwise F; valid marks 0..100
    public static char grade(int mark) {
        if (mark < 0 || mark > 100) throw new IllegalArgumentException("mark out of range");
        if (mark > 80) return 'A';
        if (mark > 70) return 'B';
        if (mark > 60) return 'C';
        return 'F';
    }
}
// 2019-20 Q7(a) — fixture + equivalence partitions + boundary values
import static org.junit.Assert.*;
import org.junit.After;
import org.junit.Before;
import org.junit.Test;

public class GraderTest {
    private int[] aMarks, bMarks, cMarks;

    @Before                                    // fixture: fresh test data before every test
    public void setUp() {
        aMarks = new int[]{81, 90, 100};       // just above 80, nominal, upper limit
        bMarks = new int[]{71, 75, 80};        // just above 70, nominal, boundary 80
        cMarks = new int[]{61, 65, 70};        // just above 60, nominal, boundary 70
    }
    @After
    public void tearDown() { aMarks = bMarks = cMarks = null; }

    @Test
    public void partitionA_above80() {
        for (int m : aMarks) assertEquals("mark " + m, 'A', Grader.grade(m));
    }
    @Test
    public void partitionB_71to80() {
        for (int m : bMarks) assertEquals("mark " + m, 'B', Grader.grade(m));
    }
    @Test
    public void partitionC_61to70() {
        for (int m : cMarks) assertEquals("mark " + m, 'C', Grader.grade(m));
    }
    @Test
    public void boundary60_isNotC() {
        assertEquals("mark 60", 'F', Grader.grade(60));
    }
    @Test(expected = IllegalArgumentException.class)
    public void invalid_aboveRange() { Grader.grade(101); }
    @Test(expected = IllegalArgumentException.class)
    public void invalid_negative() { Grader.grade(-1); }
}

(c) Steps and benefits above. Example (stack of int): (1) test push then size() == 1 → fails (no class). (2) red. (3) write Stack with push and size. (4) green. (5) refactor; next test: pop returns last pushed → red → implement pop → green; next test: pop on empty throws → implement → green; refactor array growth.

(d) 

// 2014-15 Q2(c) / 2013-14 Q3(c) — automated tester (driver) for a float sort: order + same multiset of data
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Random;

public class SortTester {
    static void sortDescending(float[] a) {              // module under test
        Arrays.sort(a);
        for (int i = 0, j = a.length - 1; i < j; i++, j--) { float t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t; }
    }
    static boolean isDescending(float[] a) {
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i - 1] < a[i]) return false;
        return true;
    }
    static boolean sameData(float[] in, float[] out) {   // 'originality': permutation of the input
        float[] x = in.clone(), y = out.clone();
        Arrays.sort(x); Arrays.sort(y);
        return Arrays.equals(x, y);
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Random r = new Random(42);
        int[] sizes = {0, 1, 2, 10, 1000};                // driver generates different sizes
        boolean all = true;
        for (int n : sizes) {
            float[] in = new float[n];
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) in[i] = r.nextInt(50) - 25 + r.nextFloat();   // duplicates and negatives
            float[] out = in.clone();
            sortDescending(out);
            boolean ok = isDescending(out) && sameData(in, out);
            all &= ok;
            System.out.println("n=" + n + (ok ? " PASS" : " FAIL"));
        }
        System.out.println(all ? "ALL PASS" : "SOME FAILED");
    }
}

(e) Cases: new queue empty; FIFO order; wrap-around of a circular buffer; dequeue from empty throws; enqueue on full throws; invalid capacity.

// 2010-11 Q6(e) — test cases for a Queue class
import static org.junit.Assert.*;
import org.junit.Before;
import org.junit.Test;

public class QueueTest {
    private BoundedQueue<Integer> q;
    @Before public void setUp() { q = new BoundedQueue<>(3); }

    @Test public void newQueue_isEmpty() { assertTrue(q.isEmpty()); assertEquals(0, q.size()); }
    @Test public void fifoOrder() {
        q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(2); q.enqueue(3);
        assertEquals(Integer.valueOf(1), q.dequeue());
        assertEquals(Integer.valueOf(2), q.dequeue());
    }
    @Test public void wrapAround_keepsOrder() {
        q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(2); q.dequeue(); q.enqueue(3); q.enqueue(4);
        assertEquals(Integer.valueOf(2), q.dequeue());
        assertEquals(Integer.valueOf(3), q.dequeue());
        assertEquals(Integer.valueOf(4), q.dequeue());
    }
    @Test(expected = IllegalStateException.class) public void dequeueEmpty_throws() { q.dequeue(); }
    @Test(expected = IllegalStateException.class) public void enqueueFull_throws() {
        q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(2); q.enqueue(3); q.enqueue(4);
    }
    @Test(expected = IllegalArgumentException.class) public void zeroCapacity_throws() { new BoundedQueue<Integer>(0); }
}

sections.title: Lesson 16 — Code Reviews: Workflow, Issues, Best Practices, Metrics
sections.html:
Opening examples (pp. 1–4): style inconsistency, a silly redundant check, a buffer overflow (unterminated msgbuf), an XSS hole (unescaped text). Code review = 'the process of analyzing code written by a teammate (i.e. a peer) to judge whether it is of sufficient quality to be integrated into the main project codebase' (p. 5).

Author writes code -> review request -> Reviewer accepts -> reviews code -> Accepted?
     ^                                                                     | no      | yes
     +---------------------- author edits code <---------------------------+        +--> approval -> merge
                                                                         (or abandon)
Simplified (p. 11): local branch -> push to Gerrit/GitHub -> reviewer notified -> approved -> push to main

History (pp. 7–8): Fagan inspection — planning, overview, preparation, meeting, rework, follow-up; improves quality but is process-heavy, meetings are hard to arrange, cost is high and adoption low. Modern tool-based review: Gerrit, Review Board, Phabricator, Crucible (p. 9). Effort (p. 10): about 6 h/week, 10–15 % of developer time — for 50,000 developers at $50/h: 50,000 × 6 × 50 = $15,000,000 per week.

Issues identified during code review (pp. 12–13)Example
Coding styleinconsistent naming/indentation
Redundant checksthe same null check twice
Project design violationUI class calls the database directly, bypassing the service layer
Misunderstood requirementsdiscount applied before tax instead of after
Critical security defectsbuffer overflow, SQL injection, XSS
Malicious codehidden back door / logic bomb
Inadequate input validationnegative quantity accepted
Unsafe methodsstrcpy, gets, eval
Lack of exception handlingfile read without try/catch or resource close

Best practices (SmartBear, pp. 14–20)

  1. Review fewer than 200–400 lines at a time (defect discovery drops after that).
  2. Authors annotate the source before the review (where to look first, why each change).
  3. Set quantifiable goals and capture metrics: inspection rate (LOC reviewed per hour), defect rate (defects found per hour of review), defect density (defects per LOC, e.g. per KLOC).
  4. Use checklists — developers repeat the same mistakes, and omissions are the hardest defects to find.
  5. Verify that defects are actually fixed (log, discuss, approve the fix).
  6. Foster a positive culture: defects are chances to improve, not a measure of the person.

Other (indirect) benefits (p. 21): project awareness, peer impression formation, consistent coding style, design discussion, knowledge dissemination.

Practice — Lesson 16

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q2(b) / 2020-21 Q6(c). (b) Actual — 2018-19 Q1(c). (c) Actual — 2017-18 Q5(c). (d) Actual — 2019-20 Q3(b). (e) Actual — 2021-22 Q8(a). (f) Actual — 2016-17 Q3(b). (g) Actual — 2012-13 Q4(a). (h) Actual — 2014-15 Q1(d).

(a) Issues commonly identified during code review — three examples. (12 / 8)

(b) Defect rate and defect density; why checklists are used in code review. (9)

(c) Indirect benefits of code review in a company, with examples. (9)

(d) Limited budget: employ reviewers for SRS, design and code, or hire more (cheaper) testers? Justify. (15)

(e) Driver and navigator in pair programming as a form of code review. (10)

(f) Checklist for a code reviewer to review the non-functional requirements. (15)

(g) Four data faults to check when inspecting a C project. (6)

(h) Scenario of reviewing a quick-sort method: participants and sample queries. (10)

Show solution

(a) Any three rows of the table, each with a two-line code example, e.g. unsafe method: strcpy(buf, input) into char buf[8] — buffer overflow → use strncpy/snprintf; inadequate validation: withdraw(amount) without checking amount > 0; lack of exception handling: FileReader opened without try-with-resources.

(b) Defect rate = defects found per hour of review (e.g. 12 defects in 3 h = 4/h). Defect density = defects per unit size (e.g. 12 defects in 2,400 LOC = 5 per KLOC). Checklists: people make the same mistakes repeatedly, and omissions (missing null checks, missing error handling) are hard to notice because the code is not there; a checklist makes reviewers look for them every time and gives consistent reviews.

(c) p. 21 list with examples: project awareness (reviewers learn what changed elsewhere); peer impression formation (trust in good engineers); consistent coding style; design discussion (better solutions proposed); knowledge dissemination (juniors learn, bus factor reduced).

(d) Keep (some) reviewers. Defects found in requirements and design reviews cost far less to fix than defects found by testers after coding (cost grows ~10× per phase); reviews also find defects testing cannot (design violations, maintainability, security holes, missing requirements) and spread knowledge. Testers still needed, so: lightweight peer reviews by the developers themselves (tool-based, checklist, < 400 LOC) instead of dedicated reviewers, reviews focused on SRS and critical modules, and the remaining budget on testers.

(e) The driver types the code; the navigator continuously reviews it — spotting bugs, thinking about design, edge cases and tests — and roles switch often. It is real-time code review: defects are caught as they are written, no separate review meeting is needed, and both share knowledge. Limits: both may share the same blind spots, so a later independent review is still useful for critical code.

(f) Performance (no N+1 queries, efficient algorithms, caching, no blocking calls in UI thread); security (input validation, parameterised queries, output encoding, secrets not hard-coded, least privilege); reliability (exception handling, resources closed, retries/timeouts); usability (clear messages, accessibility); maintainability (naming, small methods, no duplication, comments); portability (no OS-specific paths); scalability (stateless services, connection pooling); logging/auditability.

(g) Variables used before initialisation; constants not named (magic numbers); array bounds not checked (off-by-one, upper bound = size − 1); buffer overflow on character strings (missing '\0', strcpy); pointer faults (dangling or NULL pointers, memory not freed).

(h) Participants: author (explains), moderator/lead, reader, reviewers (peer developer, tester), recorder. Sample queries: Is the pivot choice safe for already-sorted input (worst case O(n²))? Does the partition handle duplicates and the 0- and 1-element arrays? Can recursion depth overflow the stack for large n? Are the indices lo/hi inclusive and is hi = n − 1 passed? Is the sort stable — is that required? Are there unit tests for empty, sorted, reverse-sorted and all-equal arrays?

sections.title: Lesson 17 — What Refactoring Is; Why, When and Its Problems
sections.html:
Memorize

Refactoring (Fowler, noun): a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior. (Verb): to restructure software by applying a series of refactorings without changing its observable behavior (p. 8).

  • External behaviour unchanged (functional requirements kept), internal structure improved — 'improving the design after it has been written' (p. 2).
  • Simple examples: consolidate duplicate conditional fragments (send() moved after the if/else, p. 3); replace magic number 9.81 with GRAVITATIONAL_CONSTANT (p. 4).
  • Dangerous: can introduce bugs; managers see time not spent on features → make it systematic, incremental and safe (p. 5).
  • Useful: designs are rarely right first time and requirements change; code often shrinks and becomes simpler (p. 6).
  • Contrast with performance optimisation: also keeps functionality but often makes code harder to understand (p. 9).
  • Safe refactoring: use named refactoring patterns, and test constantly — run the tests after every step (p. 10).
Why refactor (p. 11)When (p. 12)Problems (p. 13)
improves design (stops decay); easier to understand; helps find bugs; helps program fasterRule of Three (third duplication → refactor); when adding a function (before or after); when fixing a bug; during code reviewdatabases are tightly coupled and hard to change; published interfaces cannot change

Finding where to refactor: look for bad smells (p. 14); tools such as Codegrip, Checkstyle, PMD, FindBugs and SonarQube detect them automatically.

Note

Technical debt (2024-25 Q4(b), textbook): the future cost of rework caused by choosing a quick or easy solution now; code smells are its symptoms, refactoring is how it is repaid. Interest = the extra effort every change costs while the debt remains.

Practice — Lesson 17

(a) Actual — 2024-25 Q4(b). (b) Actual — 2017-18 Q2(c).

(a) Define code smell, tech-debt and code refactoring. Differentiate proactive and reactive risk-management strategies with examples. (15)

(b) Why is refactoring important in agile development? Examples. (7)

Show solution

(a) Code smell = a surface symptom in code that usually indicates a deeper design problem (e.g. a 200-line method, duplicated code). Technical debt = NOTE above. Refactoring = Fowler's definition. Reactive risk strategy: act only after a risk occurs (fire-fighting) — e.g. a key developer leaves and the team then scrambles to hire and learn the code. Proactive: identify, analyse and plan for risks before they happen (risk table, mitigation, monitoring, contingency) — e.g. pair programming and documentation so knowledge is shared before anyone leaves. Proactive is cheaper and is real risk management; reactive is crisis management.

(b) Agile builds the design incrementally with little up-front design, and requirements change every sprint; without refactoring the code decays into duplication and long methods, and velocity falls. Refactoring with automated tests (TDD) keeps the design simple (XP 'simple design', 'refactor mercilessly'). Examples: extract a duplicated validation into one method after the third user story needs it; replace a growing switch on payment type with polymorphic classes when a new payment method is added.

Practice — Lesson 18

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q5(a). (b) Actual — 2019-20 Q6(a). (c) Actual — 2021-22 Q6(c).

(a) Define with short code examples: shotgun surgery, parallel inheritance hierarchies, refused bequest, feature envy. (4+4+4+3)

(b) Two program snippets showing the smells Data Clump and Refused Bequest. (20)

(c) Define code smell; three examples. (10)

Show solution

(a)/(b) Each smell with before → after (compiled):

// 2019-20 Q6(a), 2022-23 Q5(a) — code smells with short examples and fixes (compile-checked)
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

// DATA CLUMP: the same three fields travel together  ->  Extract Class / Introduce Parameter Object
class MeetingBefore {
    void schedule(int startDay, int startMonth, int startYear, int endDay, int endMonth, int endYear) { }
}
class SimpleDate { final int d, m, y; SimpleDate(int d, int m, int y) { this.d = d; this.m = m; this.y = y; } }
class MeetingAfter { void schedule(SimpleDate start, SimpleDate end) { } }

// REFUSED BEQUEST: subclass inherits methods it does not want  ->  Replace Inheritance with Delegation / push down
class Bird { void fly() { System.out.println("flying"); } void eat() { } }
class PenguinBefore extends Bird {
    void fly() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException("penguins can't fly"); }   // refuses the bequest
}
abstract class Animal { void eat() { } }
class FlyingBird extends Animal { void fly() { } }
class Penguin extends Animal { void swim() { } }                                 // after: no unwanted method

// FEATURE ENVY: a method uses another class's data more than its own -> Move Method
class Customer2 { double totalSpent; int yearsAsMember;
    double loyaltyDiscount() {                                                    // after: moved here
        if (totalSpent > 1000 && yearsAsMember > 2) return totalSpent * 0.15;
        if (totalSpent > 500) return totalSpent * 0.10;
        return 0;
    }
}
class Invoice2 { double discountFor(Customer2 c) { return c.loyaltyDiscount(); } }

// SHOTGUN SURGERY: one rule copied into many classes -> Move Method / Extract Class to one place
class AccountRules { static final double MIN_BALANCE = 500;
    static void checkMinimum(double balanceAfter) {
        if (balanceAfter < MIN_BALANCE) throw new IllegalStateException("Balance would fall below " + MIN_BALANCE);
    }
}
class Debit    { void run(double bal, double amt) { AccountRules.checkMinimum(bal - amt); } }
class Transfer { void run(double bal, double amt) { AccountRules.checkMinimum(bal - amt); } }

// PARALLEL INHERITANCE HIERARCHIES: every new Employee subclass needs a new Printer subclass -> merge via polymorphism
abstract class Employee2 { abstract String report(); }           // after: each employee reports itself
class Engineer2 extends Employee2 { String report() { return "Engineer report"; } }
class Salesman2 extends Employee2 { String report() { return "Salesman report"; } }
// before: Engineer/EngineerPrinter, Salesman/SalesmanPrinter grew in parallel

public class SmellExamples {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Employee2> staff = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Engineer2(), new Salesman2()));
        for (Employee2 e : staff) System.out.println(e.report());
        Customer2 c = new Customer2(); c.totalSpent = 1200; c.yearsAsMember = 3;
        System.out.println("discount " + new Invoice2().discountFor(c));
    }
}

(c) Definition (Lesson 17) + any three rows of the table with a two-line example each.

sections.title: Lesson 19 — The Refactoring Catalogue and Worked TF Refactorings
sections.html:
Refactoring (p. 30)DoSlide example
Extract Method (pp. 31–32)turn a fragment into a method named after its purposeprint_invoice → calculate_total
Extract Class (p. 33)one class doing two jobs → move fields/methods to a new classPerson → TelephoneNumber

Replace Temp with Query (pp. 36–38)temp → private method usable elsewherebasePrice → getBasePrice()

Replace Conditional with Polymorphism (pp. 41–42)each branch → overriding methodBird.getSpeed per subclass

Introduce Parameter Object (pp. 45–46)group parameters that travel togetherDateRange(start, end, includes)
Also: Introduce Null Object, Encapsulate Collection, Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses
// Extract Variable (p. 35)
double calculatePrice(double quantity, double itemPrice) {
    double basePrice = quantity * itemPrice;
    boolean isBulkOrder = quantity > 100;
    double discountRate = isBulkOrder ? 0.9 : 0.95;
    return basePrice * discountRate;
}

Practice — Lesson 19

(a) Actual — 2022-23 Q5(b). (b) Actual — 2021-22 Q1(b). (c) Actual — 2023-24 Q8(c). (d) Actual — 2024-25 Q4(a).

(a) Which refactorings, and the refactored code: (i) renderBanner with if ((platform.toUpperCase().indexOf("MAC") > -1) && (browser.toUpperCase().indexOf("IE") > -1) && wasInitialized() && resize > 0) (ii) getSalary() with switch (type) Football / Cricket / Badminton (iii) getPayAmount() with nested if-else on isDead, isSeparated, isRetired. (6+7+7)

(b) GetSuperHeroItem.getItem(heroName) is an if-else chain (IronMan → suit, Thor → hammer, CaptainAmerica → shield, Hawkeye → arrow, else null). Rewrite it to be easier to read and maintain, with constant amortised run time. (13)

(c) Define bad smells and refactoring; identify the smells in DiscountCalculator.calculateDiscount(customerType, productType, price, customerName, customerId) (if-chain on REGULAR/PREMIUM × ELECTRONICS/GROCERY with 10/5/20/10 %) and OrderProcessor.processOrder(...) (prints customer data twice, if-chains on the same strings, compares discount == price × 0.1 / 0.15 / 0.25), and revise the code. (20)

(d) Identify five bad smells in Student (type code 1 = UG / 2 = PG, street/postOffice/district, yearWiseGpa, isFulltime for PG only, calculateFee and printDetails switching on type) and Scholarship (isRegular(Student), checkEligibility with deep nesting and duplicated CGPA loop) and refactor each. (20)

Show solution

(a) (i) Decompose Conditional / Extract Variable — name each part (isMacOs, isIE, wasResized). (ii) Replace Conditional with Polymorphism — Player subclasses override getSalary() (type code removed). (iii) Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses — return early; no temp 'result'.

// 2022-23 Q5(b) — (i) Decompose Conditional / Extract Variable, (ii) Replace Conditional with Polymorphism,
// (iii) Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses
class Banner {
    String platform = "MacOS", browser = "IE 11"; boolean initialized = true; int resize = 1;
    boolean wasInitialized() { return initialized; }
    void renderBanner() {
        final boolean isMacOs = platform.toUpperCase().indexOf("MAC") > -1;
        final boolean isIE = browser.toUpperCase().indexOf("IE") > -1;
        final boolean wasResized = resize > 0;
        if (isMacOs && isIE && wasInitialized() && wasResized) {
            System.out.println("render banner for Mac + IE");    // do something
        }
    }
}
abstract class Player {                                    // (ii)
    double baseSalary() { return 50000; }
    abstract double getSalary();
}
class FootballPlayer extends Player {
    double getWeeklyIncrement() { return 1000; }
    double getSalary() { return baseSalary() + getWeeklyIncrement() * 4; }
}
class CricketPlayer extends Player {
    double getMonthlyIncrement() { return 3000; }
    double getSalary() { return baseSalary() + getMonthlyIncrement(); }
}
class BadmintonPlayer extends Player {
    double getSalary() { return baseSalary(); }
}
class Payroll {                                            // (iii)
    boolean isDead, isSeparated, isRetired;
    double deadAmount() { return 1; } double separatedAmount() { return 2; }
    double retiredAmount() { return 3; } double normalPayAmount() { return 4; }
    double getPayAmount() {
        if (isDead) return deadAmount();
        if (isSeparated) return separatedAmount();
        if (isRetired) return retiredAmount();
        return normalPayAmount();
    }
}
public class Refactor2223 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Banner().renderBanner();
        for (Player p : new Player[]{new FootballPlayer(), new CricketPlayer(), new BadmintonPlayer()})
            System.out.println(p.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + p.getSalary());
        Payroll pr = new Payroll(); pr.isRetired = true;
        System.out.println("pay " + pr.getPayAmount());
    }
}

(b) Smells: long if-else chain (switch smell), magic strings, public fields. Refactoring: replace conditional with a lookup table (HashMap) filled once — getItem is O(1) amortised, a new hero is one register() call, and keys are lower-cased to keep equalsIgnoreCase behaviour.

// 2021-22 Q1(b) — if-else chain on names -> lookup table (HashMap): readable, O(1) amortised
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

class SuperHeroItem {
    final String name; SuperHeroItem(String n) { name = n; }
    public String toString() { return name; }
}
class GetSuperHeroItem {
    private final Map<String, SuperHeroItem> itemByHero = new HashMap<>();
    GetSuperHeroItem() {
        register("IronMan", new SuperHeroItem("suit"));
        register("Thor", new SuperHeroItem("hammer"));
        register("CaptainAmerica", new SuperHeroItem("shield"));
        register("Hawkeye", new SuperHeroItem("arrow"));
    }
    void register(String hero, SuperHeroItem item) { itemByHero.put(hero.toLowerCase(), item); }  // new hero = one call
    SuperHeroItem getItem(String heroName) {
        return heroName == null ? null : itemByHero.get(heroName.toLowerCase());   // case-insensitive, O(1)
    }
}
public class SuperHeroItems {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        GetSuperHeroItem g = new GetSuperHeroItem();
        System.out.println(g.getItem("thor") + " " + g.getItem("IRONMAN") + " " + g.getItem("Hulk"));
    }
}

(c) Smells: long parameter list and data clump (customerName, customerId, customerType); unused parameters (name and id in calculateDiscount); switch statements — if-chains on the type strings, repeated in both classes; magic numbers/strings; duplicated code (customer data printed twice); long method (processOrder); a logic bug hidden by the smells — discount is compared with price × 0.1 / 0.15 / 0.25 though the rates are 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, and doubles are compared with ==. Refactorings: Introduce Parameter Object (Customer, Product), Replace Type Code with enum + Replace Conditional with Polymorphism (rates inside CustomerType), Extract Method for printing, compute and print the rate instead of comparing doubles.

// 2023-24 Q8(c) — DiscountCalculator / OrderProcessor after refactoring
// Smells: long parameter list + data clump (customerName, customerId, customerType) -> Introduce Parameter Object Customer;
// unused parameters (name, id in calculateDiscount); switch-like if-chain on type codes -> polymorphic CustomerType enum;
// duplicated code (printing customer data twice, string comparisons repeated); magic numbers -> constants in the enum;
// long method processOrder -> Extract Method; bug: discount == price*0.15 / 0.25 never match the rates (0.05, 0.1, 0.2)
// and float comparison with == -> print the rate instead; feature envy on strings -> methods on Product/Customer.
enum ProductType { ELECTRONICS, GROCERY, OTHER }
enum CustomerType {
    REGULAR(0.10, 0.05), PREMIUM(0.20, 0.10);
    private final double electronicsRate, groceryRate;
    CustomerType(double e, double g) { electronicsRate = e; groceryRate = g; }
    double rateFor(ProductType p) {
        switch (p) {
            case ELECTRONICS: return electronicsRate;
            case GROCERY:     return groceryRate;
            default:          return 0;
        }
    }
}
class Customer {
    final String name, id; final CustomerType type;
    Customer(String name, String id, CustomerType type) { this.name = name; this.id = id; this.type = type; }
}
class Product {
    final ProductType type; final double price;
    Product(ProductType type, double price) { this.type = type; this.price = price; }
}
class DiscountCalculator {
    double discountRate(Customer c, Product p) { return c.type.rateFor(p.type); }
    double calculateDiscount(Customer c, Product p) { return p.price * discountRate(c, p); }
}
class OrderProcessor {
    private final DiscountCalculator calculator = new DiscountCalculator();
    void processOrder(Customer c, Product p) {
        double rate = calculator.discountRate(c, p);
        double discount = p.price * rate;
        printCustomer(c);
        printProduct(p);
        printPrices(p.price, discount, rate);
    }
    private void printCustomer(Customer c) {
        System.out.println("Processing order for " + c.name + " (" + c.id + "), " + c.type + " customer");
    }
    private void printProduct(Product p) { System.out.println(p.type + " item processed"); }
    private void printPrices(double price, double discount, double rate) {
        System.out.println("Original price: " + price);
        System.out.println(rate == 0 ? "No discount applied" : Math.round(rate * 100) + "% discount applied: " + discount);
        System.out.println("Final price: " + (price - discount));
    }
}
public class OrderRefactored {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderProcessor op = new OrderProcessor();
        op.processOrder(new Customer("Rina", "C-17", CustomerType.PREMIUM), new Product(ProductType.ELECTRONICS, 1000));
        op.processOrder(new Customer("Karim", "C-18", CustomerType.REGULAR), new Product(ProductType.GROCERY, 200));
        op.processOrder(new Customer("Karim", "C-18", CustomerType.REGULAR), new Product(ProductType.OTHER, 50));
    }
}

(d) Five smells → refactorings: (1) type code + switch (type 1/2 in calculateFee and printDetails) → Replace Type Code with Subclasses (UndergraduateStudent, PostgraduateStudent) + polymorphism; (2) data clump street/postOffice/district → Extract Class Address; (3) temporary field isFulltime used only for PG → move into PostgraduateStudent; (4) feature envy — Scholarship computes regularity and CGPA from Student's data → Move Method (isRegular, cgpa into Student); (5) duplicated code — CGPA loop in Student and Scholarship → Extract Method cgpa(); plus long method / deep nesting in checkEligibility → guard clauses, and magic numbers 50000/40000/48000/3.5 → named constants. ('stuent.type' typo also fixed.)

// 2024-25 Q4(a) — Student / Scholarship after refactoring
// Smells fixed: (1) type code + switch on type (UG/PG) -> Replace Conditional with Polymorphism;
// (2) data clump street/postOffice/district -> Extract Class Address; (3) feature envy: Scholarship computes CGPA and
// regularity from Student's data -> Move Method into Student; (4) duplicated code: CGPA loop in two places -> Extract Method
// cgpa(); (5) long method / deep nesting in checkEligibility -> guard clauses; also temporary field isFulltime only for PG
// -> moved into PostgraduateStudent; magic numbers -> named constants.
class Address {
    private final String street, postOffice, district;
    Address(String street, String postOffice, String district) {
        this.street = street; this.postOffice = postOffice; this.district = district;
    }
    public String toString() { return street + ", " + postOffice + ", " + district; }
}
abstract class Student {
    final String name, id;
    final int year;
    final Address address;
    private final float[] yearWiseGpa;
    Student(String name, String id, int year, Address address, float[] yearWiseGpa) {
        this.name = name; this.id = id; this.year = year; this.address = address; this.yearWiseGpa = yearWiseGpa;
    }
    float cgpa() {                                        // extracted once
        float sum = 0;
        for (float g : yearWiseGpa) sum += g;
        return yearWiseGpa.length == 0 ? 0 : sum / yearWiseGpa.length;
    }
    boolean isRegular() { return yearWiseGpa.length == year; }    // moved from Scholarship
    abstract float calculateFee();
    void printDetails() {
        System.out.println("Name: " + name);
        System.out.println("Student ID: " + id);
        System.out.println("Address: " + address);
        printSpecificDetails();
    }
    protected abstract void printSpecificDetails();
}
class UndergraduateStudent extends Student {
    private static final float UG_FEE = 50000;
    UndergraduateStudent(String n, String id, int y, Address a, float[] g) { super(n, id, y, a, g); }
    float calculateFee() { return UG_FEE; }
    protected void printSpecificDetails() { System.out.println("Undergraduate, year " + year); }
}
class PostgraduateStudent extends Student {
    private static final float HIGH_CGPA = 3.5f, PG_FEE_HIGH_CGPA = 40000, PG_FEE = 48000;
    private final boolean fulltime;
    PostgraduateStudent(String n, String id, int y, Address a, float[] g, boolean fulltime) {
        super(n, id, y, a, g); this.fulltime = fulltime;
    }
    float calculateFee() { return cgpa() > HIGH_CGPA ? PG_FEE_HIGH_CGPA : PG_FEE; }
    protected void printSpecificDetails() { System.out.println("Postgraduate, " + (fulltime ? "full-time" : "part-time")); }
}
class Scholarship {
    private static final int MIN_YEAR = 2;
    final String name; final int amount; final float cgpaThreshold;
    Scholarship(String name, int amount, float cgpaThreshold) {
        this.name = name; this.amount = amount; this.cgpaThreshold = cgpaThreshold;
    }
    boolean isEligible(Student s) {                       // guard clauses instead of nested ifs
        if (!(s instanceof UndergraduateStudent)) return false;
        if (!s.isRegular()) return false;
        if (s.year < MIN_YEAR) return false;
        return s.cgpa() >= cgpaThreshold;
    }
    void checkEligibility(Student s) {
        System.out.println(s.name + (isEligible(s) ? " is awarded scholarship: " + amount : " is not eligible."));
    }
}
public class StudentRefactored {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Address a = new Address("Road 3", "Palashi", "Dhaka");
        Student ug = new UndergraduateStudent("Asef", "2205001", 3, a, new float[]{3.6f, 3.8f, 3.7f});
        Student pg = new PostgraduateStudent("Nadia", "0423001", 1, a, new float[]{3.9f}, true);
        ug.printDetails(); System.out.println("Fee: " + ug.calculateFee());
        pg.printDetails(); System.out.println("Fee: " + pg.calculateFee());
        Scholarship s = new Scholarship("Dean's", 20000, 3.5f);
        s.checkEligibility(ug); s.checkEligibility(pg);
    }
}

sections.title: Quick Notes — Refactoring
sections.html:
Revision points for Lessons 17–19.

L17 · Basics

  • Behaviour unchanged, structure improved; small safe steps + tests after each.
  • Why: design, understanding, bugs, speed. When: rule of three, adding feature, fixing bug, review.
  • Problems: databases, published interfaces. Tech debt = cost of quick fixes.

L18 · Smells → cure

  • Duplicated → Extract Method · Long method → Extract Method · Long params / data clump → Parameter Object / Extract Class
  • Switch / type code → Polymorphism · Feature envy → Move Method · Shotgun surgery → Move into one class
  • Divergent change → Extract Class · Refused bequest → Delegation · Lazy class → Inline · Comments → Extract Method

L19 · Catalogue

  • Extract Method/Class/Variable, Replace Temp with Query, Move Method, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism,
  • Separate Query from Modifier, Introduce Parameter Object, Guard Clauses, lookup table for long if-chains.
